Lecture 1: What is React and the Declarative Model

Interview Question

CORE

What is React, and how does its declarative, component-based model differ from plain JavaScript DOM scripting?

Imagine this scenario:

  1. You built a page header that shows the user's name in a greeting and again in the corner.
  2. The user changes the name, your script updates the greeting, and the corner still shows the old name.
  3. How does every place on the page show the new name?

The page must change wherever the data appears

Most pages show the same piece of data in more than one place. A website greets the signed-in user at the top, "Welcome back, Mary", and shows the name again in the corner, "Signed in as Mary". When Mary adds her family name in her profile and becomes Mary Brooks, both places must show the new name. Every web developer meets this question: when the data changes, how does the page change with it?

The browser does not draw the HTML file directly. It reads the file and builds one object in memory for every tag, nested the way the tags are nested, so together they form a tree. Then it draws the screen from that tree. The tree is the DOM, the Document Object Model, and each object in it is a DOM node. HTML is the text we write; the DOM is what the browser builds from it and keeps. So to change what the screen shows, something must change the DOM.

The first answer is the one plain JavaScript taught you: you change the page yourself. You find the element, then you set its text.

Plain JavaScript: find the element, set its text
1const greeting = document.getElementById('greeting');
Finds <p> node by ID
2greeting.textContent = 'Welcome back, Mary Brooks';
New text on screen

document.getElementById('greeting') asks the browser for the DOM node whose id is greeting, and textContent replaces the text inside that node. Nothing else on the page changes. This is called imperative programming: you give the browser every command yourself. The word comes from the Latin imperare, "to command", the root of emperor. Like an emperor, the code orders every step. Imperative code fits well when one element changes in one place, such as a clock in the corner of a page.

The second answer is React's. Instead of the commands, you write what the element shows:

React: what the greeting shows
1<p>Welcome back, {userName}</p>

It looks like HTML, but {userName} marks a place where the value of the variable userName goes. No line finds the <p>, and no line sets its text. React reads this line, builds the <p>, and puts the current value in it. This is called declarative programming: you declare what the page should show, and React changes the DOM to match. The word comes from the Latin declarare, "to make clear, to announce". Declarative code fits when the same value shows in several places, or when many parts of the page change.

The corner works the same way:

React: what the corner shows
1<span>Signed in as {userName}</span>

The corner reads the same userName as the greeting. There is no second command to write, so there is no second command to forget. Imperative code tells the browser how to change the page, one command at a time. Declarative code says what the page shows, and React does the changing.

Two ways to update the DOM when the data changes

(1) Update the DOM with imperative programming (plain JavaScript): you give the browser every command yourself, finding each element and setting its text.

(2) Update the DOM with declarative programming (this chapter): you declare what each element should show, and React updates the DOM to match.

Declarative code still leaves room for the few jobs that need one particular element. To move the cursor into a search box, for example, React lets your code reach that one element without changing what it shows. Lecture 30 covers it.

React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces out of components. It can run a whole page, or only one part of a page that already exists. This chapter follows one idea from its first question to its last: we describe the page from data, and React makes the browser match.

This lesson answers three questions:

  • I find each element and change its text. What do I write instead in React?
  • The name shows in two places. Do I write it twice?
  • When the name changes, does React throw the header away and wipe what I typed?

The lesson builds on what you already know: HTML tags with an id attribute, and plain JavaScript, such as a variable made with const and two strings joined with +.

innerHTML replaces every node inside an element

textContent changes the text inside one node and leaves the node itself in place. innerHTML does much more. It throws away every node inside an element and builds new nodes from a string of HTML:

Plain JavaScript: rebuild the inside of the header
1const header = document.getElementById('header');
Finds <header> node by ID
2header.innerHTML = '<p>Welcome back, Mary Brooks</p>';
Replaces child nodes

After the second line, the <header> holds a new <p>, built from the string. The old <p> is gone, together with everything else that was inside the header. The screen may look the same, but every node inside the header is a new one.

One more browser word belongs here. When you click into a text box and type, that box has the focus: it is the element that receives the keys you press, and it shows a blinking cursor. Only one element on the page has the focus at a time. Click somewhere empty, and the focus goes back to the page itself.

A component is a function that returns what the page shows

In React, a page is written as components. A component is a JavaScript function whose name starts with a capital letter and which returns the markup for one piece of the page. Lecture 2 gives the rules for writing one. Here is the header from the opening, written as a component:

SiteHeader.jsx
1export default function SiteHeader() {
2 const userName = 'Mary';
The name, written once
3 return (
4 <header>
5 <p>Welcome back, {userName}</p>
6 <span>Signed in as {userName}</span>
7 <input placeholder="Search" />
8 </header>
9 );
10}

const userName = 'Mary' makes a local variable: a name for a value, inside this function. The markup after return is JSX. It looks like HTML, but it is JavaScript, as Lecture 3 explains. Inside JSX, curly braces mark a place where a JavaScript value goes, so {userName} shows "Mary" in the greeting and again in the corner. Lecture 4 shows what else the braces can hold. export default lets another file use this function, as Lecture 8 explains.

Our code never calls SiteHeader. React calls it, and React uses the JSX it returns.

A second component works the same way, this time with a number:

A second component: SiteFooter
1export default function SiteFooter() {
2 const year = 2026;
Number value placed in JSX
3 return <footer>Copyright {year}</footer>;
4}

Here {year} shows 2026. A component is a function that returns JSX, and curly braces place a value inside that JSX.

The dev server shows each saved change of a file

The code of this lesson runs in a small project prepared for you. Three files matter, and each one holds a different part of the page:

Directory
Contains component modules

Hands that empty element to React and shows the header in it

index.html is the page the browser loads, and its body holds one empty element, <div id="root"></div>. main.jsx hands that element to React and tells React to show SiteHeader inside it; Lecture 9 explains how. SiteHeader.jsx is the component we write.

index.html
1<body>
2 <div id="root"></div>
Empty container in the file
3 <script type="module" src="/src/main.jsx"></script>

You start the project with the command npm run dev. It starts a dev server, a small program on your computer that sends the project to the browser while you work. Each time you save a file, the dev server sends the new code to the open page, and the page shows the change without a reload.

To see the DOM itself, open the browser's developer tools and choose the Elements panel. It shows the DOM nodes the page has right now, which is not always what the HTML file holds. When a node changes, the panel highlights it for a moment.

Principles of React: Describing the Page from Data

Everything in this lesson comes down to one idea: we describe the page from data, and React makes the browser match.

First, declarative programming, which means describing what the page shows, not how to change it: we write what each element shows for the data, and React changes the DOM to match, so our code never finds an element by hand.

Second, a single source of truth, which means describing many places from one value: when a name appears in many places, every place reads it from one variable, so no place can show an old copy.

Third, the virtual DOM, which means describing the page again when the value changes and comparing the two descriptions: React changes only the new text, so whatever the user typed stays where it was.

QUESTION 1

The script changes the greeting and forgets the corner

The page from the opening, written in plain HTML, has a greeting and a corner, each with its own id:

index.html (plain JavaScript version)
1<p id="greeting">Welcome back, Mary</p>
2<span id="account">Signed in as Mary</span>

When Mary changes her name, a script updates the header. It finds the greeting by its id and sets its text:

Plain JavaScript: updateHeaderUser
1function updateHeaderUser(name) {
2 const greeting = document.getElementById('greeting');
3 greeting.textContent = 'Welcome back, ' + name;
Updates greeting only
4}
5
6updateHeaderUser('Mary Brooks');

After the call, the page shows "Welcome back, Mary Brooks" at the top and "Signed in as Mary" in the corner.

I find each element by its id and change its text. What do I write instead in React?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. It changes exactly the nodes it names, and it names only the greeting.

The function has one line for the greeting and none for the corner, so the corner keeps "Mary". Every new place on the page that shows the name needs one more line in this function. One forgotten line is one place on the page with the old name.

In React, we write no such function. We write SiteHeader, the component from the start of this lecture, which returns JSX with {userName} in the greeting and in the corner. React calls SiteHeader and builds the DOM nodes from the JSX it returns.

You can see this in the browser. The file index.html still holds only the empty <div id="root"></div>, yet the Elements panel shows the whole header inside it:

Elements panel
1<div id="root">
Empty element from index.html
2 <header>
Built by React
3 <p>Welcome back, Mary</p>
4 <span>Signed in as Mary</span>
Built from the same name
5 <input placeholder="Search">
6 </header>
7</div>

Every one of these nodes was built by React from the description. A search of our code finds no getElementById and no textContent, so there is no line that a new place on the page could be missing. Because the component only describes, the same data always gives the same page; Lecture 12 explains why React counts on that.

PRINCIPLE 1

Declarative programming: describing what the page shows, not how to change it

We control the page by describing what it shows from data, and we never find and change its elements by hand.

In plain JavaScript, the page changes only where our code finds an element and sets its text, so an element the code forgets keeps its old text. In React, a component returns JSX that says what each element shows for the current data. React calls the component and builds the DOM from what it returns. Our code has no line that finds or changes an element, so there is no element to forget. Reaching one element to move the cursor into it is a different job, which Lecture 30 shows.

We should do this:
function Header() {
const name = 'John';
return <p>Hello, {name}</p>;
React builds the <p>
}
We should not do this:
function updateHeader(name) {
const el = document.getElementById('hello');
el.textContent = 'Hello, ' + name;
The rest keeps old name
}
QUESTION 2

A name typed into the markup keeps the old value

A developer moves the header into React and copies the corner from the old HTML page, letters and all. The greeting reads the variable, but the corner keeps the name typed into it:

SiteHeader.jsx
1export default function SiteHeader() {
2 const userName = 'Mary Brooks';
Changed from 'Mary' and saved
3 return (
4 <header>
5 <p>Welcome back, {userName}</p>
6 <span>Signed in as Mary</span>
Pasted from the HTML page
7 <input placeholder="Search" />
8 </header>
9 );
10}

With the dev server running, the developer changes 'Mary' to 'Mary Brooks' and saves. The page now shows "Welcome back, Mary Brooks" at the top and "Signed in as Mary" in the corner.

The name shows in the greeting and in the corner. Do I write it in both places?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. The corner holds a copy of the name, and the copy did not change.

React builds every element exactly as the JSX describes it. The greeting describes its text with {userName}, so React builds it from the variable, and it shows the new name. The corner describes its text as fixed letters, "Signed in as Mary", so React builds it from those letters, on this run and on every run after it. React did nothing wrong: the JSX asked for two different names.

The fix is one line, line 6 of the file. The corner reads the same variable as the greeting:

SiteHeader.jsx
6 <span>Signed in as {userName}</span>
Signed in as Mary Brooks

Now both places are built from one variable, and the saved change shows "Mary Brooks" in both. This rule has a common name: a single source of truth. Each value lives in one place, and every part of the page reads it from there. Lecture 23 uses the same idea when two components must share a value that changes. A third place that shows the name, such as a line in the account menu, adds one more {userName} and no update code. In this lesson the name stays fixed in the code until we edit the file. A value that changes while the page is open needs state, which Lecture 14 teaches.

One variable, two places
const userName = 'Mary Brooks'
  |
  +--> <p>Welcome back, {userName}</p>
  |      shows: Welcome back, Mary Brooks
  |
  +--> <span>Signed in as {userName}</span>
         shows: Signed in as Mary Brooks

<span>Signed in as Mary</span>
  shows: Signed in as Mary (fixed text, not read from the variable)
PRINCIPLE 2

Single source of truth: describing many places from one value

When one value appears in many places, we describe every place from one variable, and we never type a copy of it.

A value often shows in more than one place, such as a name in a greeting and again in a corner of the page. A place that reads the variable in curly braces is built from it, so when the variable holds a new name, that place shows the new name. A copy typed into the markup is fixed text: it keeps the old name while the rest of the page shows the new one.

We should do this:
const name = 'John Hall';
<p>Hello, {name}</p>
Hello, John Hall
<span>Signed in as {name}</span>
Signed in as John Hall
We should not do this:
const name = 'John Hall';
<p>Hello, {name}</p>
Hello, John Hall
<span>Signed in as John</span>
Still the old name
QUESTION 3

Rebuilding the header empties the search box

The header now has a search box, and the user has typed "elections" into it. Then the name changes. In plain JavaScript, a common way to update a header is to rebuild its inside from a string with the new name:

Plain JavaScript: rebuild the header with the new name
1const name = 'Mary Brooks';
2const header = document.getElementById('header');
3header.innerHTML =
4 '<p>Welcome back, ' + name + '</p>' +
5 '<span>Signed in as ' + name + '</span>' +
6 '<input placeholder="Search">';
A new empty input node

Both names change. But the search box is empty, and the cursor no longer blinks in it: the focus has gone back to the page itself. React also builds the header from a description, so a developer who has seen this may expect React to do the same.

If React builds the header from my description, does it throw the header away when the name changes, and wipe what I typed in the search box?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted, and React does not repeat its mistake. innerHTML throws away the old search box; React keeps it.

As the start of this lecture showed, innerHTML throws away every node inside the header and builds new ones from the string. The new <input> was never typed into, so it is empty. The old one, which had the focus, is gone, so the focus has nowhere to stay but the page itself.

Now the same change in React. Type "elections" into the search box of SiteHeader, change the name on line 2 of the file, and save:

SiteHeader.jsx
2 const userName = 'Mary Brooks';
Changed from 'Mary'

The save makes React call SiteHeader again, and the function returns a whole new description of the header, with the new name in it. React compares it with the last description, element by element. The text of the <p> is different, the text of the <span> is different, and the <input> is the same. So React changes those two texts in the DOM and leaves every other node where it is. The <input> is the same DOM node as before the save, so it still holds "elections", and the cursor still blinks in it. In the Elements panel, the two names flash as they change.

What React changes when the name changes
element   last description     new description           in the DOM
<p>       Welcome back, Mary  Welcome back, Mary Brooks  text changed
<span>    Signed in as Mary   Signed in as Mary Brooks   text changed
<input>   search box           search box                same node

the same <input> node keeps "elections" and the blinking cursor

When the new description is the same as the last one, React changes no text at all. People often call the description that React compares the virtual DOM. The React documentation describes the result as "the minimal necessary operations": for this save, exactly two text changes. Lecture 15 gives each step of an update its name.

PRINCIPLE 3

The virtual DOM: describing the page again when the value changes

When the value changes, React compares the new description with the last one and changes only the new text, so whatever the user typed stays where it was.

When the data changes, React calls the component again, and the component returns a whole new description with the new value in it. React compares it with the last description, element by element. It changes the text that is new and leaves every other node where it is. A text box is still the same node, so it keeps what the user typed and keeps the focus. Rebuilding the elements with innerHTML makes new nodes, and the typed text is gone.

We should do this:
function Header() {
const name = 'John Hall';
Changed from 'John'
return (
<header>
<p>Hello, {name}</p>
Only this text changes
<input />
Keeps typed text and focus
</header>
);
}
We should not do this:
const header = document.getElementById('header');
header.innerHTML = '<p>Hello, John Hall</p><input>';
Box is empty

⚡ IN THE WILD

Does React make the page faster than plain JavaScript? No, and that is not its job. React changes the DOM with the same browser methods a script uses. On the first run it adds the nodes with appendChild(), and on the save it set the text of two nodes, exactly what a careful script would do by hand. A script that sets one text node does that same work with less code to run. React's gain is that our code no longer writes, or forgets, the update steps: it describes the page, and React works out the minimal necessary operations. So the corner is never left on the old name, and the search box is never rebuilt.
Case Study
Let's Design a Practical Example

Each question tested one principle on the smallest header that shows it. Now we build the header from the opening at its real size. Mary's name shows in three places: the greeting, the corner, and the account menu. The number of her new messages shows in two: the Messages link, and a notice below it. The header also holds the search box she types into. Each of the three steps applies one principle of this lesson, in the same order, and ends with what the page shows, so keep the dev server running and the Elements panel open.

Step 1
First, we describe the header from its data
<SiteHeader.jsx>

This step applies the first principle, declarative programming, which means describing what the page shows, not how to change it. The plain JavaScript page kept the name and the count inside its HTML, and a function such as updateHeaderUser changed them, one command per element. In React, there is no such function to bring over. We start from the data instead. The header depends on two values, who is signed in and how many messages are new, so each one gets a variable at the top of the component, and the JSX below says where each value shows:

SiteHeader.jsx
1export default function SiteHeader() {
2 const userName = 'Mary';
Who is signed in
3 const unreadCount = 3;
How many messages are new
4 return (
5 <header>
6 <p>Welcome back, {userName}</p>
7 <a href="/messages">Messages ({unreadCount})</a>
Messages (3)
8 </header>
9 );
10}

unreadCount is a number, and curly braces place it the same way SiteFooter placed year. Save the file and look at the Elements panel. The empty <div id="root"> from index.html now holds a <header> with "Welcome back, Mary" and "Messages (3)", and the file has no getElementById and no textContent. Our code describes, and React builds.

Step 2
Next, we read each value in every place that shows it
<SiteHeader.jsx>

This step applies the second principle, a single source of truth, which means describing many places from one value. The full header adds three places: the corner and the account menu show the name, and a notice repeats the count. The notice is where a copy slips in most easily. It is a whole sentence, and typing "You have 3 new messages" looks finished. That would be Question 2's mistake again, on a number this time. So every place reads its value in curly braces, and the header now runs from line 5 to line 12:

SiteHeader.jsx
5 <header>
6 <p>Welcome back, {userName}</p>
7 <span>Signed in as {userName}</span>
The corner
8 <button>{userName}</button>
The account menu
9 <a href="/messages">Messages ({unreadCount})</a>
10 <p>You have {unreadCount} new messages</p>
Not a typed 3
11 <input placeholder="Search" />
Reads no value
12 </header>

The page now shows five places built from two variables, and the component still has no update code. Plain JavaScript would need one command for each of the five places on every change, and one more command for each place someone adds later.

Why not give the account menu its own component? The header, greeting, and corner will form a tree of components, as Lecture 5 shows, but without a way to pass the name in, which Lecture 6 teaches, it would need its own copy of the name, and the copy is exactly what this step removes.

The last line, the search box, reads no variable at all. What it shows comes from the user, and Step 3 tests whether React leaves it alone.

Step 3
Finally, we change both values while the user types
<SiteHeader.jsx>

This step applies the third principle, the virtual DOM, which means describing the page again when the value changes, and it tests everything above. Type "elections" into the search box and leave the cursor in it. Then make both changes the opening promised: Mary becomes Mary Brooks, and a new message arrives, so the count goes from 3 to 4. Both values sit at the top of the component, on lines 2 and 3. Save:

SiteHeader.jsx
2 const userName = 'Mary Brooks';
Changed from 'Mary'
3 const unreadCount = 4;
Updated from 3

Before you look, predict what changes. React calls SiteHeader again, and it returns a new description with the new values in it. React compares it with the last one, place by place. Three places read userName, two read unreadCount, and the search box is the same as before. So React changes five texts in the DOM, and in the Elements panel those five values flash:

What React changes when both values change
place          last description   new description   in the DOM
greeting       Mary               Mary Brooks       text changed
corner         Mary               Mary Brooks       text changed
account menu   Mary               Mary Brooks       text changed
Messages link  3                  4                 text changed
notice         3                  4                 text changed
search box     search box         search box        same node

The box still holds "elections", and the cursor still blinks in it, because the <input> is the same DOM node it was before the save. The plain JavaScript header rebuilt with innerHTML would have emptied the box. The version that sets each text by hand would have needed five commands, with five chances to forget one.

Component Summary

main

The entry file hands the empty <div id="root"> of index.html to React and shows SiteHeader inside it. No step changed it.

SiteHeader

The header component holds the data in two variables, userName and unreadCount, and five places read them. It returns the whole header as one description and calls no DOM method. When both values changed, React changed five texts and kept the search box with what the user typed.

A developer who comes from plain JavaScript expects the update code to grow with the header: five places mean five commands for every change, and a sixth place means a sixth command that someone must remember. In React 19, the header grew from two places to five, and the update code stayed at zero lines. Each step applied one principle. The header is described from data, every place reads one variable, and a change of the data ends in exactly the texts that changed, while the search box stays as the user left it.

Where you will meet this

  1. The signed-in name: a site shows the user's name in a greeting, in the account menu, and next to every comment the user wrote. Each place reads one variable, so a name change reaches all of them at once.
  2. The cart count: a shop shows the number of items in the header and again on the checkout button. Both read the same count, so the button never promises more items than the cart holds.
  3. The search results: a results page shows "Results for elections" above the list while the same word stays in the search box. React changes the heading and leaves the box, with its cursor, as the user left it.
  4. The unread messages: a mail app shows the unread count in the browser tab and again beside the inbox. One variable feeds both, so the tab and the inbox always agree.

For the interview

The Interview Question: What is React, and how does its declarative, component-based model differ from plain JavaScript DOM scripting?

1. The Hidden Signal

The interviewer wants to hear who changes the DOM. A candidate who says "React has nicer syntax" has not answered. A strong candidate names the two models, imperative and declarative, and says what each one costs on a real page. In plain JavaScript, every update is a command we write, and every place we forget keeps old data. In React, a component describes the page for its data, and React makes the DOM match it. A strong candidate also names the one-variable rule by its common name, a single source of truth.

2. The Classic Trap

The classic trap is "React renders again, so it rebuilds the page." If that were true, every search box would lose its text each time any data changed. On our header, a saved change of the name left "elections" in the box, with its cursor. React changed two text nodes and kept the <input>.

3. What is Actually Going On

In plain JavaScript, the call to updateHeaderUser set the greeting and forgot the corner, so the page showed "Welcome back, Mary Brooks" beside "Signed in as Mary".

In React, SiteHeader keeps the name in one variable, userName, and both places read it. When the name changed to Mary Brooks, React called SiteHeader again, compared the new description with the last one, and changed exactly two texts.

The search box was the same node before and after, so it kept what was typed. People call the description React compares the virtual DOM.

4. Where It Gets Tricky

Is React a framework?

React calls itself a library for building user interfaces. It can run a whole page, or only one part of a page that already exists.

Does React stop the old name from showing up anywhere?

Only where the JSX reads the variable. A name typed into the markup as fixed text keeps the old value, even in React.

What does React change when the new description is the same as the last one?

No text at all.

Can I still call document.getElementById inside a component?

On the component's first run, its own elements are not in the page yet, so the call returns null. Lecture 10 shows the error this causes.

Glossary

  • DOM: The Document Object Model: the objects the browser builds in memory from the HTML, one for every tag, nested like the tags. The screen is drawn from the DOM, so changing the page means changing the DOM.
  • Imperative programming: Code that gives the browser every command itself, such as finding an element and setting its text. From the Latin imperare, "to command".
  • Declarative programming: Code that declares what the page should show for the current data, while React changes the DOM to match. From the Latin declarare, "to make clear, to announce".
  • Component: A JavaScript function whose name starts with a capital letter and which returns JSX for one piece of the page. React calls it; our code does not.
  • JSX: The markup a component returns. It looks like HTML but is JavaScript, and curly braces inside it place the value of a variable.
  • Virtual DOM: The common name for the description a component returns, which React compares with the last one to change only what is new in the real DOM. The React documentation calls the result "the minimal necessary operations".

Beyond the basics

  • How declarative UI compares to imperative: the React documentation's own pair of examples, a form written with commands and the same form described by its visual states, with the car and taxi pictures (see react.dev/learn/reacting-to-input-with-state).
  • What React changes in the DOM: the three steps of every screen update, and the <input> that keeps its text while the time above it changes every second (see react.dev/learn/render-and-commit).
  • Describing the UI: the chapter that turns pieces of a page into components, with the rules of JSX and curly braces (see react.dev/learn/describing-the-ui).
  • Your first component: how to write, export, and use a component, and why a whole app can be components all the way down (see react.dev/learn/your-first-component).
  • Components as formulas: why a component that only describes must give the same JSX for the same data (see react.dev/learn/keeping-components-pure).

Summary

Describing the page from data

❒ Declarative programming: describing what the page shows, not how to change it

➔ ALWAYS describe what the page shows in the JSX a component returns, and let React build the DOM from it.

➔ NEVER find and change elements by hand with document.getElementById and textContent in a page that React builds.

❒ Single source of truth: describing many places from one value

➔ ALWAYS keep a value that shows in several places in one variable, and read it with curly braces in every place.

➔ NEVER type a copy of the value into the markup; a copy keeps the old value when the variable changes.

❒ The virtual DOM: describing the page again when the value changes

➔ IF the data changes THEN describe the page from the new data and let React change only the new text.

➔ NEVER rebuild part of the page with innerHTML; it makes new nodes, and every text box inside loses what the user typed.

One description, one value, and the smallest change.

DO THIS: describe every place from one variable

code.txt
1export default function SiteHeader() {
2 const userName = 'Mary Brooks';
3 return (
4 <header>
5 <p>Welcome back, {userName}</p>
6 <span>Signed in as {userName}</span>
7 <input placeholder="Search" />
8 </header>
9 );
10}

DO NOT DO THIS: find each element and set its text by hand

code.txt
1function updateHeaderUser(name) {
2 const greeting = document.getElementById('greeting');
3 greeting.textContent = 'Welcome back, ' + name;
4}

Lecture 2: Component Anatomy and the Capitalization Rule

Interview Question

CORE

What is a React component, and what rules govern how you write and name one?

Imagine this scenario:

  1. You wrote a function that returns the markup for an article card, with a title and a short text.
  2. You save the file, and the page shows no card and no error.
  3. How does a function you write become a piece of the page?

A page is made of pieces, and each piece is a function

A site that lists articles shows the same kind of piece many times: a card for each article, a box for comments under each card, and a footer at the bottom of every page. Lecture 1 wrote one piece, the header, as one component, and main.jsx showed it. A real page needs many pieces, and some of them appear more than once. So every developer who starts with React asks the same thing: how does a function I write become a piece of the page, and how do I use it again?

The answer is one idea, and this chapter follows it from the first question to the last: a component is a function React calls. We write the function, and React calls it wherever a tag names it. Each rule of the chapter follows one tag on its way to the page: the tag itself, the first letter of its name, what the function gives back, and what happens on the next run.

This lesson answers four questions:

  • I wrote the function ArticleCard. Who calls it, and when?
  • Does it matter whether I name it articleCard or ArticleCard?
  • My markup is long. Can I start it on the line after return?
  • ArticleCard is used only inside App. Can I define it inside App?

The questions stand on what Lecture 1 established:

  • Lecture 1 (What is React): A component is a JavaScript function that returns JSX, markup that looks like HTML and describes one piece of the page. React builds the DOM, the tree of nodes the browser draws, from that description, and the Elements panel shows those nodes. export default lets another file use the function.
  • Lecture 1 (The dev server and the virtual DOM): The dev server sends each saved change to the open page. On a save, React calls the component again, compares the new description with the last one, and changes only what is new. People call that description the virtual DOM. Because React changes only what is new, a text box keeps what the user typed and keeps the focus.

A function runs only when something calls it

In plain JavaScript, the name of a function can appear in two ways, and they do different things. With parentheses after it, the name is a call: the function runs now and gives back its result. Without parentheses, the name is a reference: it stands for the function itself, which has not run.

Plain JavaScript: a call and a reference
1function sayHello() {
2 console.log('sayHello runs');
A line in the Console panel
3 return 'Hello';
4}
5const text = sayHello();
A call: it runs, text is 'Hello'
6button.addEventListener('click', sayHello);
A reference

console.log('sayHello runs') prints a message each time its line runs. The messages appear in the Console panel, next to the Elements panel in the browser's developer tools. sayHello() on the fifth line runs the function at once, so the Console panel shows "sayHello runs".

On the last line, addEventListener gets sayHello with no parentheses: the function itself. Our code never calls it there. The browser calls it later, once for each click, and each click adds one more message to the Console panel.

JavaScript names and HTML tags use different letters

Plain JavaScript names functions and variables in camelCase. The first word starts with a small letter, and every later word starts with a capital, as in sayHello or formatDate. The capitals in the middle stand up like the humps of a camel.

PascalCase starts every word with a capital, the first one too, as in ArticleCard. The name comes from the Pascal programming language, which used this style.

HTML tags are written in small letters: <article>, <footer>, <input>.

A return with nothing after it gives back undefined

A function gives back what its return names. When return names nothing, the function gives back undefined, JavaScript's value for "no value here":

Plain JavaScript: return with nothing after it
1function getTitle() {
2 return;
Ends the function here
3}
4const title = getTitle();
Title is undefined

JavaScript also lets us leave out the semicolon at the end of a line, so const city = 'Boston' works with or without one. When a line could end a statement, JavaScript ends it there, as if we had typed the semicolon. This is called automatic semicolon insertion. Most of the time it does what we meant. Question 3 shows the one place where it does not.

Many code editors run a tool called ESLint. It reads the code as we type and underlines lines that are probably mistakes, each with a short message. It does not change the code, and it does not stop the page from running.

A function defined inside another one is new on every call

A function written directly in the file, outside every other function, is at the top level of the file. JavaScript runs that line once, when the file loads, so the name stands for one function for as long as the page is open.

A function can also be written inside another function. It is then a nested function, and its line runs each time the outer function runs:

Plain JavaScript: a nested function, made on every call
1function makeGreeter() {
2 function greet() {
Runs each time makeGreeter runs
3 return 'Hello';
4 }
5 return greet;
6}
7makeGreeter() === makeGreeter();
False: two different functions

Each call of makeGreeter runs the line function greet() again and makes a new function. The two greet functions do the same work, but they are two different functions, so ===, which is true only for the very same function, gives false. A function at the top level is made once, and its name gives the same function every time.

The project for this lesson keeps every component in App.jsx

The code of this lesson runs in a small project like the one from Lecture 1. This time main.jsx shows a component called App, and every component of the lesson lives in one file, App.jsx. React allows that: a file can hold several components, and the React documentation keeps small components that work together in one file. A real app usually gives each main component its own file, such as ArticleCard.jsx, so that no file grows to hundreds of lines. This lesson keeps every component in App.jsx so that you can see all of them at once. Lecture 8 shows how to give each component its own file with import and export.

Lesson 2 project: File Explorer

ARCHITECTURAL RESPONSIBILITY

parent
The page the browser loads, with one empty element for React
src/
Directory
Contains component modules
main.jsx

Hands that empty element to React and shows App in it

main.jsx names <App />, and that tag is where every run starts. Lecture 9 explains the lines around it.

A new Vite project wraps <App /> in <StrictMode>, a development check from React. With Strict Mode on, every console.log inside a component appears twice in the Console panel while you develop. This lesson's project leaves Strict Mode out, so each message appears once. Lecture 12 explains what Strict Mode checks and why it runs each component twice.

Principles of React: A Component Is a Function React Calls

Everything in this lesson comes down to one idea: a component is a function that React calls, never our code.

First, rendering, which means React calls the component wherever a tag names it: we write the component's name as a tag in another component's markup, and React runs the function and puts what it returns on the page.

Second, PascalCase, which means React calls only the tags that start with a capital letter: a tag that starts with a small letter is read as an HTML tag, so our function never runs.

Third, automatic semicolon insertion, which means React calls the function and gets back only what starts on the return line: markup that starts on the next line is never returned, so we open the parentheses on the return line.

Fourth, top-level components, which means React calls the same function on every run: we define each component at the top level of the file, because a component defined inside another one is a new function every time, and React rebuilds everything it shows.

QUESTION 1

A component that no tag names never runs

A developer writes a card for an article. Its first line logs a message, so the Console panel shows each time the card runs:

App.jsx
1function ArticleCard() {
2 console.log('ArticleCard runs');
Shows each run
3 return (
4 <article>
5 <h2>New Park Opens Today</h2>
6 <p>The park on Main Street opens at noon.</p>
7 </article>
8 );
9}

App, the component that main.jsx shows, returns an empty <main> for now:

10export default function App() {
11 return <main></main>;
No tag names ArticleCard yet
12}

The developer saves the file. The page shows nothing, and the Console panel shows no "ArticleCard runs".

I wrote the function ArticleCard. Who calls it, and when?

ANSWER

The code works as written: nothing names the card, so nothing calls it.

A function runs only when something calls it. Our code never calls ArticleCard, and nothing in the page names it, so it never runs, and its message never appears.

To put the card on the page, App writes its name as a tag, <ArticleCard />. We want two cards, so we write the tag twice:

App.jsx
10export default function App() {
11 return (
12 <main>
13 <ArticleCard />
React calls ArticleCard here
14 <ArticleCard />
And again here
15 </main>
16 );
17}

Save, and the page shows two cards. The Console panel shows "ArticleCard runs" twice. The Elements panel shows what React built:

Elements panel
1<main>
2 <article>
From the first tag
3 <h2>New Park Opens Today</h2>
4 <p>The park on Main Street opens at noon.</p>
5 </article>
6 <article>
From the second tag
7 <h2>New Park Opens Today</h2>
8 <p>The park on Main Street opens at noon.</p>
9 </article>
10</main>

There is no <ArticleCard> tag anywhere in the DOM. The tag hands React the function itself, a reference, the same way addEventListener handed the browser sayHello. While React runs App, it finds each tag and calls ArticleCard once for it, and it builds the DOM from the <article> each call returns.

React calling a component has a name: rendering. Lecture 3 shows the call that each tag becomes. Lecture 5 calls App the parent of the two cards, and Lecture 15 names rendering as one of the steps of every update.

From the tags to the DOM
main.jsx      <App />           --> React calls App
App           <ArticleCard />   --> React calls ArticleCard  --> <article>
              <ArticleCard />   --> React calls ArticleCard  --> <article>

Console panel:   ArticleCard runs
                 ArticleCard runs
Elements panel:  <main> <article> <article>   (no <ArticleCard> tag)
PRINCIPLE 1

Rendering: React calls the component wherever a tag names it

We use a component by writing its name as a tag in another component's markup, and React calls the function once for each tag; our code never calls it.

A component is a function, and a function runs only when something calls it. The tag hands React the function itself. While React runs the component that holds the tag, it calls the function once for each tag and builds the DOM from what each call returns. A function that no tag names never runs. The DOM holds only the HTML tags the function returns, never a tag with the component's name.

We should do this:
function Greeting() {
return <p>Hello, John Hall</p>;
}
function Page() {
return <Greeting />;
React calls Greeting
}
QUESTION 2

A name with a small first letter becomes an empty HTML tag

Plain JavaScript names functions in camelCase, so a developer names the card articleCard:

App.jsx
1function articleCard() {
A small a
2 console.log('articleCard runs');
3 return (
4 <article>
5 <h2>New Park Opens Today</h2>
6 <p>The park on Main Street opens at noon.</p>
7 </article>
8 );
9}

App names the card with the same small letter:

10export default function App() {
11 return (
12 <main>
13 <articleCard />
A small a here too
14 </main>
15 );
16}

The page shows no card, and "articleCard runs" never appears. The Elements panel shows an empty element with the name in small letters:

Elements panel
1<main>
2 <articlecard></articlecard>
Empty, and all small letters
3</main>

The Console panel shows two errors from React. The first says: "<articleCard /> is using incorrect casing. Use PascalCase for React components, or lowercase for HTML elements." The second says: "The tag <articleCard> is unrecognized in this browser. If you meant to render a React component, start its name with an uppercase letter."

Does it matter whether I name it articleCard or ArticleCard?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. The card never appears, because React never calls the function.

React looks at the first letter of each tag. A small letter means an HTML tag, like <article>, so React hands the browser the text 'articleCard', not our function. The browser has no such tag, so it makes an empty element, and the Elements panel shows its name in small letters. Our function never runs, so its message never appears. The two errors in the Console panel are the only signal.

A developer who reads the errors may rename only the tag to <ArticleCard />. Then the page throws "ArticleCard is not defined", and the whole page is empty, not only the card, because App itself fails. The fix needs both names. Line 1 names the function with a capital letter:

App.jsx
1function ArticleCard() {
A capital A here
2 console.log('ArticleCard runs');

Line 13, in App, writes the tag the same way:

App.jsx
13 <ArticleCard />
And a capital A here

Now the card appears, and the Console panel shows "ArticleCard runs". This is why component names use PascalCase: one capital letter tells React, and every reader, that the tag is ours and not an HTML tag. Lecture 3 shows that the call for <articleCard /> takes a text, while the call for <ArticleCard /> takes our function.

PRINCIPLE 2

PascalCase: React calls only the tags that start with a capital letter

We start a component's name with a capital letter, in the function and in the tag, because a tag with a small first letter is read as an HTML tag and our function never runs.

React decides what a tag is by its first letter. A capital letter hands React our function, and React calls it. A small letter means an HTML tag, so the browser makes an element with that name. An unknown name gives an empty element, and our function never runs. Renaming the tag without the function leaves the name undefined, and the whole page fails.

We should do this:
function ProfileCard() {
return <p>John Hall</p>;
}
<ProfileCard />
React calls ProfileCard
We should not do this:
function profileCard() {
return <p>John Hall</p>;
}
<profileCard />
an empty HTML tag; the function never runs
QUESTION 3

A return alone on its line gives back nothing

The card's markup grows, and a developer moves it to the line after return, so it lines up neatly:

App.jsx
1function ArticleCard() {
2 return
The statement ends here
3 <article>
4 <h2>New Park Opens Today</h2>
5 <p>The park on Main Street opens at noon.</p>
6 </article>;
7}

App still names <ArticleCard />. The page shows an empty <main>. The Console panel shows no error, and the terminal where the dev server runs shows no warning. Only an editor that runs ESLint underlines the <article> line, with the message "Unreachable code".

My markup is long. Can I start it on the line after return?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. The function gives back nothing, so React has nothing to show.

return alone on its line can end a statement, so automatic semicolon insertion ends it there, as if we had typed return;. The function gives back undefined, as getTitle did at the start of this lecture, and the markup below is never reached. React called ArticleCard and got nothing back, so it shows nothing in the card's place.

Nothing is wrong in JavaScript's eyes, so no error appears anywhere. ESLint is the one tool that notices: it marks the lines below return as "Unreachable code", code that can never run.

The fix is to open a parenthesis on the return line. The statement cannot end while a parenthesis is open, so it goes on until the markup is closed:

App.jsx
1function ArticleCard() {
2 return (
The parenthesis opens here
3 <article>
4 <h2>New Park Opens Today</h2>
5 <p>The park on Main Street opens at noon.</p>
6 </article>
7 );
8}

The card appears again. Markup that fits on the return line needs no parentheses, such as return <footer>Latest Articles, 2026</footer>; The parentheses are for markup that starts on the next line.

PRINCIPLE 3

Automatic semicolon insertion: React calls the function and gets back only what starts on the return line

When the markup does not fit on the return line, we open the parentheses on the return line, because a return alone on its line gives back nothing.

JavaScript ends a return that stands alone on its line, as if a semicolon followed it. The function gives back undefined, and the markup below it never runs. React gets nothing, so it shows nothing, and no error appears. A parenthesis opened on the return line keeps the statement going until the markup is closed.

We should do this:
function Greeting() {
return (
the statement goes on
<section>
<h2>Hello, John Hall</h2>
</section>
);
}
We should not do this:
function Greeting() {
return
gives back undefined
<section>
<h2>Hello, John Hall</h2>
</section>;
}
QUESTION 4

A card defined inside App loses the typed comment on every save

The card now has a comment box. ArticleCard is used only by App, so a developer writes it inside App, the way plain JavaScript often keeps a helper inside the only function that uses it:

App.jsx
1export default function App() {
2 function ArticleCard() {
Defined inside App
3 return (
4 <article>
5 <h2>New Park Opens Today</h2>
6 <input placeholder="Write a comment" />
7 </article>
8 );
9 }

Below the card, App returns it:

10 return <main><ArticleCard /></main>;
React calls the inner card
11}

The first run looks right. The developer types "See you there" into the comment box, then changes the title in the file to "New Park Opens on Saturday" and saves. The new title shows, but the comment box is empty, and the cursor is gone.

ArticleCard is used only inside App. Can I define it inside App?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. Every run of App makes a new ArticleCard, and React rebuilds the card from scratch.

As in Lecture 1, the save makes React call App again. This run reaches the line function ArticleCard() and makes a new function, just as each call of makeGreeter made a new greet. React compares the new description with the last one and finds a different function in the card's place.

To React, a different function is a different component. So it removes the old <article>, with its <input>, and builds new nodes. The new box was never typed into, so it is empty, and the old box, which had the focus, is gone.

The fix is to move ArticleCard out of App, to the top level of the file:

App.jsx
1function ArticleCard() {
At the top level, beside App
2 return (
3 <article>
4 <h2>New Park Opens Today</h2>
5 <input placeholder="Write a comment" />
6 </article>
7 );
8}

App keeps only the tag:

9export default function App() {
10 return <main><ArticleCard /></main>;
Only the tag stays here
11}

Now type "See you there" again, change the title, and save. The box still holds "See you there", and the cursor still blinks in it. React found the same ArticleCard in the card's place, so it changed only the title text. On a save, the dev server matches each top-level component of the file to its old version by its name. A nested component has no such match.

What React finds in the card's place on the save
ArticleCard is   last run      this run      in the DOM
inside App       function #1   function #2   new <article>, empty box
at top level     ArticleCard   ArticleCard   same <input>, "See you there" kept

The save is not the only time App runs again. Lecture 14 shows a component running again while the page is open, when its data changes, and a nested card would lose the typed text there too. Lecture 24 explains how React matches components from one run to the next. And a card that needs data from App gets it through props, which Lecture 6 teaches, not by living inside App.

PRINCIPLE 4

Top-level components: React calls the same function on every run

We define every component at the top level of the file, beside the others, and never inside another component.

React compares the new description with the last one, and it knows a component by its function. A component defined inside another one is made again on each run of the outer component, so React finds a different function in the same place. It removes the old elements and builds new ones, and a text box loses what the user typed and the focus. A component at the top level is made once, so React finds the same function and keeps its elements.

We should do this:
function SearchBox() {
return <input placeholder="Search" />;
}
function Profile() {
return <SearchBox />;
the same SearchBox on every run
}
We should not do this:
function Profile() {
function SearchBox() {
a new SearchBox on every run
return <input placeholder="Search" />;
}
return <SearchBox />;
}

⚡ IN THE WILD

Can I call ArticleCard() myself instead of writing the tag? It works today, and that is the trap. If App writes {ArticleCard()} inside <main>, the page shows the same card, and the Console panel shows "ArticleCard runs". But our code ran the function while App was running, so React received only the <article> it returned. React never learned that a component was there. The React documentation's rule is short: Never call component functions directly. Use every component as a component tag, so React decides when to call it. The cost of the hand call shows once a component keeps its own data, which Lecture 37 explains.
Case Study
Let's Design a Practical Example

Each question tested one rule on a single card. Now we build a small but whole article page: a heading, an article card with a comment box under it, and a footer. That is four components in one file: App, ArticleCard, CommentBox, and Footer. Each of the four steps applies one principle of this lesson, in the same order, and ends with what the page shows, so keep the dev server running and both the Elements panel and the Console panel open.

Before you save, predict the order of the messages. React calls App first, because main.jsx names it. In App's markup it finds <ArticleCard /> and calls the card, and in the card's markup it finds <CommentBox /> and calls the box. So the Console panel shows "App runs", "ArticleCard runs", and "CommentBox runs", in that order. The Elements panel shows <main>, <h1>, <article>, <h2>, <p>, and <input>, and no tag with a component's name. Our code called none of the three functions.

Step 2
Next, we name our footer with a capital letter
<App.jsx>

This step applies the second principle, PascalCase, which means React calls only the tags that start with a capital letter. The page needs a footer, and the best name for our component is the same word as the HTML tag it returns. The capital letter alone keeps the two apart. We write it above App, from line 15:

App.jsx
15function Footer() {
16 console.log('Footer runs');
17 return <footer>Latest Articles, 2026</footer>;
Fits on the return line
18}

App names our footer below the card. The footer took lines 15 to 18, so App moved down and now starts on line 19:

App.jsx
22 <main>
23 <h1>Latest Articles</h1>
24 <ArticleCard />
25 <Footer />
Ours: a capital F
26 </main>

Save. "Footer runs" appears after the other three messages, and the Elements panel shows one <footer> with "Latest Articles, 2026".

Had App written <footer /> with a small f, the browser would have made an empty HTML footer, and our function would never have run. This time React would have printed no error at all, because <footer> is a real HTML tag. That is Question 2's mistake in its quietest form, and the capital letter is the only thing that prevents it.

Step 3
Then, we open the parentheses on the return line as the footer grows
<App.jsx>

This step applies the third principle, automatic semicolon insertion, which means React calls the function and gets back only what starts on the return line. The team wants a contact link in the footer. The markup no longer fits on the return line, so it moves inside parentheses, and the parenthesis opens on the return line:

App.jsx
15function Footer() {
16 console.log('Footer runs');
17 return (
Two lines now, so it opens here
18 <footer>
19 <p>Latest Articles, 2026</p>
20 <a href="/contact">Contact us</a>
21 </footer>
22 );
23}

Save, and the footer shows "Latest Articles, 2026" and the link "Contact us". Had the <footer> started on the line after a bare return, the whole footer would have vanished with no error, as the card did in Question 3. One line needed no parentheses; two lines need them.

Step 4
Finally, we keep every component at the top level while the reader types
<App.jsx>

This step applies the fourth principle, top-level components, which means React calls the same function on every run, and it tests everything above. CommentBox is used only inside ArticleCard, which tempts us to write it there. It stays at the top level, beside the other three.

Now test it. Type "See you there" into the comment box and leave the cursor in it. Then change the title, on line 9, and save:

App.jsx
9 <h2>New Park Opens on Saturday</h2>
Was New Park Opens Today

Before you look, predict what happens. The Console panel shows all four messages again, so React called every component again. Each time, it found the same function in the same place: the same ArticleCard, the same CommentBox, the same Footer. So React changed only the title text and kept every other node.

What React finds on the save
component     last run       this run       in the DOM
ArticleCard   ArticleCard    ArticleCard    title text changed
CommentBox    CommentBox     CommentBox     same <input>, "See you there" kept
Footer        Footer         Footer         nothing changed

The box still holds "See you there", and the cursor still blinks in it. With CommentBox written inside ArticleCard, the same save would have emptied the box and taken the cursor away, as the nested card did in Question 4.

Component Summary

main

The entry file names <App />, so every run starts with App. No step changed it.

App

Four top-level components. App names <ArticleCard /> and <Footer />, and ArticleCard names <CommentBox />. React called them in the order of their tags, and none of them is called by our code. The footer's markup opens its parentheses on the return line. When the title changed, React changed one text and kept the comment box with what the reader typed.

A developer who comes from plain JavaScript brings four habits: call each function where its markup should go, name it like any other function, start long markup on a fresh line, and keep a helper inside the only function that uses it. Each habit breaks a component in its own way. A call hides the component from React, a small letter turns it into an empty HTML tag, a bare return gives back nothing, and a nested definition empties the comment box on every run. In React 19, the four steps avoided all four: each piece is a tag, each name starts with a capital letter, each long return opens its parentheses on the return line, and each component sits at the top level, so the page kept what the reader typed.

Where you will meet this

  1. A list of cards: a site that lists articles, a shop, or a feed writes one card component and names its tag once for each item. Lecture 6 shows how each card gets its own text.
  2. Names that match HTML tags: most apps have a Header, a Footer, a Button, or a Form component. The capital letter is the only thing that tells React to call ours instead of making the HTML tag.
  3. A card that vanished after a reformat: a teammate moves the markup to the line after return to make it easier to read, and the card is gone with no error. ESLint's "Unreachable code" points at the line.
  4. A chat box that keeps emptying: a message box defined inside the chat window component loses the half-typed message every time the window runs again. Moving it to the top level fixes it.

For the interview

The Interview Question: What is a React component, and what rules govern how you write and name one?

1. The Hidden Signal

The interviewer wants to hear who calls the component. A candidate who says "a component is a function that returns HTML" has given half an answer. A strong candidate says that our code never calls it: we write its name as a tag, React calls it, and that call is called rendering. A strong candidate also treats the capital letter as a rule React acts on, not a matter of style.

2. The Classic Trap

The classic trap is "capitalization is just a naming convention." On our page, <articleCard /> showed no card, the Elements panel held an empty <articlecard> element, and the function never ran. A convention would not change what the browser builds.

3. What is Actually Going On

A tag with a capital letter hands React the function itself. While React renders the parent, it calls the function once for each tag and builds the DOM from what it returns. A return alone on its line gives back undefined, so React shows nothing.

A component defined inside another one is a new function on every run of the outer one. React finds a different function in the same place, removes the old elements, and builds new ones, so a comment box loses what was typed.

4. Where It Gets Tricky

Is <ArticleCard /> the same as ArticleCard()?

The page can look the same, but with the call, React never learns that a component was there. The React documentation says never to call component functions directly, and Lecture 37 shows the cost.

Why does every message appear twice in a new project?

A new Vite project turns on Strict Mode, which runs each component twice while you develop. Lecture 12 explains why.

Can several components live in one file?

Yes. This lesson keeps four in App.jsx, each at the top level. Real apps keep small components that work together in one file too, while each main component usually gets its own. Lecture 8 shows how to split them into files.

Does a component that gives back undefined throw an error?

No. React 19 shows nothing in its place and prints no error, which is why the bare return is hard to find.

Glossary

  • Component: A JavaScript function whose name starts with a capital letter and which returns JSX for one piece of the page. React calls it; our code does not.
  • Component tag: A component's name written as a tag, such as <ArticleCard />, in another component's markup. It hands React the function.
  • Rendering: React calling a component to find out what it shows.
  • camelCase: The usual style for JavaScript names: the first word starts with a small letter, and every later word with a capital, as in formatDate.
  • PascalCase: A style where every word starts with a capital, as in ArticleCard. Component names use it.
  • undefined: JavaScript's value for "no value here". A function whose return names nothing gives it back.
  • Automatic semicolon insertion: JavaScript ending a statement at the end of a line, as if a semicolon were there, when the line could end it.
  • ESLint: A tool that reads code as we write it and underlines likely mistakes, such as "Unreachable code".
  • Top level: The part of a file outside every function. A function written there is made once.
  • Strict Mode: A development check from React that runs each component twice, so every console.log in a component appears twice.

Beyond the basics

  • Your first component: how to define, use, and nest components, with the three pitfalls of this lesson and four challenges (see react.dev/learn/your-first-component).
  • Render and commit: what rendering means, told as a kitchen where React is the waiter and components are the cooks (see react.dev/learn/render-and-commit).
  • React calls Components and Hooks: the rule "Never call component functions directly", with the reasons behind it (see react.dev/reference/rules/react-calls-components-and-hooks).
  • Keeping components pure: what Strict Mode checks when it runs each component twice (see react.dev/learn/keeping-components-pure).
  • Preserving and resetting state: how React matches components from one run to the next, and why a nested definition loses the typed text (see react.dev/learn/preserving-and-resetting-state).

Summary

A component is a function React calls

❒ Rendering: React calls the component wherever a tag names it

➔ ALWAYS use a component by writing its name as a tag, such as <ArticleCard />, in another component's markup.

➔ NEVER call a component function yourself, such as {ArticleCard()}; let React call it.

❒ PascalCase: React calls only the tags that start with a capital letter

➔ ALWAYS start a component's name with a capital letter, in the function and in the tag.

➔ NEVER give a component a name with a small first letter; React reads its tag as an HTML tag, and the function never runs.

❒ Automatic semicolon insertion: React calls the function and gets back only what starts on the return line

➔ IF the markup does not fit on the return line THEN open the parentheses on the return line.

➔ NEVER leave return alone on its line; the function gives back undefined, and nothing shows.

❒ Top-level components: React calls the same function on every run

➔ ALWAYS define every component at the top level of the file, beside the others.

➔ NEVER define a component inside another component; it is new on every run, and its text boxes lose what the user typed.

One tag, one capital letter, one return line, and one function at the top.

DO THIS: a top-level component with a capital letter, used as a tag

5 <input placeholder="Write a comment" />
6 </article>
7 );
8}
9
10export default function App() {
11 return <main><ArticleCard /></main>;
12}

DO NOT DO THIS: a nested component with a small letter and a bare return

code.txt

2 function articleCard() {
3 return
4 <article>
5 <h2>New Park Opens Today</h2>
6 </article>;
7 }
8 return <main><articleCard /></main>;
9}

Lecture 3: JSX Syntax and the Single-Root Rule

Interview Question

CORE

What is JSX, what syntax rules must every snippet follow, and how do Fragments group elements without wrapper nodes?

Imagine this scenario:

  1. You copy the markup of an article card from the old site and paste it into a component.
  2. You save, and instead of the card, a dark box with red text covers the page.
  3. What changes when HTML moves into a component?

Most React work starts from HTML that already exists

Most React work does not start from an empty file. It starts from markup that already exists: a page of an old site, a design a teammate wrote in HTML, or an example copied from the web. Our site is moving to React, and its old pages are plain HTML files. In Lecture 2, every component we wrote was small and clean. Now the markup comes from somewhere else, and it was written for the browser, not for React. So every developer who moves a site to React asks the same thing: what changes when HTML moves into a component?

The answer is one idea, and this chapter follows it from the first question to the last: JSX looks like HTML, but it is JavaScript: each tag becomes a call that builds an object. Each rule of the chapter follows one block of pasted HTML on its way to the page: the tag, its end, the return, the group, its attributes.

This lesson answers five questions:

  • My component returns something that looks like HTML. Is it HTML?
  • My HTML has <img> with no closing tag. Why does the build stop?
  • I pasted a heading and a paragraph after return. Why does the build fail?
  • So I wrap everything in a <div>?
  • Can I keep class and for from my HTML?

The questions stand on what Lectures 1 and 2 established:

  • Lecture 1 (What is React): A component is a JavaScript function that returns JSX, markup that describes one piece of the page. React builds the DOM, the tree of nodes the browser draws, from that description, and the Elements panel shows those nodes. The dev server sends each saved change to the open page.
  • Lecture 2 (Component anatomy): We write a component's name as a component tag, such as <ArticleCard />, and React calls the function. That call is called rendering. A capital first letter tells React that the tag is ours, and long markup starts on the return line with return ( console.log prints a message in the Console panel, and our projects leave Strict Mode out, so each message appears once.

An object keeps values under names

A JavaScript object keeps several values together, each under a name. Each name with its value is a property. We write an object with curly braces, and we read a property with a dot:

Plain JavaScript: an object and its properties
1const article = {
2 title: 'Ten easy summer recipes',
A property named title
3 topic: 'Food',
4};
5console.log(article.title);
Ten easy summer recipes

The object holds two properties, title and topic. article.title reads the first one, so the Console panel shows "Ten easy summer recipes". A property name is a JavaScript name, so it follows the same rules as the name of a variable.

The dev server changes our files before the browser gets them

The browser does not read App.jsx as we wrote it. When the page asks for the file, the dev server reads it, rewrites it into plain JavaScript, and sends the result. This rewriting is called the build. The command npm run build does the same for every file at once, when the site is ready to publish.

The Sources panel of the browser's developer tools, next to the Elements panel and the Console panel, shows each file the browser received. Opening App.jsx there shows the result of the build, not our file.

When the build cannot read a file, nothing in that file runs. Vite then covers the page with a dark box, the error overlay. It shows the message, the file, and the line where the build stopped. The overlay goes away once we fix the file and save.

HTML lets some tags stay open

Some HTML tags can never hold anything inside them: <img>, <br>, and <input>. They are called void elements, and HTML lets us write them without a closing tag. HTML even lets us leave some other tags open, such as <li> and <p>, because the browser closes them when the next one starts.

CSS can style only the direct children of an element

A new Vite project has a stylesheet, index.css, and main.jsx loads it with one line, so its rules apply to the whole page. Ours styles a list of featured articles:

index.css
1.articles {
2 display: flex;
The items sit in a row
3 gap: 24px;
4 padding: 0;
5 list-style: none;
6}
7.articles > li {
Only the direct children
8 border: 1px solid #999;
9 padding: 8px;
10}

display: flex turns the list into a flex layout: its children sit side by side in a row, with 24 pixels between them. The > in .articles > li makes it a child selector. It gives a border only to an <li> that sits directly inside the list, not to one that sits deeper.

Some words belong to JavaScript itself

JavaScript keeps some words for itself, such as return, function, class, and for. They are called reserved words. class starts a class definition, and for starts a loop, so neither can be the name of a variable.

HTML has two families of attributes whose names contain a dash. aria-* attributes, such as aria-label, describe an element to screen readers. data-* attributes, such as data-year, store our own values on an element.

The project for this lesson

The code runs in the same small project as Lecture 2. Every component lives in App.jsx, and main.jsx shows App. As in Lecture 2, one file is a choice for learning, so that you see every component at once. A real app gives each main component its own file, and Lecture 8 shows how. Two images sit in the public folder. Vite serves each file there at the root of the site, so /library.jpg is the library photo.
