Principles of React: JSX Is JavaScript

Everything in this lesson comes down to one idea: JSX looks like HTML, but it is JavaScript.

First, the JSX transform, which means each tag becomes a JavaScript call that returns an object: the build rewrites every tag as a call, and React builds the page from the objects.

Second, closed tags, which means JavaScript must know where each tag ends: every tag needs a closing tag or a slash, the image and the line break too.

Third, a single root, which means a JavaScript function returns one value: a component gives back one element that holds the rest.

Fourth, Fragments, which means one JavaScript value that adds no element to the page: when the page needs no extra box, an empty tag groups the elements instead.

Fifth, camelCase attributes, which means each attribute becomes a JavaScript property name: class becomes className, and for becomes htmlFor.

QUESTION 1

A tag in JSX becomes a call that returns an object

A developer pastes the markup of an article card into ArticleCard. Curious about what the markup really is, the developer stores it in a variable, logs it, and returns it:

App.jsx
1function ArticleCard() {
2 const card = (
JSX stored in a variable
3 <article>
4 <h2 className="title">City Library Extends Its Hours</h2>
5 <p>The library now stays open until nine.</p>
6 </article>
7 );
8 console.log(card);
9 return card;
10}

className is how JSX writes the class of HTML, and Question 5 explains why. App shows the card:

11export default function App() {
12 return <main><ArticleCard /></main>;
React calls ArticleCard
13}

The developer saves. The card appears, with its title and its text. The Console panel does not show the markup as text. It shows an object.

My component returns something that looks like HTML. Is it HTML?

ANSWER

The code works as written: the card appears, and the Console panel shows an object.

Open the object in the Console panel. It has a type and props, and inside props, children holds two more objects, one for each inner tag. Here it is, shortened, with dots in place of the two texts:

Console panel: the logged card, shortened
1{
2 type: 'article',
The outer tag
3 props: {
4 children: [
One object for each inner tag
5 { type: 'h2', props: { className: 'title', children: '...' } },
6 { type: 'p', props: { children: '...' } },
7 ],
8 },
9}

So JSX is not HTML. Open App.jsx in the Sources panel to see what the browser received. Every tag is gone. In its place is a call of a function from React, _jsxDEV:

Sources panel: App.jsx as the browser received it, shortened
1const card = _jsxDEV("article", {
The <article> tag
2 children: [
3 _jsxDEV("h2", {
4 className: "title",
5 children: "City Library Extends Its Hours",
6 }),
7 _jsxDEV("p", { children: "The library now stays open until nine." }),
8 ],
9});

The build rewrote each tag as a call. The tag's name became the first argument, and its attributes and its content became the properties of an object, the second argument. This rewrite is called the JSX transform. The dev server also added an import line at the top of the file, which loads _jsxDEV from React, and it added the file name and the line of each tag, for error messages. When we run npm run build, the calls use a shorter function, jsx, without those extras.

Each call returns a plain object, the one the Console panel showed. React calls it a React element. When React renders the component, it reads these objects and builds the DOM from them, so the browser never receives a tag at all.

This keeps a promise from Lecture 2. In the Sources panel, the tag in App became a call too, and the first letter decides what the call takes:

Sources panel: two tags and their calls
1_jsxDEV(ArticleCard, {})
<ArticleCard />: our function
2_jsxDEV("articleCard", {})
<articleCard />: only a text

A capital letter hands the call our function, so React can call it. A small letter hands it a text, the name of an HTML tag. The object has a few more fields than type and props, which Lecture 76 explains. JSX can also show the value of a variable inside curly braces, which Lecture 4 teaches.

PRINCIPLE 1

The JSX transform: each tag becomes a JavaScript call that returns an object

We read JSX as JavaScript: the build turns each tag into a call, the call returns an object that describes the element, and React builds the DOM from those objects.

The browser never reads JSX. The build rewrites each tag as a call of a function from React. The tag's name, its attributes, and its content go into the call, and the call returns a plain object, a React element. React reads these objects and builds the DOM. So JSX can go wherever a JavaScript value can go: after a return, or in a variable.

We should do this:
function Greeting() {
const note = <p className="note">Hello, John Hall</p>;
an object
return note;
}
QUESTION 2

An open img tag stops the build

The card should show a photo of the library. The old site's HTML has it, so a developer pastes it as it is:

App.jsx
1function ArticleCard() {
2 return (
Pasted from the old site
3 <article>
4 <img src="/library.jpg" alt="The city library">
5 <h2>City Library Extends Its Hours</h2>
6 </article>
7 );
8}

The developer saves, and the page stays empty. The error overlay covers it, with two messages. The first one points at two lines:

Vite error overlay: the first message, shortened
[PARSE_ERROR] Expected corresponding JSX closing tag for 'img'.
 4 │       <img src="/library.jpg" alt="The city library">
   │        ─┬─
   │         ╰─── Opened here
 6 │     </article>
   │       ───┬───
   │          ╰───── Expected `</img>`

The second message says "Unexpected token. Did you mean {'}'} or &rbrace;?", and it points at line 8, the closing brace of the function.

My HTML has <img> with no closing tag. Why does the build stop?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. The build stops at the <img>, so nothing in the file runs.

Each tag becomes a call, and the build must know where the call's content ends. After an open tag, it reads everything as the content of that tag until it finds the closing tag. HTML knows that <img> is a void element, but the build does not make that exception. So the <h2> became the content of the <img>, and at </article> the build was still waiting for </img>. That is what the two marks in the overlay say: the tag was opened here, and its end was expected there.

The second message comes from the same mistake. The build lost its place and reached the closing brace of the function as if it were text inside the markup. That line has no mistake of its own, so we fix the first message and the second one goes away.

The fix is a slash before the >. A tag that closes itself has no content, so the build knows at once where it ends:

App.jsx
1function ArticleCard() {
2 return (
Every tag closed
3 <article>
4 <img src="/library.jpg" alt="The city library" />
5 <h2>City Library Extends Its Hours</h2>
6 </article>
7 );
8}

Save, and the photo and the title appear. <br> and <input> fail the same way, and so does an <li> or a <p> left open, as HTML allows. Any tag may close itself, such as <div className="spacer" />

PRINCIPLE 2

Closed tags: JavaScript must know where each tag ends

We close every tag, with a closing tag or with a slash, <img /> and <br /> too, because JavaScript must know where each tag ends.

The build reads everything after an open tag as its content, until it finds the closing tag. JSX makes no exception for void elements, so an open image swallows the tags below it, and the build stops at the next closing tag. Nothing in the file runs, and the overlay names the open tag. A slash closes a tag that holds nothing.

We should do this:
<section>
<img src="/john.jpg" alt="John Hall" />
closed with a slash
<p>John Hall<br />Boston</p>
</section>
We should not do this:
<section>
<img src="/john.jpg" alt="John Hall">
waits for </img>
<p>John Hall<br>Boston</p>
</section>
QUESTION 3

Two tags side by side after return stop the build

Another card on the old site has no <article> around it, only a heading and a paragraph. A developer pastes both after return:

App.jsx
1function ArticleCard() {
2 return (
Two tags side by side
3 <h2>City Library Extends Its Hours</h2>
4 <p>The library now stays open until nine.</p>
5 );
6}

The page stays empty, and the overlay shows "Adjacent JSX elements must be wrapped in an enclosing tag." under the <p>. Below it is a line of help: "Did you want a JSX fragment <>...</>?"

I pasted a heading and a paragraph after return. Why does the build fail?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. The function tries to give back two values, and the build stops before anything runs.

Each tag becomes one call, and one call gives one value. A JavaScript function gives back one value with return, so the build cannot turn two calls side by side into one return. HTML allows any number of tags next to each other, but a function's return does not.

One element around both is one call. The two inner calls become its content, its children, exactly as the <h2> and the <p> did in the object of Question 1:

App.jsx
1function ArticleCard() {
2 return (
One root: the article
3 <article>
4 <h2>City Library Extends Its Hours</h2>
5 <p>The library now stays open until nine.</p>
6 </article>
7 );
8}

Save, and the card appears. The help line in the overlay pointed at a second way to give one root, and Question 4 takes it up.

PRINCIPLE 3

Single root: a JavaScript function returns one value

We return one root from every component, one element that holds the rest, because a JavaScript function returns one value.

Each tag becomes one call, and each call gives one value. A function returns one value, so a component returns one tag, and that tag holds the others as its children. Two tags side by side are two values, and the build stops before anything runs. The root is usually an element the page needs anyway, such as an article or a section.

We should do this:
return (
<section>
one root
<h2>John Hall</h2>
<p>Author of 12 articles</p>
</section>
);
We should not do this:
return (
<h2>John Hall</h2>
<p>Author of 12 articles</p>
a second value
);
QUESTION 4

A div inside a list breaks the list's layout

The home page shows the featured articles in a row, with the list from index.css. App owns the list, and a new component, FeaturedArticles, returns its items. Two <li> side by side would stop the build, so a developer wraps them in a <div>, as one often does in HTML:

App.jsx
1function FeaturedArticles() {
2 return (
One root for the two items
3 <div>
4 <li>Ten easy summer recipes</li>
5 <li>New park opens today</li>
6 </div>
7 );
8}

App places the articles inside the styled list:

9export default function App() {
10 return (
The list styled by index.css
11 <main>
12 <ul className="articles">
13 <FeaturedArticles />
14 </ul>
15 </main>
16 );
17}

The build passes, and the Console panel stays clean. But the two articles stack one above the other, and neither has a border. The Elements panel shows why:

Elements panel: with the div
1<ul class="articles">
2 <div>
The only child of the list
3 <li>Ten easy summer recipes</li>
4 <li>New park opens today</li>
5 </div>
6</ul>

So I wrap everything in a <div>?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. The <div> gives one root, but it also lands on the page, between the list and its items.

A <div> is a real element, so React builds it in the DOM. The flex layout arranges the children of the list, and the list now has one child, the <div>. The two items sit inside the <div>, one below the other. The child selector .articles > li looks for an <li> directly inside the list, finds none, and gives no border.

What we need is one value for the return and nothing on the page. That is a Fragment, written as an empty tag, <> and </>:

App.jsx
1function FeaturedArticles() {
2 return (
One value, and no element
3 <>
4 <li>Ten easy summer recipes</li>
5 <li>New park opens today</li>
6 </>
7 );
8}

A Fragment is one call, like any tag, so the build accepts it as one root. Its type is React's Fragment, and React does not build an element for it. It puts the Fragment's children straight into the parent:

Elements panel: with the Fragment
1<ul class="articles">
2 <li>Ten easy summer recipes</li>
A direct child: a border
3 <li>New park opens today</li>
4</ul>

Save, and the two articles sit side by side, each with its border. App is now the parent of FeaturedArticles, and Lecture 5 draws that tree. An element is still the right root when the page needs the box, as the <article> was in Question 3. A Fragment cannot take a key, which Lecture 11 explains when it renders lists.

PRINCIPLE 4

Fragments: one JavaScript value that adds no element to the page

When the elements need one root but the page needs no extra box, we group them with a Fragment, <> and </>, and we keep an element only when the page needs the box.

A wrapping element is a real node in the DOM, between the parent and the children. Inside a list, a table, or a flex row, it breaks the layout, because the styles look for direct children. A Fragment is one call, so it gives one root, but React builds no element for it and puts its children straight into the parent. An element stays right when the page needs it, for its meaning or for a style.

We should do this:
function NameCells() {
return (
<>
no element in the DOM
<td>John</td>
<td>Hall</td>
</>
);
}
We should not do this:
function NameCells() {
return (
<div>
a div inside the table row
<td>John</td>
<td>Hall</td>
</div>
);
}
QUESTION 5

class and for work, and the console fills with errors

The old site has a newsletter form. A developer pastes it into SignUp, with the attributes it had in HTML:

App.jsx
1function SignUp() {
2 return (
Pasted with its HTML attributes
3 <form>
4 <label class="label" for="email">Your email</label>
5 <input id="email" type="email" tabindex="0" />
6 </form>
7 );
8}

The page looks right, and a click on the label puts the cursor in the box. But the Console panel shows three errors. The first one says: "Invalid DOM property class. Did you mean className?" The other two say the same for for, with htmlFor, and for tabindex, with tabIndex.

Can I keep class and for from my HTML?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. The page works, but each HTML name is the wrong name in JSX, and each one adds an error to the console.

The attributes of a tag become the properties of an object, as className did in Question 1. A property name is a JavaScript name, and class and for are reserved words in JavaScript. So React uses the names that the DOM itself gives these two properties, className and htmlFor. Other attribute names of several words use camelCase, so tabindex becomes tabIndex.

React 19 still sets the wrong names on the element. That is why the page looks right and the label still works. Only the console shows the mistake, and a console full of these errors hides the one error that matters.

The fix uses the JavaScript names. The aria-* and data-* attributes are the exception: they keep their dashes, as in HTML:

App.jsx
1function SignUp() {
2 return (
Aria-label and data-form-id keep their dashes
3 <form aria-label="Newsletter" data-form-id="7">
4 <label className="label" htmlFor="email">Your email</label>
5 <input id="email" type="email" tabIndex="0" />
6 </form>
7 );
8}

Save, and the Console panel is empty. The Elements panel still shows class="label" and for="email", because React writes the HTML names into the page. Lecture 83 lists the other renamed attributes, and attributes written on the tag of our own component become its props, which Lecture 6 teaches.

PRINCIPLE 5

camelCase attributes: each attribute becomes a JavaScript property name

We write each attribute as a JavaScript property name: className for class, htmlFor for for, camelCase for names of several words, and dashes only in aria-* and data-*.

The attributes of a tag become the properties of the object the call receives, so they follow the rules of JavaScript names. The words class and for are reserved in JavaScript, so React uses className and htmlFor, the names the DOM gives these properties. Names of several words use camelCase. React 19 still sets an HTML name on the element, so the page looks right, and only the console shows an error.

We should do this:
<form className="contact">
className, not class
<label htmlFor="name">Name</label>
<input id="name" placeholder="John Hall" data-user-id="7" />
</form>
We should not do this:
<form class="contact">
an error in the console
<label for="name">Name</label>
<input id="name" placeholder="John Hall" data-user-id="7" />
</form>

⚡ IN THE WILD

Old tutorials import React at the top of every file. Do I need that line? Not for JSX. Older tutorials start each component file with import React from 'react' because the old transform turned every tag into a call of React.createElement, and that call needs React in the file. React 19 requires the new JSX transform, which adds its own import of the JSX functions, as the Sources panel showed in Question 1. That is why our files never import React and still work. A file still imports by name the other things it uses from React, which Lecture 8 shows.

Each of the five steps applies one principle of this lesson, in the same order, and ends with what the screen shows, so keep the dev server running and both the Elements panel and the Console panel open.

A <div> would add an element that nothing uses, and a <main> would wrongly put the header and the footer inside the main content. So the parts go into a Fragment. The old HTML is now JSX: every tag a call, every tag closed, one root in each component, no extra box, and JavaScript names.

Component Summary

main

The entry file loads index.css and names <App />. No step changed it.

App

Two top-level components. SearchBox returns one <section> that holds the search form and its hint. App returns a Fragment with the header, <SearchBox />, and the footer, so the three parts sit directly in the root. Every tag is closed, and every attribute has its JavaScript name; aria-label and data-year keep their dashes.

A developer who comes from HTML brings five habits: read the markup as HTML, leave void elements open, put tags side by side, wrap a group in a <div>, and keep the HTML attribute names. Each habit meets JavaScript in its own way. The markup is a list of calls, an open tag hides where a call ends, two tags side by side are two values, a <div> lands on the page and breaks a layout, and class fills the console with errors. In React 19, the five steps followed the build from one message to the next, and the old page now runs as two components with a clean console.

Where you will meet this

  1. A designer's HTML mockup: a design arrives as an HTML file, and every page of it goes through the same five checks as the home page of our site.
  2. A snippet copied from the web: examples from CSS libraries are written in HTML, full of class and open <input> tags. Each one needs className and a slash.
  3. A table row component: a component that returns several <td> cells for a row needs a Fragment, because a <div> inside a <tr> breaks the table.
  4. An old tutorial: a file that starts with import React from 'react' comes from the time before the new JSX transform.
  5. An icon pasted from a design tool: SVG markup brings attributes such as stroke-width, which JSX writes as strokeWidth.

For the interview

The Interview Question: What is JSX, what syntax rules must every snippet follow, and how do Fragments group elements without wrapper nodes?

1. The Hidden Signal

The interviewer wants to hear what JSX turns into. A candidate who says "JSX is HTML inside JavaScript" has described how it looks. A strong candidate says that the build turns each tag into a function call, that the call returns a plain object, and that React builds the DOM from those objects, so the browser never sees JSX. Every rule then follows from that one fact.

2. The Classic Trap

The classic trap is "JSX is just HTML with a few differences." On our page, an open <img> stopped the build, two tags side by side stopped it again, and class filled the console with errors. HTML accepts all three. JavaScript does not.

3. What is Actually Going On

Each tag becomes a call, so the build must know where its content ends, and every tag must be closed. Each call is one value, and a function returns one value, so a component returns one root.

A Fragment is a call with React's Fragment type. It gives one root, and React puts its children straight into the parent, so nothing extra lands in the DOM. The attributes become the properties of an object, so they take JavaScript names: className, htmlFor, and camelCase.

4. Where It Gets Tricky

Does a Fragment appear in the Elements panel?

No. React builds no element for it. Its children sit directly inside the parent, as the two articles did in the list.

Can I keep the HTML comments of my old page?

No. A comment written as in HTML stops the build with "HTML comments are not allowed in modules". A comment in JSX needs curly braces, which Lecture 4 teaches.

Does class break the page?

No. React 19 still sets it on the element, and the page looks right. The Console panel shows an error that asks for className.

Can a Fragment take a key?

The empty tag cannot. The long form, written with the name Fragment, can, and Lecture 11 shows it in a list.

Glossary

  • Object: A JavaScript value that keeps several values together, each under a name.
  • Property: One name and its value inside an object, such as title: 'Ten easy summer recipes'
  • Build: The rewriting of our files into plain JavaScript, done by the dev server for each file the page asks for, and by npm run build for the whole site.
  • Sources panel: The panel of the browser's developer tools that shows each file the browser received, after the build.
  • Error overlay: The dark box Vite puts over the page when the build cannot read a file. It shows the message, the file, and the line.
  • JSX transform: The step of the build that rewrites each JSX tag as a call of a function from React.
  • React element: The plain object a JSX call returns. It describes one element with a type and props.
  • Void element: An HTML element that can hold nothing, such as <img>, <br>, or <input>. HTML lets it stay open; JSX does not.
  • Fragment: An empty tag, <> and </>, that groups elements into one root and adds no element to the page.
  • Flex layout: A CSS layout, set with display: flex, that puts the children of an element in a row.
  • Child selector: A CSS selector with >, such as .articles > li, that matches only the direct children of an element.
  • Reserved word: A word JavaScript keeps for itself, such as class or for, which cannot be a variable name.
  • className and htmlFor: The JSX names of the HTML attributes class and for.

Beyond the basics

  • Writing markup with JSX: the three rules of JSX, why several tags need a wrapper, and a challenge that converts HTML to JSX (see react.dev/learn/writing-markup-with-jsx).
  • Fragment: the empty tag, the long form with a key, and what a Fragment keeps from one render to the next (see react.dev/reference/react/Fragment).
  • React 19 Upgrade Guide: why React 19 requires the new JSX transform (see react.dev/blog/2024/04/25/react-19-upgrade-guide).
  • Common components: every attribute name that React accepts on HTML elements (see react.dev/reference/react-dom/components/common).

Summary

JSX looks like HTML, but it is JavaScript

❒ The JSX transform: each tag becomes a JavaScript call that returns an object

➔ ALWAYS read JSX as JavaScript: each tag is a call that returns an object, and React builds the DOM from the objects.

➔ NEVER expect the browser to receive the tags; open the Sources panel to see the calls it got.

❒ Closed tags: JavaScript must know where each tag ends

➔ ALWAYS close every tag, with a closing tag or a slash, such as <img />, <br />, and <input />.

➔ NEVER leave a void element open as HTML allows; the build stops, and nothing in the file runs.

❒ Single root: a JavaScript function returns one value

➔ ALWAYS return one root that holds the rest of the component's markup.

➔ NEVER return two tags side by side; they are two values, and the build stops.

❒ Fragments: one JavaScript value that adds no element to the page

➔ IF the elements need one root but the page needs no extra box THEN group them with <> and </>.

➔ IF the page needs the box, for its meaning or a style, THEN keep an element such as <section> as the root.

❒ camelCase attributes: each attribute becomes a JavaScript property name

➔ ALWAYS write className for class, htmlFor for for, and camelCase for names of several words.

➔ NEVER rename aria-* and data-* attributes; they keep their dashes.

One call per tag, every tag closed, one root, no extra box, and JavaScript names.

6 </section>
7 );
8}

code.txt

2 return (
3 <label for="query">Words to find</label>
4 <input id="query" type="search">

Lecture 4: JavaScript Expressions in JSX with Curly Braces

Interview Question

CORE

How do you use JavaScript expressions inside JSX with curly braces?

Imagine this scenario:

  1. You move an article into a component, and its title, its author, and the address of its photo now sit in variables at the top of the function.
  2. You write the title into the markup, save, and the page shows the word title; the photo is a broken image.
  3. How does markup that looks like HTML read the values that live in JavaScript?

A page shows values that live in JavaScript

Almost nothing on a real page is typed once and left alone. An article card shows a title, the author's name, the date, and a photo, and each of them comes from somewhere: a database, a form, a calculation. In JavaScript, a value like that lives in a variable. In Lecture 3, every tag we pasted from the old site held fixed text, and every attribute held a fixed value in quotes. Every value in this lesson is fixed in local variables. A value that changes over time while the user interacts with the page requires state, which Lecture 14 introduces. So every React developer meets the same question: how does markup that looks like HTML read the values that live in JavaScript?

The answer is one idea, and this chapter follows it from the first question to the last: curly braces open a window to JavaScript: the code inside runs when React calls the component, and its value takes the place of the braces. Each rule of the chapter follows one value through that window: where it opens, in the text or in an attribute; what it holds, an expression or a comment; and what comes out, a value the page shows or an object it does not.

This lesson answers six questions:

  • Lecture 1 wrote {userName}. What do the braces actually do, and what stays text?
  • My image address is in a variable. How do I put it into src?
  • The label should say Live now only when the article is live. Can I write an if inside the braces?
  • The HTML I pasted in Lecture 3 has comments. How do I keep a note in my markup?
  • My label says Live: {isLive}. Why does the page show only Live:?
  • Why does my date crash the page, and why do some attributes have two pairs of braces?

The questions stand on what Lectures 1, 2, and 3 established:

  • Lecture 1 (What is React): A component describes what the page shows, and React builds the DOM from that description. A local variable made with const holds a value inside the component, and {userName} showed that value in the greeting and in the corner. This chapter explains what those curly braces do.
  • Lecture 2 (Component anatomy): React calls our component wherever a tag names it; that call is rendering. console.log prints in the Console panel, once per call in this course's projects. A function returns undefined when it gives back nothing.
  • Lecture 3 (JSX syntax): The build turns each tag into a call that returns an object, a React element, and the Sources panel shows those calls. An object keeps values under names, its properties. When the build cannot read a file, Vite's error overlay covers the page. Attributes are JavaScript names, such as className.

Some code gives back a value, and some code only does a job

JavaScript code comes in two kinds. An expression is code that gives back a value: 540, wordCount, wordCount / 200, and Math.ceil(wordCount / 200) are all expressions. A statement is code that does a job and gives back nothing we can keep: const makes a variable, if decides whether to run some lines, and for repeats them. A simple test tells them apart: an expression can stand on the right of =, and a statement cannot.

Plain JavaScript: expressions and a statement
1const wordCount = 540;
2const readTime = Math.ceil(wordCount / 200);
3
3if (readTime > 2) {
A statement: it gives back no value
4 console.log('A long read');
5}

wordCount / 200 gives back 2.7, and Math.ceil rounds it up, so readTime holds 3. The if checks whether readTime is more than 2 and runs the line inside, so the Console panel shows "A long read". We could write const result = Math.ceil(wordCount / 200) but never const result = if (readTime > 2) ...

The ternary operator chooses one of two values

Sometimes the value depends on a yes-or-no question. The ternary operator asks it in one expression: a condition, a question mark, the value for yes, a colon, and the value for no. Because it gives back a value, it can stand on the right of =, where an if cannot:

Plain JavaScript: a ternary chooses a value
1const isLive = false;
2const label = isLive ? 'Live now' : 'Recorded';
Recorded

The condition isLive is tested. Because it is false, the expression chooses 'Recorded' and stores it in label.

Two ways to build a text from pieces

An address such as /images/library-hours.jpg is often built from a fixed start, a value, and a fixed end. String concatenation joins texts with +. A template literal does the same in one text: it is written between backticks, and ${...} inside it puts in the value of an expression:

Plain JavaScript: concatenation and a template literal
1const imageId = 'library-hours';
2const first = '/images/' + imageId + '.jpg';
3const second = `/images/${imageId}.jpg`;
The same text

Both approaches produce the identical string /images/library-hours.jpg.

JavaScript has values for yes, no, and nothing

A yes-or-no value is a boolean: true or false. A variable such as isLive holds one. JavaScript also has two values that mean "nothing here": undefined, which Lecture 2 met as the result of a function that gives back nothing, and null, which we write on purpose when a value is missing.

A date is an object

JavaScript keeps a date in a Date object. new Date(2026, 9, 15) makes October 15, 2026; the months count from 0, so 9 is October. A date is an object, not a text, so to show it we ask it for a text: toLocaleDateString('en-US') gives back '10/15/2026'.

Some HTML attributes take a yes or a no, and one takes CSS

Some HTML attributes are on or off. A boolean attribute such as disabled works by being there: <button disabled> is disabled, and so is <button disabled="false">, because the browser looks only at whether the attribute exists, not at its text.

The style attribute sets CSS on one element: in HTML it holds CSS text, such as style="color: gray". A class in a stylesheet is the usual way to style; style is for a value that only this element has.

The project for this lesson

The code runs in the same small project as Lectures 2 and 3. Every component lives in App.jsx, and main.jsx shows App. As in Lecture 2, one file is a choice for learning, so that you see every component at once. A real app gives each main component its own file, and Lecture 8 shows how. The public folder holds two photos: the author's photo, served at /samantha-robinson.jpg, and the article's photo, served at /images/library-hours.jpg.

Principles of React: Curly Braces Open a Window to JavaScript

Everything in this lesson comes down to one idea: curly braces open a window to JavaScript, and the value of the code inside takes their place.

The first two principles say where the window opens. First, embedding expressions, which means curly braces put a JavaScript value where the text goes: the name of a variable in braces shows its value, and everything outside the braces stays text. Second, dynamic attributes, which means curly braces put a JavaScript value where the attribute value goes: the whole value goes in one pair of braces, with no quotes, and quotes stay for fixed text.

The next two say what the window holds. Third, expressions, not statements, which means curly braces hold code that produces a value: a variable, a sum, a call, or a choice with a question mark, but never a statement such as if. Fourth, JSX comments, which means curly braces hold a comment the page never shows: a note in the markup goes inside braces, between a slash and a star.

The last two say what comes out. Fifth, rendered values, which means curly braces show strings and numbers, and nothing for true, false, null, and undefined: a value the reader must see becomes text first. Sixth, double curlies, which means curly braces pass an object only to an attribute that expects one: an object is never shown as text, and the style attribute takes one inside a second pair of braces.

QUESTION 1

Curly braces put a value into the text, and a line break takes a space away

A developer creates ArticleCard with local variables for the title, the author, the word count, and the reading time computed from it:

App.jsx
1function ArticleCard() {
2 const title = 'City Library Extends Its Hours';
3 const author = 'Samantha Robinson';
4 const wordCount = 540;
5 const readTime = Math.ceil(wordCount / 200);
3

The component returns an article with the title, the author's name, and the reading time formatted across two lines:

6 return (
7 <article>
8 <h2>{title}</h2>
9 <p>By {author}</p>
Joins text with variable
10 <p>
11 {readTime}
Line break drops space
12 min read
13 </p>
14 </article>
15 );

App renders the card:

16}
17export default function App() {
18 return <main><ArticleCard /></main>;
React calls ArticleCard
19}

The developer saves. The card appears on screen, showing the title and "By Samantha Robinson". But the reading time at the bottom reads "3min read" without a space between the number and the word.

Lecture 1 wrote {userName}. What do the braces actually do, and what stays text?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. The title and the author's name are right, but a space is missing in the reading time.

Open App.jsx in the Sources panel to see how the build rewrote the markup. Inside the call, children receives the variable itself without quotes:

Sources panel: the heading call with curly braces
1_jsxDEV("h2", { children: title })
Passes the variable

Contrast that with writing <h2>title</h2> without braces:

Sources panel: the heading without braces
1_jsxDEV("h2", { children: "title" })
Passes fixed text

When React calls ArticleCard, the code in the braces runs, and its value takes their place. Text outside the braces stays text. In <p>By {author}</p> children becomes ["By ", author], so React joins the text "By " with the value of author. A function called inside curly braces runs during rendering, so it must only compute and return without side effects, a rule Lecture 12 explores under component purity. Calling new Date() directly while rendering produces a different time on every call, which is why our example in Question 6 uses a fixed date.

The missing space comes from JSX whitespace rules. JSX removes line breaks and the whitespace around them between an expression and adjacent text. Because {readTime} sits on one line and min read sits on the next, the build removes the newline, and the two tokens touch on screen.

The fix puts them on a single line, <p>{readTime} min read</p> or keeps a space on purpose with {' '}, a string holding one space:

App.jsx
1function ArticleCard() {
2 const readTime = 3;
3 return (
4 <p>{readTime} min read</p>
Keeps the space on screen
5 );
6}

Save, and the page shows "3 min read". Code formatters such as Prettier often insert {' '} automatically when breaking long lines, ensuring that spaces are never dropped.

PRINCIPLE 1

Embedding expressions: curly braces put a JavaScript value where the text goes

We put a value from JavaScript into the text by writing it in curly braces; everything outside the braces stays text, and the code inside runs each time React calls the component.

Curly braces between JSX tags create an evaluation window. The JavaScript expression inside the braces is evaluated on every render cycle, and its result takes the place of the braces in the DOM. Any text outside the braces remains literal text. When an expression and text are separated by a line break, JSX strips the intervening whitespace, so spaces between values and words must be kept explicitly on the same line or with a spaced string expression.

We should do this:
const minutes = 4;
<p>{minutes} min read</p>
shows 4 min read
We should not do this:
const minutes = 4;
<p>
{minutes}
min read
shows 4min read
</p>
QUESTION 2

A variable in quotes is only text

The developer now wants to show photos in the card: the author's avatar and a photo of the library. Both addresses live in variables:

App.jsx
1function ArticleCard() {
2 const avatarUrl = '/samantha-robinson.jpg';
3 const imageId = 'library-hours';
4 return (
5 <article>
6 <img src="{avatarUrl}" alt="Author" />
Passes literal braces
7 <img src="/images/{imageId}.jpg" alt="Library" />
Literal id
8 </article>
9 );
10}

The developer saves. Neither photo loads; both appear as broken image icons.

My image address is in a variable. How do I put it into src?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. Both image elements fail to load their source files.

Inspect the Elements panel. The markup reveals that the browser received the literal text inside quotes:

Elements panel: literal strings in attributes
1<img src="{avatarUrl}" alt="Author">
Requests /%7BavatarUrl%7D
2<img src="/images/{imageId}.jpg" alt="Library">

Quotes always pass fixed text in JSX, whether or not curly braces are written inside them. When the browser attempts to fetch src="{avatarUrl}", it requests /%7BavatarUrl%7D from the dev server, which does not exist. Similarly, src="/images/{imageId}.jpg" asks for the literal filename {imageId}.jpg.

Curly braces only open a JavaScript window in attributes when placed directly after the equals sign without quotes. To pass a single variable, write src={avatarUrl}. To build an attribute from multiple pieces, write one complete JavaScript expression inside the braces using concatenation or a template literal:

App.jsx
1function ArticleCard() {
2 const avatarUrl = '/samantha-robinson.jpg';
3 const imageId = 'library-hours';
4 return (
5 <article>
6 <img src={avatarUrl} alt="Author" />
Evaluates variable path
7 <img src={`/images/${imageId}.jpg`} alt="Library" />
Valid path
8 </article>
9 );
10}

The same rule applies to boolean attributes. In HTML, writing disabled="false" still disables a button because the browser checks whether the attribute is present, not what text it holds. React warns in the console: "Received the string false for the boolean attribute disabled. Did you mean disabled={false}?". Writing disabled={false} tells React to omit the attribute from the DOM completely.

PRINCIPLE 2

Dynamic attributes: curly braces put a JavaScript value where the attribute value goes

We give an attribute a value from JavaScript by writing the whole value in one pair of curly braces, right after the equals sign and with no quotes, and we keep quotes for fixed text.

Attributes in JSX accept either quotes for literal string values or curly braces for dynamic JavaScript values. Putting quotes around curly braces treats the braces as literal characters. To evaluate an expression for an attribute, place the curly braces directly against the equals sign with no quotes. When combining fixed paths with variables, construct the entire string inside the single pair of braces using template literals or string concatenation.

We should do this:
const photoUrl = '/john-hall.jpg';
<img src={photoUrl} alt={name} />
loads the photo
We should not do this:
const photoUrl = '/john-hall.jpg';
<img src="{photoUrl}" alt="{name}" />
broken image
QUESTION 3

An if inside the braces stops the build

The article card should display "Live now" when an article is live, and show "Recorded" otherwise. A developer tries to write an if statement inside the curly braces:

App.jsx
1function ArticleCard() {
2 const isLive = false;
3 return (
4 <article>
5 <h2>City Library Extends Its Hours</h2>
6 <p>{if (isLive) { 'Live now' }}</p>
Statement stops the build
7 </article>
8 );
9}

The developer saves. The page goes completely blank, and Vite's error overlay covers the screen.

The label should say Live now only when the article is live. Can I write an if inside the braces?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. The build fails immediately with a parse error:

Vite error overlay: unexpected token
[PARSE_ERROR] Unexpected token
 5 │       <p>{if (isLive) { 'Live now' }}</p>
   │           ─┬─
   │            ╰─── Expected an expression, found 'if'

Recall from Lecture 3 that JSX tags become function calls. The content between tags becomes the children argument of that call. In JavaScript, arguments to a function can only be expressions, code that computes and produces a value.

An if statement is a control flow statement. It executes actions, but it produces no value that can be assigned or passed. JavaScript does not allow a statement to stand where an expression is expected, so the compiler halts before generating any runnable code. for loops and variable declarations with const fail for the same reason.

To choose between values inside JSX braces, use the ternary operator because it is an expression that yields a value:

App.jsx
1function ArticleCard() {
2 const isLive = false;
3 return (
4 <article>
5 <h2>City Library Extends Its Hours</h2>
6 <p>{isLive ? 'Live now' : 'Recorded'}</p>
Ternary yields a value
7 </article>
8 );
9}

Save, and the page renders "Recorded". If the logic requires multiple statements or complex branches, execute the if statement above the return in standard JavaScript, assign the result to a local variable, and reference that variable inside the braces:

App.jsx
1function ArticleCard() {
2 const isLive = false;
3 let status = 'Recorded';
Sets local variable
4 if (isLive) {
5 status = 'Live now';
6 }
7 return (
8 <p>{status}</p>
Reads the computed string
9 );
10}

Curly braces can contain any JavaScript expression: mathematical calculations like {Math.ceil(wordCount / 200)}, method calls like {title.toUpperCase()}, or function invocations. However, curly braces cannot replace tag names: writing <{tag}> is illegal syntax and stops the build.

PRINCIPLE 3

Expressions, not statements: curly braces hold code that produces a value

We put only an expression, code that produces a value, inside curly braces: a variable, a sum, a call, or a ternary; a statement such as if goes above the return, and its result goes into the braces through a variable.

Curly braces in JSX compile to object property assignments or function call arguments, which only accept expressions. Statements like if, for, let, or const do not evaluate to values and trigger parse errors at build time. When conditional logic must reside directly inside JSX markup, use ternary expressions. When logic spans multiple statements, compute the result into a local variable before the return statement and pass that variable into the JSX braces.

We should do this:
const isOnline = true;
<p>{isOnline ? 'Online' : 'Away'}</p>
shows Online
We should not do this:
const isOnline = true;
<p>{if (isOnline) { 'Online' }}</p>
build stops

A pasted HTML comment stops the build

The HTML of the old site contained comments documenting sections of the page. A developer pastes one of those comments into ArticleCard:

App.jsx
1function ArticleCard() {
2 return (
Pasted from the old site
3 <article>
4 <!-- the title from the old site -->
5 <h2>City Library Extends Its Hours</h2>
6 </article>
7 );
8}

The developer saves. Once again the page goes blank, and Vite's error overlay reports a parse failure:

Vite error overlay: HTML comments
[PARSE_ERROR] HTML comments are not allowed in modules
 4 │       <!-- the title from the old site -->
   │        ───────────────────────────────────
   │        Did you mean to use a JSX comment '{/* ... */}'?

The HTML I pasted in Lecture 3 has comments. How do I keep a note in my markup?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. The build rejects HTML comment syntax.

Between JSX tags, the compiler expects either valid child tags or literal text nodes. <!-- is an HTML syntax construct that is not part of the JavaScript language. Because JSX files are parsed as JavaScript ES modules, HTML comment tags cause the parser to fail.

The developer might next try writing two slashes, as in standard JavaScript:

App.jsx
1function ArticleCard() {
2 return (
The next attempt
3 <article>
4 // the title from the old site
5 <h2>City Library Extends Its Hours</h2>
6 </article>
7 );
8}

This compiles without error, but it creates a silent visual bug. Because the slashes sit between JSX tags, the compiler treats them as plain text. The page visibly displays "// the title from the old site" directly above the heading:

Elements panel: two slashes printed as text
1<article>
2 <h2>City Library Extends Its Hours</h2>
The title from the old site <!-- printed directly on screen
3</article>

To leave a note inside JSX markup, open a JavaScript window with curly braces and write a standard multi-line comment: {/* comment */}:

App.jsx
1function ArticleCard() {
2 return (
A note inside braces
3 <article>
4 {/* the title from the old site */}
5 <h2>City Library Extends Its Hours</h2>
6 </article>
7 );
8}

Because the comment is inside curly braces, JavaScript parses it as a comment. Because a comment produces no value, the braces evaluate to nothing, and React adds no text node or element to the DOM:

Elements panel: comment adds no element
1<article>
Comment produced zero DOM nodes
2 <h2>City Library Extends Its Hours</h2>
3</article>

Outside of JSX tags, above the return statement, standard single-line // and multi-line /* */ comments work as expected.

PRINCIPLE 4

JSX comments: curly braces hold a comment the page never shows

We write a note between tags as a JavaScript comment inside curly braces, {/* */}; an HTML comment stops the build, and two slashes alone print on the page.

HTML comment syntax is prohibited in JSX modules and stops the compiler. Placing standard JavaScript double slashes directly between JSX tags causes them to render as visible text nodes on the page. To write an authentic comment inside JSX markup, wrap a multi-line comment block in curly braces. The braces switch context into JavaScript, where the comment is parsed and discarded without emitting any DOM nodes.

We should do this:
<article>
{/* contact details */}
<p>John Hall</p>
nothing in the DOM
</article>
We should not do this:
<article>
<!-- contact details -->
<p>John Hall</p>
the build stops
</article>
QUESTION 5

A boolean in the braces shows nothing

The developer adds a status indicator to show whether the library is open for live consultations:

App.jsx
1function ArticleCard() {
2 const isLive = false;
3 return (
4 <article>
5 <h2>City Library Extends Its Hours</h2>
6 <p>Live: {isLive}</p>
Boolean renders nothing
7 </article>
8 );
9}

The developer saves. The card appears, but the paragraph reads only "Live: " with a blank space where the boolean should be. The Console panel shows zero warnings or errors.

My label says Live: {isLive}. Why does the page show only Live:?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. The boolean value is completely invisible on the page.

In JavaScript, console.log(false) prints the word "false" to the console. React behaves differently. React renders strings and numbers as visible text nodes, but it intentionally ignores true, false, null, and undefined:

What JSX renders for each JavaScript value
Value        Inside braces         What appears on screen
'text'       {'text'}              text
42           {42}                  42
0            {0}                   0
true         {true}                (nothing)
false        {false}               (nothing)
null         {null}                (nothing)
undefined    {undefined}           (nothing)

React skips booleans, null, and undefined so that conditional rendering expressions can output nothing when a condition is not met. If false rendered as the word "false", writing {isLoggedIn && <UserMenu />} would print "false" on screen for logged-out visitors. An array of strings in braces shows its items joined, while turning an array of data into a list of elements with keys is the subject of Lecture 11.

Notice that the number 0 is not ignored. 0 is a number, and numbers always render on screen. Lecture 10 explores how this distinction impacts conditional rendering bugs.

This silent omission also hides typos. If you reference {author.nmae} instead of {author.name}, the expression evaluates to undefined, and React renders an empty string without warning.

When you want a boolean value to be visible to the user, convert it to a string explicitly using a ternary operator:

App.jsx
1function ArticleCard() {
2 const isLive = false;
3 return (
4 <article>
5 <h2>City Library Extends Its Hours</h2>
6 <p>Live: {isLive ? 'Yes' : 'No'}</p>
Converts boolean to text
7 </article>
8 );
9}

Save, and the paragraph reads "Live: No". If a function identifier is placed inside braces without parentheses, such as {formatDate}, React renders nothing and logs an explicit warning: "Functions are not valid as a React child. ... Or maybe you meant to call this function rather than return it.". Always invoke functions with parentheses: {formatDate()}.

PRINCIPLE 5

Rendered values: curly braces show strings and numbers, and nothing for true, false, null, and undefined

We expect strings and numbers to show as text, and true, false, null, and undefined to show nothing, so a value the reader must see, such as yes or no, becomes text before it reaches the braces.

React transforms strings and numbers into text nodes in the DOM, including zero and NaN. To make conditional rendering seamless, React intentionally suppresses booleans, null, and undefined, rendering no DOM nodes for them without error. When boolean states or missing values must be visible to the end user, convert them into string literals before rendering by using ternary operators or explicit formatting functions.

We should do this:
const isVerified = false;
<p>
Verified: {isVerified ? 'Yes' : 'No'}
shows Verified: No
</p>
We should not do this:
const isVerified = false;
<p>Verified: {isVerified}</p>
shows Verified:
QUESTION 6

A date in the braces empties the page

The developer wants to display the date the library article was published:

App.jsx
1function ArticleCard() {
2 const publishedAt = new Date(2026, 9, 15);
3 return (
4 <article>
5 <h2>City Library Extends Its Hours</h2>
6 <p>Published {publishedAt}</p>
Object crashes the render
7 </article>
8 );
9}

The developer saves. The entire page goes blank. The Elements panel shows an empty root container, and the Console panel displays a fatal runtime exception:

Console panel: object as React child
Uncaught Error: Objects are not valid as a React child (found: [object Date]).
If you meant to render a collection of children, use an array instead.

The developer also notices that some React tutorials use double curly braces on attributes: <p style={{ color: 'gray' }}>

Why does my date crash the page, and why do some attributes have two pairs of braces?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. Placing an object directly between JSX tags crashes the render.

In JavaScript, a Date instance looks like a readable timestamp when logged, but it is a complex JavaScript object. An object has no single canonical text representation. Rather than making an arbitrary guess, React throws a runtime error when an object is passed as a child between tags.

Because this application does not yet have an error boundary to catch the failure, React unmounts the entire component tree, leaving the page completely empty. Lecture 72 teaches how error boundaries contain these errors.

To render information from an object, you must extract a primitive string or number. For dates, call formatting methods such as toLocaleDateString():

App.jsx
1function ArticleCard() {
2 const publishedAt = new Date(2026, 9, 15);
3 const formatted = publishedAt.toLocaleDateString('en-US');
4 return (
5 <article>
6 <h2>City Library Extends Its Hours</h2>
7 <p>Published {formatted}</p>
Formats date to string
8 </article>
9 );
10}

Save, and the paragraph displays "Published 10/15/2026". For regular objects like { name: 'Samantha Robinson' } access the individual property: {author.name}.

The double curly braces seen in attributes are not a special language feature. They are simply an ordinary JavaScript object literal placed inside a standard JSX attribute window:

Double braces taken apart
style={ { color: 'gray' } }
       │ └─────────────┘ │
       │   an object     │
       └─────────────────┘
         the JSX window

The outer braces open the JavaScript expression window for the attribute. The inner braces define an inline object literal with CSS properties. The style attribute expects an object mapping CSS properties to values, so passing an object to it is valid:

App.jsx
1function ArticleCard() {
2 return (
3 <article>
4 <h2 style={{ color: 'gray' }}>
Style object
5 City Library Extends Its Hours
6 </h2>
7 </article>
8 );
9}

React reads the object and applies style="color: gray;" to the HTML element. In React, style="color: gray" throws an error because the style prop expects an object mapping CSS properties to values. Style properties use camelCase names, and Lecture 83 teaches the full rules of the style attribute and when to prefer CSS classes. Attempting to write <h2>{{title}}</h2> between tags fails with the same "Objects are not valid as a React child" error, because the inner braces construct an object where React expects renderable text.

PRINCIPLE 6

Double curlies: curly braces pass an object only to an attribute that expects one

We show a field of an object or a formatted string, never the object itself, and we pass an object only to an attribute that expects one, such as style, where the outer braces open the window and the inner braces write the object.

Plain JavaScript objects and Date instances have no default text representation and cannot be rendered directly as JSX children. Placing an object between tags throws a runtime error that unmounts the component tree. Always extract primitive values or call formatting methods before rendering. Double curly braces are not special syntax; they represent an object literal passed inside a single JSX attribute evaluation window.

We should do this:
const joinedAt = new Date(2024, 2, 5);
<p style={{ color: 'gray' }}>
Member since {joinedAt.toLocaleDateString('en-US')}
</p>
shows date in gray
We should not do this:
const joinedAt = new Date(2024, 2, 5);
<p>Member since {joinedAt}</p>
crashes the render

⚡ IN THE WILD

Does a string that holds HTML tags show as HTML? A reader's comment might arrive from an API containing HTML markup, such as '<b>Updated</b>'. A developer might expect the browser to render bold text. However, React writes every string into the page as literal text, creating a text node rather than parsing HTML elements. The browser displays the literal angle brackets and letters <b>Updated</b> and the Elements panel shows &lt;b&gt;Updated&lt;/b&gt;. This automatic escaping is a built-in security feature that protects users from Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) attacks. Lecture 48 covers dangerouslySetInnerHTML, the explicit property used when raw HTML must be injected intentionally.
Case Study
Let's Design a Practical Example

Each question tested one rule on a small card. Now we build the featured article of the home page at its real size. The old site typed every value into the markup: the title twice, once as text and once as the photo's description, the author, the reading time, and the photo's address. This time every value comes from a variable, and the card gains a status label, the date, and the number of comments. The three steps follow the three parts of this lesson: where the braces open, what they hold, and what comes out. Keep the dev server running and the Elements panel and the Console panel open.

Step 1
First, we open the braces in the text and in the attributes
<App.jsx>

This step applies the first two principles: Embedding expressions and Dynamic attributes. On the legacy site, every value was hardcoded into the markup. We move those values into local variables declared at the top of FeaturedArticle: title, author, imageId, and readTime.

In the return markup, curly braces replace the fixed text for the title and author. For the image, src evaluates a template literal inside one pair of curly braces, `src={/images/${imageId}.jpg}, while alt dynamically receives title`. The reading time and its text label stay together on a single line, preserving the space.

11 />

Next, we compute what goes inside the braces

This step applies the third and fourth principles: Expressions, not statements and JSX comments. The reading time should be computed from the actual word count of the article rather than typed as a fixed number. We declare wordCount (540 words) and isLive (false). Because variable declarations and calculations are statements, we compute readTime above the return using Math.ceil(wordCount / 200).

In the markup, we display a status label. Because an if statement cannot sit inside JSX braces, we evaluate a ternary expression: {isLive ? 'Live now' : 'Recorded'} We also add a note above the status line using JSX comment syntax: {/* the label follows isLive */}

In FeaturedArticle, lines 5 to 7 declare the new variables and calculation, replacing the old line 5:

Step 3
Finally, we turn each value into something the page can show
<App.jsx>

This step applies the fifth and sixth principles: Rendered values and Double curlies. The card now receives a publication date and a comment count: commentCount (0) and publishedAt (new Date(2026, 9, 15)).

If we rendered {publishedAt} directly, the Date object would crash React and blank the screen. Instead, we call publishedAt.toLocaleDateString('en-US') to provide a formatted string. The commentCount number can be rendered directly because numbers, including 0, are visible. Finally, we style the status label dynamically: when live, it renders in red; when recorded, it renders in gray. Because inline styles require a JavaScript object mapping CSS properties, we pass an object literal using double curly braces: style={{ color: isLive ? 'red' : 'gray' }}

In FeaturedArticle, lines 8 and 9 introduce the comment count and publication date:

App.jsx

19 </p>

Component Summary

main

The entry file loads index.css and names <App />. No step changed it.

App

FeaturedArticle declares values as variables above the return and reads them through curly braces. App renders FeaturedArticle inside a main landmark.

A developer coming from HTML or templating libraries brings three ingrained habits: expect quotes to read variables, put statements such as if inside braces, and expect objects like dates to print automatically. Each habit meets JavaScript in its own way. Quotes always pass fixed text, statements produce no value and halt the build, and objects cannot be converted to text and crash the render. In React 19, the three steps followed the thread: opening the braces in text and attributes, computing expressions and notes inside them, and ensuring that every value that reaches the page is a string or a number.

Where you will meet this

  1. A product card: formatting a price from a numeric variable into currency text, and choosing an in-stock label with a ternary.
  2. An avatar image: constructing a dynamic image source URL from a user ID using a template literal inside one pair of braces.
  3. An article's date: converting a Date object from an API response into a readable string using toLocaleDateString().
  4. A status pill: toggling between active and inactive color styles on an element using style={{ color: isActive ? 'green' : 'gray' }}
  5. Markup imported from an HTML template: cleaning up old <!-- --> comments and replacing them with {/* */} annotations.

For the interview

The Interview Question: How do you use JavaScript expressions inside JSX with curly braces?

1. The Hidden Signal

The interviewer wants to hear that curly braces are not template markers: they are an evaluation window into JavaScript that becomes an argument in a function call. A strong candidate explains that braces accept only expressions that produce values, and that the resulting value takes the place of the braces when React renders the component.

2. The Classic Trap

The classic trap is saying "You can write any JavaScript inside JSX braces." You cannot write statements such as if, for, or const inside braces because statements produce no value; they cause build errors. A second trap is believing that {{ }} is a special syntax, rather than an object literal passed to an attribute window.

3. What is Actually Going On

Braces open a JavaScript window in two places: between tags as children, and after an attribute equals sign as a prop. Between tags, React converts strings and numbers into text, while silently skipping true, false, null, and undefined. Objects, including Date instances, cannot be converted to text and crash the render with an error. In attributes, braces pass raw JavaScript values directly, without quotes.

4. Where It Gets Tricky

Why does {false} render nothing while {0} renders 0?

React treats boolean values, null, and undefined as invisible values so conditional expressions can render nothing cleanly. Numbers are treated as visible content, so 0 is converted to the character "0".

Why does rendering a Date object crash the whole component?

React does not guess how an object should look as text. It throws "Objects are not valid as a React child", which removes the entire component tree unless caught by an error boundary.

What does src="{avatarUrl}" actually pass to the browser?

It passes the literal string "{avatarUrl}". The browser encodes the braces and requests /%7BavatarUrl%7D, resulting in a broken image. Dynamic attributes must omit quotes: src={avatarUrl}.

How do you write a comment inside JSX markup?

Between tags, you open curly braces and write a multi-line JavaScript comment: {/* comment */}. Plain <!-- --> comments cause a syntax error, and // comments render as visible text on the page.

Glossary

  • Expression: JavaScript code that produces a value, such as wordCount / 200, Math.ceil(x), or a ternary.
  • Statement: JavaScript code that performs an action without producing a value, such as if, for, or const.
  • Ternary operator: An expression that tests a condition and produces one of two values, written as condition ? yes : no.
  • Template literal: A string written between backticks that evaluates expressions inside ${...}.
  • Boolean: A JavaScript value representing true or false.
  • null: A JavaScript primitive representing the intentional absence of any object value.
  • JSX comment: A comment inside JSX markup written as {/* ... */} within curly braces.
  • Double curlies: The appearance of an object literal passed directly into a JSX attribute window, as in style={{ color: 'gray' }}.
  • Date: A JavaScript built-in object that represents a single moment in time.

Beyond the basics

  • JavaScript in JSX with Curly Braces: Where to use curly braces, passing strings with quotes, and using double curlies (see react.dev/learn/javascript-in-jsx-with-curly-braces).
  • Writing Markup with JSX: The foundational syntax rules of JSX and why it differs from HTML (see react.dev/learn/writing-markup-with-jsx).
  • Conditional Rendering: How ternaries and the logical AND operator work inside JSX expressions (see react.dev/learn/conditional-rendering).
  • Common components: Documentation on the style prop and how React maps style objects to DOM elements (see react.dev/reference/react-dom/components/common).

Summary

Curly braces open a window to JavaScript

❒ Embedding expressions: curly braces put a JavaScript value where the text goes

➔ ALWAYS write dynamic text inside curly braces between tags.

➔ NEVER put a line break between a value and text if you want a space; use {' '} if formatters break the line.

❒ Dynamic attributes: curly braces put a JavaScript value where the attribute value goes

➔ ALWAYS pass JavaScript values to attributes using curly braces right after = with no quotes.

➔ NEVER put quotes around curly braces or variable names in attributes; quotes always pass fixed text.

❒ Expressions, not statements: curly braces hold code that produces a value

➔ ALWAYS place expressions such as variables, calculations, calls, and ternaries inside curly braces.

➔ NEVER put statements such as if, for, or const inside braces; put them above the return.

❒ JSX comments: curly braces hold a comment the page never shows

➔ ALWAYS write notes between tags as {/* ... */} inside curly braces.

➔ NEVER write HTML comments <!-- --> or bare // between JSX tags.

❒ Rendered values: curly braces show strings and numbers, and nothing for true, false, null, and undefined

➔ ALWAYS convert booleans to visible text using a ternary if the user needs to see yes or no.

➔ NEVER expect true, false, null, or undefined to render text on the screen.

❒ Double curlies: curly braces pass an object only to an attribute that expects one

➔ ALWAYS format dates and read object properties before placing them between tags.

➔ NEVER pass an object or a Date directly between tags; pass an object only to attributes like style.

The text or an attribute, an expression or a comment, and a value the page can show.

DO THIS: curly braces for dynamic values, expressions, and style objects

code.txt
1function ArticleCard() {
2 const title = 'City Library Extends Its Hours';
3 const isLive = false;
4 return (
5 <article>
6 <h2>{title}</h2>
7 <p style={{ color: 'gray' }}>{isLive ? 'Live now' : 'Recorded'}</p>
8 </article>
9 );
10}

DO NOT DO THIS: quotes around variables, statements in braces, or objects in text

code.txt
1function ArticleCard() {
2 const title = 'City Library Extends Its Hours';
3 const isLive = false;
4 return (
5 <article>
6 <h2>"{title}"</h2>
7 <p style="color: gray">{if (isLive) { 'Live' }}</p>
8 </article>
9 );
10}
THE HTML OR TEMPLATE HABITTHE JSX RULE
Where it opensQuotes around variables or template syntax like ${val}Braces between tags for text,
or right after = with no quotes
What it holdsTemplate statements, if tags,
or <!-- --> comments		One expression that produces a value,
or a {/* */} comment
What comes outEverything converted to text,
including dates and objects		Strings and numbers become text;
booleans hide; objects crash

Lecture 5: UI as a Tree and Component Hierarchy

Interview Question

CORE

How does React organize nested components into a tree, and why does hierarchy dictate data flow?

Imagine this scenario:

  1. The page has grown: a header with the site name, a list of articles with each article's title and author, and a box of popular articles, each in its own component in App.jsx.
  2. The article card needs the topic that App declares; you write it in braces, save, and the whole page goes blank.
  3. How do components fit together, and how does a value reach the part of the page that shows it?

A page grows from a few components into many

In Lecture 2, the article page had three components: App, an article card, and a comment box. A real home page has many more: a header with a menu, a list of articles, the author's name under each article, a box of popular articles, and a footer. In our project they all sit side by side in App.jsx, one function after another, like a flat list. But the page is not flat: the author's name sits inside the article, and the article sits inside the list. So every React developer meets the same question: how do the components fit together, and how does a value reach the part of the page that shows it?

The answer is one idea, and this chapter follows it from the first question to the last: the page is a tree of components: each component's markup names its children, and React builds the page from the root down. The chapter follows the tree from its shape to its use: how it grows, where it is cut, and what travels along it.

This lesson answers three questions:

  • I have five components side by side in App.jsx. How does React know which goes where?
  • My App now holds the whole home page. Should I cut it up, and where?
  • ArticleCard needs the topic that App declares. Can it just read it?

The questions stand on what Lectures 1, 2, 3, and 4 established:

  • Lecture 1 (What is React): A local variable made with const holds a value inside the component. In plain JavaScript, document.getElementById finds an element on the page, and textContent reads its text.
  • Lecture 2 (Component anatomy): React calls a component wherever a tag names it, and console.log in its body shows each call in the Console panel, once per call in this course's projects. Every component is defined at the top level of the file; a component defined inside another one is made again on every run, and loses what the reader typed.
  • Lecture 3 (JSX syntax): A Fragment, <> and </>, groups elements without adding one to the page.
  • Lecture 4 (JavaScript expressions in JSX with curly braces): {topic} puts the value of a variable into the text, and the code inside the braces runs each time React calls the component.

A variable lives inside the function that declares it

A variable declared with const inside a function exists only while that function runs, and only the code inside that function can see it. This part of the code where a name can be used is called the variable's scope. A variable declared at the top level of a file, outside every function, can be seen by every function of that file.

Plain JavaScript: a variable stays in its function
1const siteName = 'Latest Articles';
The whole file sees it
2function header() {
3 const topic = 'Sport';
Only header sees it
4 return siteName + ', ' + topic;
5}
6function footer() {
7 return siteName + ', ' + topic;
Topic is not defined
8}

header() gives back "Latest Articles, Sport". footer() stops with "topic is not defined": topic exists only inside header. JavaScript calls this kind of error a ReferenceError: the code uses a name that does not exist where it is written. siteName works in both, because it sits at the top level.

A tree has a root, branches, and leaves

Folders on a computer form a tree: one folder at the top holds others, and they hold more. The same words name any tree. The root is the one at the top. Each item is the parent of the items directly inside it, and those are its children. Children of the same parent are siblings. An item near the root is top-level, and an item that holds nothing is a leaf.

One function, one job

A long function that does many things is hard to read and hard to change, because every change risks the other things it does. Programmers split it so that each function has one job, and this habit has a name: separation of concerns. A function with one job gets a name that says the job, such as formatDate or sendEmail.

The project for this lesson

The code runs in the same small project as Lectures 2 to 4. Every component lives in App.jsx, and main.jsx shows App. As in Lecture 2, one file is a choice for learning, so that you see every component at once. A real app gives each main component its own file, and Lecture 8 shows how. Each component logs its name, so the Console panel shows the order in which React calls them.

Principles of React: The Page Is a Tree of Components

Everything in this lesson comes down to one idea: the page is a tree of components, and React builds it from the root down.

First, the render tree, which means each component's markup names its children: App is the root, every component is the parent of the components its markup names, and React calls them branch by branch.

Second, component boundaries, which means one branch of the tree for each part of the page with its own job: the header, the list of articles, and the article each get a component, nested where they sit on the page.

Third, data flow, which means a value travels down the tree, never across it: a component cannot read a variable of its parent or of its neighbor, so a value they share starts above them both.

QUESTION 1

React calls the components in the order of the tree

A developer writes the home page in App.jsx with six component functions. Each component logs its name to the Console panel so the execution order is visible:

App.jsx
1function SiteHeader() {
2 console.log('SiteHeader runs');
Leaf component
3 return <header><h1>Latest Articles</h1></header>;
4}
5function AuthorName() {
6 console.log('AuthorName runs');
Leaf component
7 return <p>By Samantha Robinson</p>;
8}

ArticleCard logs its execution, renders the title, and nests <AuthorName />:

9function ArticleCard() {
10 console.log('ArticleCard runs');
Parent of author name
11 return (
12 <article>
13 <h2>City Library Extends Its Hours</h2>
14 <AuthorName />
Child of card
15 </article>
16 );
17}

PopularArticles renders the side box:

18function PopularArticles() {
19 console.log('PopularArticles runs');
Leaf component
20 return <aside><h3>Popular articles</h3></aside>;
21}

ArticleList groups ArticleCard and PopularArticles inside a <main> tag:

22function ArticleList() {
23 console.log('ArticleList runs');
Parent of card and popular articles
24 return (
25 <main>
26 <ArticleCard />
First child
27 <PopularArticles />
Second child
28 </main>
29 );
30}

Finally, App renders SiteHeader and ArticleList inside a Fragment:

31export default function App() {
32 console.log('App runs');
Root component
33 return (
34 <>
35 <SiteHeader />
First child
36 <ArticleList />
Second child
37 </>
38 );
39}

The developer saves. The page displays the site header, the article with its author's name, and the side box. In the Console panel, the messages appear in this order: "App runs", "SiteHeader runs", "ArticleList runs", "ArticleCard runs", "AuthorName runs", "PopularArticles runs".

I have five components side by side in App.jsx. How does React know which goes where?

ANSWER

The code works as written. The page displays the complete layout, and the Console panel shows that React called the components in the order of the tree, not the order of the file.

The file starts with SiteHeader on line 1, but the first message in the console is "App runs". React starts at App because main.jsx names <App />. App is the root of the tree.

Inside App, the return markup names <SiteHeader /> and <ArticleList />. Because App names them, they are App's children, and App is their parent. SiteHeader and ArticleList share the same parent, so they are siblings.

React calls SiteHeader first. SiteHeader returns native HTML tags (<header> and <h1>), naming no further components. It is a leaf of the tree, so React finishes that branch. Next, React calls ArticleList. Its markup names <ArticleCard /> and <PopularArticles />. Before calling PopularArticles, React dives into ArticleCard. Inside ArticleCard, the markup names <AuthorName />. React calls AuthorName, which is a leaf. Only after completing the entire ArticleCard branch does React call its sibling, PopularArticles.

This branching structure is the render tree. App sits at the root, top-level components branch below it, and leaf components sit at the tips. React keeps this tree as real data in memory, and React Developer Tools draws it in its Components tab, which Lecture 64 explores.

Notice that the render tree holds only React components. The Elements panel in the browser shows only the HTML tags they returned: <header>, <main>, <article>, <p>, and <aside>. No component names appear in the DOM.

Each component tag creates a distinct place in the tree. If <ArticleCard /> were named twice inside ArticleList, React would create two nodes in the tree, and "ArticleCard runs" would print twice. When a component chooses different children based on state, the tree changes from one render to the next, which Lecture 10 teaches. And when components move into separate files that import each other, they form a module dependency tree, which Lecture 8 explores.

The render tree and the call order
1. App (root)
              /             \
    2. SiteHeader      3. ArticleList
                           /          \
                4. ArticleCard      6. PopularArticles
                      |
                5. AuthorName
PRINCIPLE 1

The render tree: each component's markup names its children

root component the top component in the tree that React mounts into the page
render tree the hierarchy of components created by nested tags in JSX
child components components named inside a parent component's markup
leaf components components at the ends of branches that name no other components

We read the components a component's markup names as its children: App is the root, each component is the parent of the ones it names, and React calls them from the root down, finishing one branch before the next.

We might expect React to call components from top to bottom as they appear in the file. But the file order plays no part. React begins at the root component named in main.jsx and builds the render tree by reading which component tags appear inside each component's markup. When a component returns other component tags, those become its child components. React calls each child and traverses down that entire branch to its leaf components before moving to the next sibling branch. The browser DOM receives only the native HTML tags the components return.

We should do this:
function ProfilePage() {
return (
<>
<ProfileHeader />
first child branch
<ContactList />
second child branch
</>
);
}
QUESTION 2

One long App shows the same page

A developer considers writing the entire home page as one single App component that returns all the markup in a single function:

App.jsx
1export default function App() {
2 return (
3 <>
4 <header>
5 <h1>Latest Articles</h1>

6 </header>
7 <main>
8 <article>

The rest of the markup follows, containing the title, the author's name, and the side box:

9 <h2>City Library Extends Its Hours</h2>

11 </article>
