The developer saves. The page displays the exact same layout as Question 1. Opening the Elements panel reveals the exact same DOM structure: <header>, <main>, <article>, <p>, <aside>.

My App now holds the whole home page. Should I cut it up, and where?

ANSWER

The code works as written. React builds the exact same page from one function or from six.

Looking only at the browser screen or the Elements panel, you cannot tell the two files apart. React creates identical DOM elements whether they come from one large component or a tree of smaller ones. So the reason to cut a page into components is for the code and the developers who maintain it, not for the browser.

In one long App, a single function handles five distinct jobs at once: the site header, the list of articles, the individual article, the author line, and the side box. If you need to change how the author's name looks, you must read through the site header and side box to find the right lines.

The official documentation in Thinking in React starts every app the same way: draw a box around each part of the design and give each box a name. The core rule behind this is separation of concerns: giving each piece of code one clear, focused job.

When breaking up a page, create one component for each part of the page that has its own distinct job, nested where that part sits on the page:

  • SiteHeader holds the site header.
  • ArticleList organizes the list of articles.
  • ArticleCard presents one article.
  • AuthorName displays the author line.
  • PopularArticles handles the side box.

A part of the page deserves its own component whenever it has a distinct job, even if it is used only once. The author's name stays a separate component because it represents an independent concern inside every card.

Conversely, do not create a component for every individual tag. An <h2> that serves only as the title of ArticleCard stays inside ArticleCard until it grows a job of its own. Just as Thinking in React keeps a table header inside the table until it develops its own independent logic, keep minor tags inside their parent.

The real cost of keeping everything in one giant App becomes obvious in Lecture 6, when each part of the page needs its own data.

Component boundaries drawn around page jobs
+---------------------------------------------------+
| SiteHeader: site header ("Latest Articles")       |
+---------------------------------------------------+
| ArticleList                                       |
|  +------------------------+  +------------------+ |
|  | ArticleCard: article   |  | PopularArticles: | |
|  |  +-------------------+ |  | side box         | |
|  |  | AuthorName        | |  +------------------+ |
|  +--+-------------------+-+                       |
+---------------------------------------------------+
PRINCIPLE 2

Component boundaries: one branch of the tree for each part of the page with its own job

separation of concerns organizing code so each component handles one distinct responsibility

We give each part of the page with its own job its own component, nested where the part sits on the page, and we keep a small piece inside its parent until it grows a job of its own.

React produces the identical DOM from one long component or from many small ones. We divide the UI into separate components to practice separation of concerns, ensuring each function has one understandable responsibility. Give each section with an independent role its own component, nested where it appears on the page. A component that performs a distinct job is worth creating even if it is rendered in only one place. Keep minor tags inside their parent until they develop independent logic or formatting needs.

We should do this:
function ProfilePage() {
return (
<main>
<ProfileHeader />
owns name and photo
<ContactList />
owns email and phone
</main>
);
}
QUESTION 3

A child cannot read its parent's variable

Now that the page is cut into components, the developer wants ArticleCard to show the topic, "Sport". App declares topic as a local variable:

App.jsx
1function ArticleCard() {
2 return (
3 <h2>{topic} articles</h2>
ReferenceError: topic not defined
4 );
5}
6export default function App() {
7 const topic = 'Sport';
Local variable inside App
8 return <main><ArticleCard /></main>;
9}

The developer saves. The page crashes and turns completely blank. Opening the Console panel reveals a red error message: ReferenceError: topic is not defined React also logs a message suggesting adding an error boundary to handle rendering failures.

ArticleCard needs the topic that App declares. Can it just read it?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. ArticleCard cannot see a variable declared inside App.

Because <ArticleCard /> appears inside App's return markup, it is tempting to assume that ArticleCard can read App's variables, the way a nested JavaScript function reads outer variables.

But a JSX tag is not code inside App's function: it is only an instruction telling React to call ArticleCard. Both ArticleCard and App are defined as separate functions at the top level of the file. As shown in the runway, a variable declared with const inside a function exists only in that function's scope. When React calls ArticleCard, topic does not exist in its scope. JavaScript throws a ReferenceError, and because nothing catches it, the entire page unmounts and goes empty.

Reaching across horizontally to a sibling fails for the exact same reason: ArticleList cannot read a local variable declared inside its sibling SiteHeader.

Reaching across using traditional browser DOM methods fails too. If SiteHeader tries to read its neighbor's rendered text using document.getElementById('topic').textContent JavaScript throws:

TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'textContent')

This happens because when React calls SiteHeader, the component tree is still being evaluated. No DOM elements exist on the page yet (as Lecture 15 explains in the render and commit lifecycle). Moreover, code that runs while React calls the components must not depend on other components having run, a requirement Lecture 12 explores with pure functions.

Another tempting fix is to declare ArticleCard directly inside App. While JavaScript function nesting would allow ArticleCard to read topic, this breaks the core rule from Lecture 2: defining a component inside another component recreates it on every run, resetting its state and destroying what the user typed.

Instead, data in React must flow in one direction: down the tree. A shared value must start above all components that need it.

For a fixed value that the entire file needs and that never changes, the immediate solution within this lesson's scope is to declare const topic = 'Sport'; at the top level of the file, outside of every function:

App.jsx
1const topic = 'Sport';
File-level scope
2function ArticleCard() {
3 return (
4 <h2>{topic} articles</h2>
Reads top-level constant
5 );
6}

Now ArticleCard displays "Sport articles". When data varies between cards or changes over time, it originates in the closest common parent and travels down through props, which Lecture 6 teaches.

Data flow: downward from above, never across
[ const topic = 'Sport' ] (top-level file scope)
       |
       +-------------------------------+
       |                               |
       v (reads in scope)              v (reads in scope)
      App                         ArticleCard
       |                               ^
       +--- X (topic is private) ------+
         (cannot read parent variable)
PRINCIPLE 3

Data flow: a value travels down the tree, never across it

scope the area of code where a declared variable can be accessed

We start a value that several components need above all of them and let it travel down the tree; a component never reads a variable of its parent or of its neighbor, and never reads another component's text from the page.

A component is a top-level function that sees only its own local variables and variables declared at the file level. Writing a component tag inside another component does not share JavaScript scope. A child cannot access variables declared inside its parent, and siblings cannot read from each other. DOM lookups like document.getElementById fail during rendering because HTML elements do not exist yet. Values that multiple components share must start above them in the hierarchy and travel down.

We should do this:
const ownerName = 'John Hall';
top-level file scope
function ProfileHeader() {
return <h1>{ownerName}</h1>;
reads file scope
}
function ContactList() {
return <p>{ownerName}</p>;
reads file scope
}
We should not do this:
function ProfilePage() {
const ownerName = 'John Hall';
private to ProfilePage
return <ContactList />;
}
function ContactList() {
return <p>{ownerName}</p>;
ownerName not defined
}

⚡ IN THE WILD

Is the render tree the same as the tree of my files? In Lecture 8, we will move each component into its own file, and those files will import one another. It is natural to expect the tree of files to look exactly like the render tree. However, these are two distinct trees. The files and their import statements form a module dependency tree. A build tool or bundler (such as Vite) reads the module dependency tree to determine which JavaScript files to bundle and send to the browser. In contrast, the render tree is created at runtime by React as it executes JSX tags and builds the component hierarchy. The two trees do not always match. A component can render children that it never imported directly, as Lecture 7 demonstrates when passing nested JSX via the children prop. Furthermore, conditional rendering can alter branches of the render tree dynamically while the module dependency tree remains fixed.

Step 3
Finally, we send the topic down to both ends of the tree
<App.jsx>

This step applies the third principle: Data flow: a value travels down the tree, never across it.

We want to show the topic ("Sport") in two places: in the site header ("Latest Sport Articles") and in the newsletter sign-up ("Get the Sport articles by email."). These two components (SiteHeader and NewsletterBox) sit at opposite ends of the render tree. If we declared const topic = 'Sport'; inside SiteHeader, NewsletterBox could never access it because components cannot read across sibling branches.

What happens if topic stays inside SiteHeader? React tries to render NewsletterBox, finds that topic is not defined, attempts the render pass once more (logging each component message twice), throws ReferenceError: topic is not defined and the page goes blank.

Because the topic is a fixed value that the entire page needs and that does not change between instances, we declare it at the top level of App.jsx, on line 1, outside of every component. Adding line 1 pushes every subsequent line down by one, bringing the file to 72 lines.

Line 1 declares the topic constant:

App.jsx
1const topic = 'Sport';
File-level constant

In SiteHeader, line 10 reads {topic} in the site header:

App.jsx
10 <h1>Latest {topic} Articles</h1>
Reads file scope

In NewsletterBox, line 52 reads {topic} in the sign-up paragraph:

App.jsx
52 return <p>Get the {topic} articles by email.</p>;
Reads file scope

Save the file. The page displays "Latest Sport Articles" in the site header and "Get the Sport articles by email." in the footer. Both ends of the tree successfully read the value. In Lecture 6, when the topic changes dynamically between pages, it will originate in App and travel downward as a prop.

Component Summary

main

The entry file names <App /> as the root of the tree. No step changed it.

App

Top-level constant topic sits at line 1. App renders SiteHeader (with MainMenu), ArticleList (with ArticleCard and PopularArticles), and SiteFooter (with NewsletterBox).

A developer who views App.jsx as a flat list of functions expects the file order to determine how elements appear and assumes components in the same file can freely share variables. In React 19, the three steps followed the thread: the render tree determined the execution order regardless of file layout, component boundaries divided the page by responsibility rather than arbitrary tags, and the shared topic reached both ends of the tree by starting above them. Each component remains focused on its single job, ready to receive dynamic props in Lecture 6.

Where you will meet this

  1. Designing layout trees: drawing boxes on a designer's mockup to establish parent-child boundaries before writing any component code.
  2. Page frame architecture: structuring a global app shell containing a Header, Sidebar, ContentArea, and Footer wrapped around page views.
  3. User profile dashboards: sharing the signed-in user's name across navigation bars, welcome banners, and activity cards without horizontal coupling.
  4. DevTools component inspection: using the Components tab in React Developer Tools to navigate the live render tree and track component hierarchies.
  5. DOM selection debugging: diagnosing and fixing bugs where a component attempts to read sibling state using document.getElementById during render.

For the interview

The Interview Question: How does React organize nested components into a tree, and why does hierarchy dictate data flow?

1. The Hidden Signal

The interviewer wants to hear that you distinguish between code file layout and the runtime render tree, and that you understand why React enforces unidirectional downward data flow. A junior candidate assumes components execute in file order or that functions in the same file can share local state. A senior engineer explains that JSX tags build a hierarchical render tree with App at the root, and that React traverses this tree depth-first.

2. The Classic Trap

The classic trap is believing that nesting a component tag inside JSX creates a lexical JavaScript closure. Writing <ArticleCard /> inside App does not give ArticleCard access to App's local variables; both functions sit at file scope. A second trap is reaching across sibling components using document.getElementById during render. Because React evaluates component functions before committing elements to the DOM, querying uncommitted elements returns null and crashes execution.

3. What is Actually Going On

React builds a tree of component instances based on JSX nesting. React calls the root component first and traverses down each branch, evaluating every child and descendant leaf before moving to the next sibling branch. Because each component is a separate top-level function, its scope is isolated. A component can only access its own local variables, file-level constants, or values passed explicitly from above. Therefore, any data needed by multiple components must originate in their closest common ancestor and flow downward.

4. Where It Gets Tricky

Does the order of component definitions in a file affect the render order?

No. The file order is completely irrelevant to the render sequence. React begins execution at the root component declared in main.jsx and calls child components strictly according to the JSX tree hierarchy.

If a component tag is written twice in JSX, is it one node or two?

It creates two distinct nodes in the render tree. React treats each JSX tag invocation as an independent component instance with its own execution and lifecycle, even though both share the same function definition.

Why can a nested JavaScript function read outer variables, but a child component in JSX cannot?

A nested function physically sits inside the outer function's body, creating a lexical closure. In contrast, React components are defined as separate top-level functions. Writing <Child /> in JSX merely creates a React element descriptor; it does not place Child's code inside the parent's function scope.

Where must a value live if two sibling components need to display it?

It must live above both of them: either as a file-level constant if it never changes, or in their closest common parent component, passed downward to each sibling via props (Lecture 6) or lifted state (Lecture 23).

Glossary

  • Render tree: The runtime hierarchy of React components created by nested component tags in JSX, starting from the root component.
  • Root component: The top-level component in the render tree that React mounts directly into the browser page container.
  • Parent and child components: A relationship where a parent component's return markup includes the tag of a child component.
  • Sibling components: Components that share the same immediate parent component in the render tree.
  • Top-level and leaf components: Top-level components sit near the root of the tree, while leaf components sit at the tips of branches and render only native HTML tags.
  • Separation of concerns: The design principle of organizing code so that each component encapsulates exactly one distinct responsibility.
  • Scope: The physical region of JavaScript code where a declared variable can be accessed.
  • ReferenceError: A JavaScript runtime error thrown when code attempts to access a variable name that has not been declared in the current scope.

Beyond the basics

  • Understanding Your UI as a Tree: How React models component relationships and renders the UI tree (see react.dev/learn/understanding-your-ui-as-a-tree).
  • Thinking in React: Step 1: Breaking the user interface into a component hierarchy (see react.dev/learn/thinking-in-react).
  • Your First Component: Nesting components properly and organizing component files (see react.dev/learn/your-first-component).
  • Passing Props to a Component: How values travel down the component tree to configure child components (see react.dev/learn/passing-props-to-a-component).

Summary

The page is a tree of components

❒ The render tree: each component's markup names its children

➔ ALWAYS determine component hierarchy by reading JSX nesting rather than the order of functions in the file.

➔ NEVER assume components execute in file order; React calls them from the root down, completing one branch before the next.

❒ Component boundaries: one branch of the tree for each part of the page with its own job

➔ ALWAYS extract a separate component for each distinct responsibility, even if used only once.

➔ NEVER create components for every individual HTML tag; keep subordinate markup inside its parent until it develops its own job.

❒ Data flow: a value travels down the tree, never across it

➔ ALWAYS declare shared values above all components that need them and pass them downward.

➔ NEVER attempt to read a parent's local variable, reach across to a sibling, or query uncommitted DOM elements.

The tree grows by nesting, is cut by job, and carries values down.

DO THIS: compose components in a hierarchy with shared values defined above them

1const topic = 'Sport';
2function SiteHeader() {
3 return <header><h1>Latest {topic} Articles</h1></header>;
4}
5function ArticleCard() {
6 return <article><p>{topic} articles</p></article>;
7}
8export default function App() {
9 return (
10 <>
11 <SiteHeader />
12 <ArticleCard />
13 </>
14 );
15}

DO NOT DO THIS: reach across components or declare variables inside parent functions

code.txt
1function ArticleCard() {
2 return <article><p>{topic} articles</p></article>;
3}
4export default function App() {
5 const topic = 'Sport';
6 return (
7 <>
8 <header><h1>Latest Articles</h1></header>
9 <ArticleCard />
10 </>
11 );
12}

JSX branches depth-first
Where it is cutEither one massive function
or a component per tag		One component per distinct job;

Lecture 6: Passing Data with Props and the Read-Only Contract

Interview Question

CORE

How do you pass data into a component, and why can a component never change its own props?

Imagine this scenario:

  1. The article list needs three articles, so you write <ArticleCard /> three times.
  2. You save, and the page displays the exact same hardcoded article title three times.
  3. How does each copy of a component receive its own title, author, and reading time?

One component displays many different articles

An article list displays the same card frame again and again: the same layout, but a different title, a different author, and a different reading time. In Lecture 5, ArticleCard held its title inside its own markup, so every copy showed the same text. Declaring a constant at the top of the file does not solve this either: a file-level variable gives every copy the exact same value. In Lecture 5, we saw that a value that belongs to the page starts in a parent component and travels down the tree. So every React developer meets the same question: how does each copy of a component receive its own distinct values?

The answer is one idea, and this chapter follows it from the first question to the last: props are a component's arguments: the parent writes them on the tag, and the component reads them as one object. The chapter follows the life of one prop: written on the tag, read in the function, missing from the tag, and kept unchanged.

This lesson answers four questions:

  • My three ArticleCards show the same story. How do I give each its own headline?
  • How do I get title out of the props?
  • What if a parent leaves out a prop?
  • Can the card change its own title, to show it in capitals?

The questions stand on what earlier lessons established:

  • Lecture 3 (JSX syntax): An object keeps values under names, called its properties. The build turns each JSX tag into a call, and npm run build makes the production files for the published site.
  • Lecture 4 (JavaScript expressions in JSX with curly braces): Quotes pass text strings, and curly braces pass a JavaScript value, such as a number or an object literal. In React rendering, null and undefined display nothing, while an object cannot be shown as text: React stops with "Objects are not valid as a React child".
  • Lecture 5 (UI as a tree and component hierarchy): Components form a render tree with App at the root. A component sees only its own variables, so a shared value needed by several components starts above them in the tree and travels downward.

A function's parameters receive the values of a call

A JavaScript function lists variable names inside its parentheses: its parameters. When other code calls the function, the values supplied in that call are its arguments, and each parameter takes the argument provided in its matching position.

Plain JavaScript: parameters and arguments
1function headline(title, readTime) {
2 return title + ', ' + readTime + ' min read';
Formats parameters
3}
4headline('Rail Strike Ends', 5);
Arguments for first call
5headline('New Park Opens Today', 2);
Arguments for second call

In this function, title and readTime are parameters. In the first call, the string 'Rail Strike Ends' and the number 5 are arguments. The second call passes different arguments to produce a different result.

Destructuring takes properties out of an object by name

Reading several properties from an object often takes multiple lines of repetitive assignments, such as const title = article.title; JavaScript destructuring extracts properties in a single statement: variable names placed inside curly braces on the left side of an assignment extract the matching property names from the object on the right side. If an extracted property does not exist on the object, it receives undefined, unless a default value follows the variable name after an equals sign.

Plain JavaScript: destructuring with a default
1const article = { title: 'Rail Strike Ends', readTime: 5 };
2const { title, readTime, topic = 'News' } = article;
Unpacks properties
3console.log(title, readTime, topic);
Logs unpacked values

The curly braces on the left extract title and readTime directly from the object. Because topic is absent on article, it takes the default value 'News'. The exact same destructuring syntax works inside a function's parameter list, unpacking an incoming argument object directly.

Two operators fall back to a default value

JavaScript provides two operators to supply fallback values when a variable might be empty: logical OR (||) and nullish coalescing (??).

Plain JavaScript: fallbacks with OR and nullish coalescing
1const missingTime = undefined;
2const zeroTime = 0;
3console.log(missingTime ?? 3);
3: nullish coalescing fills fallback
4console.log(zeroTime || 3);
5console.log(zeroTime ?? 3);
0: nullish coalescing preserves valid 0

The logical OR operator (a || b) returns b whenever a is falsy: 0, an empty string "", null, false, and undefined all trigger the fallback. The nullish coalescing operator (a ?? b) returns b only when a is strictly null or undefined. Because 0 is a valid number of minutes for a short update, 0 ?? 3 preserves 0, whereas 0 || 3 mistakenly replaces it with 3.

Some objects cannot be changed

JavaScript strings provide built-in methods to transform text. Calling 'Rail Strike Ends'.toUpperCase() returns a brand-new uppercase string 'RAIL STRIKE ENDS' while leaving the original string completely unchanged.

Plain JavaScript: frozen objects and string methods
1const text = 'Rail Strike Ends';
2const upper = text.toUpperCase();
Returns new string without modifying text
3const settings = Object.freeze({ readTime: 3 });
4settings.readTime = 5;
Throws TypeError in strict mode / modules

JavaScript can lock an object using Object.freeze(). Once an object is frozen, modifying or reassigning its properties is forbidden. In JavaScript ES modules, which all modern React files are, attempting to mutate a frozen property throws a TypeError. However, this freeze is shallow: if an object contains nested objects or arrays, those inner structures remain mutable.

A Vite application runs two distinct environments. The development server runs a development build with extra runtime checks to catch bugs early. The production command npm run build generates a production build that omits these extra checks so the application runs as fast and lean as possible in production.

The project for this lesson

The code runs in the same project as Lectures 2 to 5. Every component lives in App.jsx, and main.jsx renders App. As in Lecture 2, keeping all components in one file is a choice for learning so that you see every component at once. A real application gives each main component its own file, and Lecture 8 shows how to split components using import and export.

ARCHITECTURAL RESPONSIBILITY

src/

Contains component modules
main.jsx

Mounts App as the root of the render tree
App.jsx
child
Every component for this lesson, in one file until Lecture 8

Principles of React: Props Are a Component's Arguments

Everything in this lesson comes down to one idea: props are a component's arguments, written by the parent and read by the component as one object.

First, props, which means the attributes on a component's tag arrive as one object, its only argument: each card gets its own headline because each tag carries its own.

Second, destructuring, which means the component names the props it reads, inside curly braces in its parameter list: without the braces, the whole object lands in the first name.

Third, default values, which means the component names a fallback for a prop the tag leaves out: the fallback fills a missing prop, but not a null and not a zero.

Fourth, read-only props, which means the component reads its props and never changes them: to show a value differently, it makes a new variable.

QUESTION 1

Three tags carry three stories, and the card ignores them

A developer wants to render three distinct article cards on the page. In App.jsx, App renders three <ArticleCard /> tags, giving each tag its own title attribute and readTime attribute. In ArticleCard, the developer accepts props, logs it to the Console panel, but continues to return fixed markup:

App.jsx
1function ArticleCard(props) {
2 console.log('ArticleCard props:', props);
Logs input props object
3 return <h2>City Library Extends Its Hours</h2>;
4}

In App, three tags specify three different headlines and reading times:

5export default function App() {
6 return (
7 <main>
8 <ArticleCard
9 title="City Library Extends Its Hours"
10 readTime={3}
11 />
First card attributes

The remaining two tags complete the list:

12 <ArticleCard title="Rail Strike Ends" readTime={5} />
13 <ArticleCard
14 title="New Park Opens Today"
15 readTime={2}
16 />
Third card
17 </main>
18 );
19}

The browser page displays the exact same heading "City Library Extends Its Hours" three times with zero errors or warnings. But when opening the Console panel, three different JavaScript objects appear: { title: 'City Library Extends Its Hours', readTime: 3 } { title: 'Rail Strike Ends', readTime: 5 } and { title: 'New Park Opens Today', readTime: 2 }

My three ArticleCards show the same story. How do I give each its own headline?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. ArticleCard ignores its input argument and renders fixed markup.

React collects every attribute written on a component tag into a single JavaScript object, called props, and passes that object as the single argument to the component function. Writing attributes on a tag does not alter the DOM on its own; it merely delivers the data to the component. Because ArticleCard never read from its props argument, it rendered the same hardcoded text on every call.

The fix is to read the properties from the props object inside JSX curly braces: props.title and props.readTime. Once ArticleCard reads from props, each card displays its own title and reading time.

App.jsx
1function ArticleCard(props) {
2 return (
3 <article>
4 <h2>{props.title}</h2>
5 <p>{props.readTime} min read</p>
Reads props object
6 </article>
7 );
8}

Passing values follows the rules established in Lecture 4: quotes pass text strings, while curly braces pass dynamic JavaScript expressions. If you write readTime="5", the value arrives as the string "5", and {props.readTime + 1} produces "51 min read". Writing readTime={5} delivers the actual number 5, so {props.readTime + 1} calculates 6. Props can carry any JavaScript value: numbers, booleans, arrays, or objects like writer={{ name: 'Samantha Robinson', city: 'Denver' }} Content written between opening and closing tags arrives through a specialized prop named children, which Lecture 7 explores.

How React collects tag attributes into props objects
TAG ON CALL SITE                       PROPS OBJECT PASSED TO COMPONENT
<ArticleCard title="News" readTime={3} />  -->  { title: 'News', readTime: 3 }
<ArticleCard title="Park" readTime={2} />  -->  { title: 'Park', readTime: 2 }
PRINCIPLE 1

Props: the attributes on a component's tag arrive as one object, its only argument

props the single object React passes to a component holding all tag attributes

We give each copy of a component its own values by writing them as attributes on its tag; React collects them into one object, the props, and passes it as the component's only argument.

We might expect attributes written on a component tag to appear automatically on the page. But a component tag is a function call descriptor, not an HTML element. React gathers every attribute written on the tag into a single props object and passes that object as the component function's only argument. A component displays nothing from its tag until its function body explicitly reads from that object. Quotes pass literal text strings, while curly braces pass evaluated JavaScript values such as numbers, arrays, and objects.

We should do this:
function ContactCard(props) {
return <p>{props.name}, {props.city}</p>;
reads props from tag
}
<ContactCard name="John Hall" city="Austin" />;
passes attributes
We should not do this:
function ContactCard(props) {
return <p>John Hall, Austin</p>;
hardcoded fixed values
}
<ContactCard name="Mary Jones" city="Denver" />;
tag values ignored
QUESTION 2

Two names in the parentheses crash the page

Typing props. before every variable feels verbose. A developer with standard JavaScript habits decides to list parameters individually in the component definition:

App.jsx
1function ArticleCard(title, readTime) {
2 return (
3 <article>
4 <h2>{title}</h2>
Crashes: object is not valid child
5 <p>{readTime} min read</p>
6 </article>
7 );
8}

Save the file. The browser screen immediately goes blank, and the Console panel logs a fatal error: Uncaught Error: Objects are not valid as a React child (found: object with keys {title, readTime})

How do I get title out of the props?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. React passes all props inside a single object rather than separate arguments.

In plain JavaScript, functions often accept multiple arguments. But React component functions always receive exactly one argument: the props object. When ArticleCard(title, readTime) declares two parameters, JavaScript assigns the first argument (the entire props object { title: '...', readTime: 5 }) to title. The second parameter readTime receives undefined. When React attempts to render {title} inside <h2>, it encounters a plain JavaScript object. As Lecture 4 demonstrated, React forbids rendering objects directly as text children to prevent accidental data corruption, and the application crashes.

The fix is parameter destructuring: wrapping the parameter names in curly braces function ArticleCard({ title, readTime }) The curly braces instruct JavaScript to unpack the properties title and readTime directly from the single incoming props object into local variables.

App.jsx
1function ArticleCard({ title, readTime }) {
2 return (
3 <article>
4 <h2>{title}</h2>
5 <p>{readTime} min read</p>
Unpacked from props
6 </article>
7 );
8}

The destructured parameter names must match the attribute names written on the tag. If a tag writes title="Rail Strike Ends" but the component destructures { headline }, the variable headline evaluates to undefined, and the heading renders completely blank without an error. Destructuring props in the parameter list is the standard idiom in modern React applications.

PRINCIPLE 2

Destructuring: the component names the props it reads, inside curly braces in its parameter list

destructuring unpacking properties from an object directly into named variables

We read props by naming them inside curly braces in the parameter list, ({ title, readTime }), with the same names the tag uses.

We might expect a component to accept several arguments like a standard JavaScript function. But React always passes exactly one argument: the props object. If we declare parameters without curly braces, the first parameter absorbs the entire object, and subsequent parameters become undefined. When the component attempts to render that first parameter, React crashes because objects cannot be rendered directly as text. We use destructuring by wrapping parameter names in curly braces ({ title, readTime }), extracting values by name to match the tag attributes.

We should do this:
function ContactCard({ name, city }) {
destructures props by name
return <p>{name}, {city}</p>;
displays each unpacked value
}
We should not do this:
function ContactCard(name, city) {
receives entire object in name
return <p>{name}</p>;
crashes: object is not valid React child
}
QUESTION 3

A prop the tag leaves out leaves a hole

A developer renders <ArticleCard title="Rail Strike Ends" /> omitting the readTime attribute. Remembering an older tutorial, the developer attaches a defaultProps property to ArticleCard to provide a fallback:

App.jsx
1function ArticleCard({ title, readTime }) {
2 return <p>{title}: {readTime} min read</p>;
Shows " min read"
3}
4ArticleCard.defaultProps = { readTime: 3 };
Ignored in React 19

App renders the card without a reading time:

5export default function App() {
6 return <ArticleCard title="Rail Strike Ends" />;
ReadTime omitted
7}

The browser displays "Rail Strike Ends: min read" with an empty hole where the number should be. React 19 displays no warning in the console, completely ignoring the defaultProps assignment.

What if a parent leaves out a prop?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. An omitted prop evaluates to undefined, which renders as empty space.

When a parent component omits an attribute from a JSX tag, that property is absent from the props object, so destructuring assigns it undefined. As Lecture 4 showed, React renders undefined as empty text. Furthermore, React 19 officially removed support for defaultProps on function components, rendering older tutorial patterns useless.

The fix is to assign a default value directly inside the destructuring braces using the equals sign: function ArticleCard({ title, readTime = 3 }) If the parent tag omits readTime or explicitly passes readTime={undefined}, JavaScript fills the fallback value 3.

App.jsx
1function ArticleCard({ title, readTime = 3 }) {
2 return (
3 <article>
4 <h2>{title}</h2>
5 <p>{readTime} min read</p>
Defaults to 3 when omitted
6 </article>
7 );
8}

A default value activates only when the prop is undefined or omitted. If a parent passes readTime={null}, the value is explicitly defined as null, so the default 3 does not trigger, and the card renders empty text. If a parent passes readTime={0}, 0 is a valid number, so the card renders "0 min read". Avoid using legacy logical OR fallbacks like readTime || 3 in component bodies, because 0 || 3 mistakenly replaces a valid zero with 3. Use default values whenever a prop has a natural, predictable fallback.

Fallback behavior for missing and defined props
PROP WRITTEN ON TAG         VALUE OF readTime    readTime = 3 RENDERS
(omitted attribute)         undefined            3 min read (default used)
readTime={undefined}        undefined            3 min read (default used)
readTime={null}             null                   min read (null shows nothing)
readTime={0}                0                    0 min read (zero preserved)
PRINCIPLE 3

Default values: the component names a fallback for a prop the tag leaves out

default value a fallback assigned when an attribute is missing or undefined

When a component has a sensible fallback, we write it beside the prop's name, readTime = 3, and we remember that it fills only a missing or undefined prop, never null or 0.

When a tag omits an attribute, the destructured prop evaluates to undefined, producing empty gaps in the rendered text. React 19 ignores legacy defaultProps declarations on function components. When a prop has a sensible fallback, assign a default value directly inside the parameter destructuring braces using =. The fallback activates only when the prop is omitted or explicitly passed as undefined. Real values like null or 0 are preserved.

We should do this:
function ContactCard({ name, phone = 'not listed' }) {
fallback
return <p>{name}: {phone}</p>;
shows fallback when omitted
}
We should not do this:
function ContactCard({ name, phone }) {
no fallback provided
return <p>{name}: {phone}</p>;
leaves empty text when omitted
}
QUESTION 4

Changing a prop crashes in development and ships in production

A designer requests that every article title appear in capital letters. A developer decides to transform the title in place by assigning to props.title:

App.jsx
1function ArticleCard(props) {
2 props.title = props.title.toUpperCase();
Throws TypeError in dev
3 return <h2>{props.title}</h2>;
4}

In the local development server, the page goes blank, and the Console panel throws TypeError: Cannot assign to read only property 'title' of object '#<Object>' But when the developer runs npm run build and tests the production build with npm run preview, the error disappears, and the headlines display in uppercase letters.

Can the card change its own title, to show it in capitals?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. React freezes the props object in development, and mutating props violates component purity.

Props belong to the parent component that created them. A child component is a pure function that must treat its incoming arguments as read-only. To catch accidental mutations during development, React runs Object.freeze() on every props object. Modifying a frozen object in an ES module triggers a TypeError. However, to maximize speed in production, React omits Object.freeze(). The mutation silently succeeds in production, meaning an application that passed code review can ship with hidden state corruption.

The danger is worse with object props. Because React's development freeze is shallow, nested objects are never frozen. If ArticleCard receives a writer object and executes writer.name = writer.name.toUpperCase() neither development nor production throws an error. But this mutates the shared object in browser memory, unexpectedly altering the author name across every other component on the page that references that same object, such as an AuthorBox.

App.jsx
1function ArticleCard({ writer }) {
2 writer.name = writer.name.toUpperCase();
Shallow mutation succeeds
3 return <h2>By {writer.name}</h2>;
4}

The fix is to derive a new local variable during render: const headline = title.toUpperCase()

App.jsx
1function ArticleCard({ title }) {
2 const headline = title.toUpperCase();
Derives local uppercase value
3 return <h2>{headline}</h2>;
Leaves props object untouched
4}

Deriving a local variable leaves the incoming props completely untouched. As Lecture 12 explains in detail, React components must remain pure, never mutating any inputs during rendering. If a displayed value must change dynamically over time in response to user actions, the parent component must pass new props, or the component must manage local state, which Lecture 14 introduces. Choosing which elements to render based on props using conditionals is covered in Lecture 10.

Shallow freeze leaves nested objects mutable
props object (FROZEN by React in dev)
+------------------------------------+
| title: "New Park Opens Today"      |
| writer: [Ref: Object in memory] ---+--> writer object (NOT FROZEN)
+------------------------------------+    +----------------------------+
                                          | name: "Samantha Robinson"  |
                                          +----------------------------+
                                                    ^
                                          AuthorBox | also points here
PRINCIPLE 4

Read-only props: the component reads its props and never changes them

read-only an object whose properties cannot be modified after creation

We never change a prop or an object inside one; to show a value differently, we make a new variable, const headline = title.toUpperCase(), and a value that must change comes from the parent.

We might expect to modify a component's props like any ordinary JavaScript object. But props belong to the parent that declared them. In development, React freezes the props object, making it read-only and throwing a TypeError on assignment. Production builds skip this freeze for speed, allowing bugs to ship silently. The freeze is also shallow, so mutating an object inside a prop corrupts data across every component sharing that reference. To format a value differently, derive a new local variable.

We should do this:
function ContactCard({ name }) {
const upper = name.toUpperCase();
derives new local variable
return <p>{upper}</p>;
leaves original props untouched
}
We should not do this:
function ContactCard(props) {
props.name = props.name.toUpperCase();
throws TypeError in dev
return <p>{props.name}</p>;
}

⚡ IN THE WILD

Are props the same as HTML attributes? On a built-in HTML tag like <img src="/photo.jpg" alt="Site logo" /> the attributes look identical to props. We might wonder if React treats them the same way. However, there is a fundamental difference. On built-in HTML elements, React only accepts the specific attributes defined by the HTML standard and applies them directly to the browser DOM node. On our own custom components, we can invent any prop names we want. React does not send custom props to the DOM; it simply bundles all attributes into a single props object and hands it to our component function. Our component decides what to do with each value. Props can carry any JavaScript value: text strings, numbers, objects, arrays, and even functions, which Lecture 13 uses to handle user clicks.

App

A developer coming from plain JavaScript expects functions to accept multiple positional arguments and assumes input objects can be modified freely. In React 19, the four steps demonstrated the unidirectional props contract: attributes written on tags arrived as a single props object, parameter destructuring extracted values cleanly by name, default values filled omitted properties without hiding zeros, and derived local variables formatted output while preserving props immutability.

Where you will meet this

  1. Product catalog grids: passing unique item titles, prices, and stock counts down to reusable product card components.
  2. Configurable design system buttons: providing default values for button variants (variant = 'primary') and sizes (size = 'medium').
  3. User profile badges: receiving user data objects and extracting display names and avatars without mutating the cached user object.
  4. Data table cells: formatting raw timestamps into localized date strings inside cell components using derived variables.
  5. Upgrading legacy codebases: removing obsolete React 18 defaultProps declarations and migrating to standard JavaScript destructuring defaults.

For the interview

The Interview Question: How do you pass data into a component, and why can a component never change its own props?

1. The Hidden Signal

The interviewer is probing your understanding of unidirectional data flow and functional purity. A junior candidate treats props merely as HTML attributes and assumes a component can update its own props when its data changes. A senior engineer explains that props represent immutable input snapshots owned exclusively by the parent component. They articulate that maintaining props as read-only objects is essential for pure render contracts, predictable component re-rendering, and preventing cross-tree state corruption.

2. The Classic Trap

The classic trap is believing that props can be modified locally like ordinary JavaScript object arguments. Candidates often propose mutating a prop in place to format text or toggle a value. In development, React catches this by freezing the props object, triggering a fatal TypeError. However, because production builds omit Object.freeze() for performance, direct mutation appears to work in production while corrupting shared object references. Another trap is confusing missing props with null: a default value = fallback triggers only on undefined, leaving null values unchanged.

3. What is Actually Going On

When React evaluates JSX, it compiles element attributes into a plain JavaScript object and passes it as the first argument to the child component function. In development, React executes Object.freeze() on this props object. Because the freeze is shallow, nested objects remain technically mutable, but mutating them breaks component purity. When a component needs to display data differently, it derives a new local variable. When data must actually change over time, the change must be triggered in the parent via state, flowing downward as fresh props on the next render pass.

4. Where It Gets Tricky

Why does function Card(title, readTime) fail to receive two arguments?

React components always receive exactly one argument: the props object. In this definition, JavaScript binds the entire props object { title: '...', readTime: 5 } to the parameter title, while readTime remains undefined. Attempting to render {title} inside JSX crashes because React cannot render objects as text children.

Does a destructuring default value replace a null prop?

No. JavaScript destructuring default values ({ readTime = 3 }) trigger strictly when the incoming property is undefined or omitted entirely. If a parent explicitly passes readTime={null}, null is a defined value, so the default does not activate and readTime remains null.

Why does mutating props.title throw an error in development but succeed in production?

In development, React calls Object.freeze(props) to catch impure side effects early. In production, React skips Object.freeze() to maximize rendering performance. In an ES module, modifying a frozen object throws a TypeError. In production, the assignment succeeds silently, masking bugs that corrupt application state.

What happens when a child component mutates a nested object prop?

Because Object.freeze() is shallow, nested objects are not frozen even in development. If a child modifies user.name = 'New Name', the change mutates the underlying object in shared memory. Every other component in the tree that reads from that same user reference will display the mutated data, causing cross-tree state drift.

Glossary

  • Props: The single, read-only JavaScript object passed by React to a component function containing all attributes declared on its JSX tag.
  • Parameter and argument: Parameters are variable names declared in a function signature; arguments are the concrete values passed during an invocation.
  • Destructuring: A JavaScript syntax that unpacks properties from an object directly into distinct, named local variables.
  • Default value: A fallback value assigned during destructuring that activates only when a property is omitted or equals undefined.
  • Nullish coalescing: The JavaScript operator ?? that returns its right-hand operand only when its left-hand operand is null or undefined.
  • Frozen object: A JavaScript object locked by Object.freeze() whose properties cannot be added, removed, or reassigned.
  • TypeError: A standard JavaScript runtime error thrown when an operation cannot be performed, such as mutating a frozen property in strict mode.
  • Development and production builds: Development builds include runtime sanity checks like object freezing; production builds omit them for speed.

Beyond the basics

  • Passing Props to a Component: How to pass, read, and forward props, specify defaults, and understand how props change over time (see react.dev/learn/passing-props-to-a-component).
  • Components and Hooks must be pure: The immutability contract of props and state and why mutating inputs causes rendering bugs (see react.dev/reference/rules/components-and-hooks-must-be-pure).
  • createElement and frozen props: The official React API specification documenting why the props object is frozen in development mode (see react.dev/reference/react/createElement).
  • React 19 upgrade guide: The official announcement detailing the removal of propTypes and defaultProps on function components (see react.dev/blog/2024/04/25/react-19-upgrade-guide).

Summary

Props are a component's arguments

❒ Props: the attributes on a component's tag arrive as one object, its only argument

➔ ALWAYS pass data to child components by writing descriptive attributes on their JSX tags.

➔ NEVER assume writing attributes on a JSX tag updates the screen automatically; the child component must explicitly read and render those values.

❒ Destructuring: the component names the props it reads, inside curly braces in its parameter list

➔ ALWAYS wrap prop parameter names in curly braces ({ title, readTime }) to unpack the incoming props object directly.

➔ NEVER list multiple unbracketed parameters (title, readTime) in a component signature; the entire props object collapses into the first name.

❒ Default values: the component names a fallback for a prop the tag leaves out

➔ IF a prop has a natural fallback THEN assign a default value beside the prop name ({ readTime = 3 }) during destructuring.

➔ NEVER rely on legacy defaultProps in React 19, and never use || when zero is a valid numeric prop value.

❒ Read-only props: the component reads its props and never changes them

➔ ALWAYS compute derived values using new local variables const headline = title.toUpperCase() during rendering.

➔ NEVER assign to props.title or mutate nested object props; modifying props violates component purity and causes cross-tree corruption.

Written on the tag, read by name, filled when missing, and never changed.

DO THIS: read props by destructuring, assign defaults, and derive new values

code.txt
1function ArticleCard({ title, readTime = 3 }) {
2 const headline = title.toUpperCase();
3 return (
4 <article>
5 <h2>{headline}</h2>
6 <p>{readTime} min read</p>
7 </article>
8 );
9}
10export default function App() {
11 return <ArticleCard title="Rail Strike Ends" />;
12}

DO NOT DO THIS: mutate props or rely on separate function parameters

code.txt
1function ArticleCard(title, readTime) {
2 title = title.toUpperCase();
3 return (
4 <article>
5 <h2>{title}</h2>
6 <p>{readTime} min read</p>
7 </article>
8 );
9}
10export default function App() {
11 return <ArticleCard title="Rail Strike Ends" />;
12}

Lecture 7: Container Composition with Children and Prop Spreading

Interview Question

CORE

How do the children prop, spread attributes, and default values work?

Imagine this scenario:

  1. The article list shows three kinds of article: one with text, one with a photo, and one with a quote.
  2. With one prop per piece, the card grows twenty specialized props and breaks whenever content changes.
  3. How does one card component show different content each time?

One card design, different content each time

Every website shows the same kind of card many times. A shop shows each product in the same frame, and an article site shows each story in the same box. The design stays the same; only the content changes. So every React developer meets the same question: how does one card component show different content each time?

React gives two answers. The first one you know from Lecture 6: the card takes a prop and places the value in its own markup.

Option 1: a prop
1<ContentCard name="John Hall" />
Passes data through an attribute

Inside ContentCard, the code is <p>My name is {name}</p> The card decides what the content looks like, and the caller only gives the value. This fits when every use has the same shape, such as a price tag that always shows a name and a price.

The second answer is to write the content between the card's tags.

Option 2: content between the tags
1<ContentCard>
2 <p>My name is John Hall</p>
Content placed between tags
3</ContentCard>

Look at what sits between <ContentCard> and </ContentCard>: the whole element <p>My name is John Hall</p> React takes everything written between the opening tag and the closing tag and hands it to the card as a prop. With a prop from Lecture 6, the information sits in an attribute whose name we choose; here it sits between the tags, and the prop's name is always children. Inside the card, the code is just {children}. Here the caller writes the content, and the card only gives the design around it.

In this chapter, we write one React component that keeps the design the same and lets each article decide its own content. In React, this approach is enabled by a prop named children. We will see it with one child, with several, and with none, then when to keep a prop beside it, and how the card passes on the attributes it does not use.

Two ways to show different content in one card

(1) Show different content with props (Lecture 6): the caller passes values in attributes whose names we choose, and the card decides how they look.

(2) Show different content with children (this chapter): the caller writes the content between the card's tags, and the card decides only the design around it.

The idea this chapter follows from the first question to the last: a component can be a frame the caller fills: what the caller writes between its tags arrives as children, and the frame decides where it goes. The chapter follows one tag from the inside out: the content between the tags, the choice between content and props, and the attributes on the tag.

This lesson answers three questions:

  • I put a headline between <CardContainer> and </CardContainer>. Where does it go?
  • One story has a photo, another a quote, another only text. Do I add a prop for each?
  • Callers want a className and an aria-label on the card. Do I list each one?

The questions stand on what earlier lessons established:

  • Lecture 3 (JSX syntax): Each tag becomes a call, and the content inside a tag becomes its children in the object, as the browser inspect tools reveal. className is JSX's name for class, and aria-* and data-* attributes keep their hyphens.
  • Lecture 4 (JavaScript expressions in JSX with curly braces): In React rendering, undefined displays nothing, and the plus operator (+) joins strings together.
  • Lecture 5 (UI as a tree and component hierarchy): Nesting component tags creates the component render tree, with App at the root.
  • Lecture 6 (Passing data with props and the read-only contract): The attributes on a component's tag arrive as one object, the props, read by destructuring in the parameter list. A default value, className = '', fills a prop that is missing or undefined. Props are read-only and never mutated.

An array keeps several values in order

An array in JavaScript holds multiple values in an ordered sequence, enclosed in square brackets: ['Rail Strike Ends', 'New Park Opens Today'] Each item occupies a numeric index, starting at index 0.

Plain JavaScript: an array of items
1const articles = ['Rail Strike Ends', 'New Park Opens Today'];
2console.log(articles[0]);
'Rail Strike Ends': first item at index 0
3console.log(articles.length);
2: total number of items

When a caller nests two or more elements between component tags, React groups those elements into an array and hands that array to the component as children. Lecture 11 shows how to transform arrays of dynamic data into elements using .map().

Three dots collect the rest and spread it out

The three-dot syntax (...) performs two distinct jobs in modern JavaScript depending on where it appears.

Plain JavaScript: rest syntax
1const story = { title: 'Rail Strike Ends', id: 'top', section: 'News' };
2const { title, ...rest } = story;
Unpacks title and collects remaining
3console.log(rest);
{ id: 'top', section: 'News' }

When used on the left side of an assignment or inside a function's parameter destructuring list, ...rest is called rest syntax. It extracts the named properties and gathers all remaining properties into a new object. When placed on a JSX tag, {...rest} is called spread syntax. It takes every property from that object and applies it as an attribute on the JSX element.

The project for this lesson

The code runs in the same small project as Lectures 2 to 6. Every component lives in App.jsx, and main.jsx renders App. As in Lecture 2, keeping all components in one file is a choice for learning so that you see every component at once. A real application gives each main component its own file, and Lecture 8 shows how to split components using import and export. The photo card loads /images/park.jpg, stored in the public folder.

Principles of React: A Component Is a Frame the Caller Fills

Everything in this lesson comes down to one idea: a component can be a frame that the caller fills.

First, the children prop, which means the content between a component's tags arrives as one prop: the frame shows it wherever it writes children in braces, and nowhere if it forgets.

Second, composition, which means children when the caller decides the content, props when the frame decides its shape: the body of a story goes between the tags, and its title stays a prop.

Third, prop spreading, which means the attributes the frame does not use pass on to its element: the rest goes on with three dots, the attribute written last wins, and a class both sides set is joined.

QUESTION 1

The card shows nothing of what sits between its tags

A developer builds a container component named CardContainer to wrap article content in a styled card border. In App.jsx, App places a heading <h2>New Park Opens Today</h2> between the opening and closing tags of <CardContainer>:

App.jsx
1function CardContainer(props) {
2 return <article className="card" />;
PROBLEMATIC: empty container
3}

In App, the heading is nested inside the container:

4export default function App() {
5 return (
6 <CardContainer>
7 <h2>New Park Opens Today</h2>
Nested between tags
8 </CardContainer>
9 );
10}

Save the file. The browser displays an empty card box on screen with zero text. Furthermore, if a child component like <AuthorName /> is nested between the tags, its console.log never fires; the child component is never even called.

I put a headline between <CardContainer> and </CardContainer>. Where does it go?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. CardContainer ignores its children prop and renders an empty container.

In native HTML, content placed between <div> tags appears automatically in the browser. But in React, writing <CardContainer> does not render a DOM element directly; it instructs React to call the CardContainer component function. As Lecture 3 demonstrated during JSX compilation, React gathers whatever sits between a component's tags into a property on the props object named children: _jsxDEV(CardContainer, { children: ... })

A container component displays nothing from between its tags until its return markup explicitly renders {children} inside curly braces. Because CardContainer never included {children}, React dropped the nested content entirely, and the nested <h2> was never evaluated.

The fix is to destructure children from props and render {children} inside the <article> tag:

App.jsx
1function CardContainer({ children }) {
2 return (
3 <article className="card">
4 {children}
Renders nested content
5 </article>
6 );
7}

The prop children can take multiple structural shapes depending on what the caller passes: a single element arrives as an element object, multiple sibling elements arrive as an array of elements, plain text arrives as a string, and omitting inner content leaves children as undefined. React handles each shape seamlessly when placed in JSX curly braces {children}. However, calling children.map() directly inside a component crashes with children.map is not a function when a single child element is passed, because a single element is not an array.

The four shapes children can take
CONTENT NESTED BETWEEN TAGS          VALUE OF children IN COMPONENT
<Card><h2>Park</h2></Card>           element object: { type: 'h2', ... }
<Card><h2>Park</h2><p>Text</p></Card> array of 2 elements: [ {..}, {..} ]
<Card>Direct text</Card>             string: "Direct text"
<Card></Card>                        undefined (renders nothing)
PRINCIPLE 1

The children prop: the content between a component's tags arrives as one prop

children the prop React automatically populates with content between component tags

We read what the caller writes between a component's tags as the prop children, and we place {children} where the content belongs; a frame that never writes it drops the content without a warning.

We might expect content placed between a component's opening and closing tags to render automatically like HTML. But a component tag is a function call. React bundles whatever is nested between those tags into a specialized prop named children. A container component displays nothing from between its tags until its function body explicitly renders {children}. If the container omits {children}, all nested elements are dropped silently and never execute.

We should do this:
function Panel({ children }) {
return <section className="panel">{children}</section>;
renders slot
}
We should not do this:
function Panel() {
return <section className="panel"></section>;
PROBLEMATIC: drops children
}
QUESTION 2

A prop for every piece leaves an empty byline

An article list needs to show multiple story formats: a standard text article with an author byline, a photo article with no author, and a quote article. Following the pattern from Lecture 6, a developer creates a rigid ArticleCard that takes individual props for every layout element:

App.jsx
1function ArticleCard({ title, author }) {
2 return (
3 <article className="card">
4 <h2>{title}</h2>
5 <p>By {author}</p>
PROBLEMATIC: shows 'By ' when omitted
6 </article>
7 );
8}

App renders two article cards, but the photo update has no author:

9export default function App() {
10 return (
11 <>
12 <ArticleCard title="Rail Strike Ends" author="James Smith" />
13 <ArticleCard title="New Park Opens Today" />
Author omitted
14 </>
15 );
16}

The second card displays "New Park Opens Today" followed by "By " with an empty hole. When designers ask to add photo cards, quote cards, and video badges, the component accumulates twenty optional props, creating brittle, tangled markup.

One story has a photo, another a quote, another only text. Do I add a prop for each?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. A rigid component couples container layout to specific content fields.

When a component accepts a dedicated prop for every piece of content, it must hardcode where and how each piece renders. If a story omits a piece, the hardcoded markup leaves an empty label on screen. If a new content format is introduced, the card must add new props, causing the component to grow uncontrollably.

The solution is composition: use props for fixed data that every card shares and that the container positions, and use children for variable body content that changes from use to use. Every article requires a title rendered at the top of the card, so title remains a prop. But whether the body contains a paragraph, an author byline, an image, or a blockquote is decided by the caller between the tags.

App.jsx
1function CardContainer({ title, children }) {
2 return (
3 <article className="card">
4 <h2>{title}</h2>
Fixed title slot
5 {children}
Flexible content slot
6 </article>
7 );
8}

Now, the weather update simply places no author between its tags, so no empty byline appears. The photo article nests an <img>, and the quote article nests a <blockquote>. As react.dev emphasizes, components with a children prop act as visual frames with an open slot. Conditional rendering of fallback slots is covered in Lecture 10.

Rigid card with fixed slots vs flexible container frame
RIGID CARD (prop for every piece)    CONTAINER FRAME (children for content)
+---------------------------------+  +---------------------------------+
| title prop -> <h2>{title}</h2>  |  | title prop -> <h2>{title}</h2>  |
| author prop-> <p>By {author}</p>|  | {children} -> flexible slot for |
| (shows "By " when prop missing) |  |   photo, quote, or author text  |
+---------------------------------+  +---------------------------------+
PRINCIPLE 2

Composition: children when the caller decides the content, props when the frame decides its shape

composition combining flexible content slots with fixed container framing

We pass content that changes from use to use as children, and we keep a prop for what every use must have and the frame must place, such as the title.

Creating dedicated props for every possible variation creates bloated, rigid components that break when designs evolve. When a component hardcodes layout slots, omitting a prop leaves dangling labels on screen. Practice composition by using props for fixed values that every instance requires in a standardized location, and use children for variable content that changes from instance to instance.

We should do this:
function ProfileCard({ title, children }) {
return (
<article className="card">
<h2>{title}</h2>
title placed by frame
{children}
body provided by caller
</article>
);
}
We should not do this:
function ProfileCard({ title, phone }) {
return (
<article className="card">
<h2>{title}</h2>
<p>Phone: {phone}</p>
PROBLEMATIC: shows empty gap
</article>
);
}
QUESTION 3

The caller's class replaces the card's own

The featured top story on the page needs an accessibility label aria-label="Top story", an anchor id="top-story", and an extra highlight class className="featured". A developer collects remaining props using rest syntax and spreads them onto the card:

App.jsx
1function CardContainer({ children, ...rest }) {
2 return (
3 <article className="card" {...rest}>
4 {children}
PROBLEMATIC: overrides card class
5 </article>
6 );
7}

App passes the extra attributes to the featured container:

8export default function App() {
9 return (
10 <CardContainer className="featured" id="top-story" aria-label="Top story">
11 <h2>Park Opens Today</h2>
PROBLEMATIC: base style lost
12 </CardContainer>
13 );
14}

The id and aria-label reach the <article> element. But inspecting the element in the browser Elements panel reveals class="featured": the base "card" class disappeared completely, stripping away borders, padding, and layout shadows.

Callers want a className and an aria-label on the card. Do I list each one?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. Spreading rest after a class attribute overrides it, and joining an undefined class prints "undefined".

In JSX, attributes are evaluated in sequential order from left to right, and whichever attribute is written last wins. In <article className="card" {...rest}> the spread syntax unpacks the caller's className="featured" after className="card", completely replacing "card" with "featured". If you swap the order to <article {...rest} className="card"> the card preserves "card" but discards the caller's "featured" class entirely.

When both the container and the caller need to apply CSS classes, the container must concatenate them: className={'card ' + className} However, if a caller passes no class, className is undefined, and string concatenation turns it into class="card undefined". To prevent this bug, provide a default value in the destructuring parameter list: className = ''.

App.jsx
1function CardContainer({ children, className = '', ...rest }) {
2 return (
3 <article className={'card ' + className} {...rest}>
4 {children}
Joined classes with fallback
5 </article>
6 );
7}

Notice that we unpack children and className first and spread only ...rest. If a component spreads all props directly with <article {...props}>, it accidentally forwards children into the DOM as an attribute and leaks non-standard props (like isFeatured), causing React to log React does not recognize the isFeatured prop on a DOM element Rest syntax ensures only valid, unconsumed attributes reach the underlying DOM node.

PRINCIPLE 3

Prop spreading: the attributes the frame does not use pass on to its element

rest syntax collecting unextracted properties into a single remaining object

We take out the props the frame uses and pass only the rest to its element with {...rest}; the attribute written last wins, so a class the frame and the caller both set is joined, with an empty default for the caller who sets none.

Extra attributes written on a component tag do not reach underlying HTML elements automatically. Use rest syntax in parameter destructuring ({ children, className = '', ...rest }) to extract known container props while capturing remaining attributes in rest. Spread {...rest} onto the element. Because the last attribute written wins, join container and caller classes explicitly, using an empty default string to prevent class="card undefined".

We should do this:
function Panel({ children, className = '', ...rest }) {
return (
<section className={'panel ' + className} {...rest}>
{children}
joins classes and spreads rest
</section>
);
}
We should not do this:
function Panel({ children, ...rest }) {
return (
<section className="panel" {...rest}>
{children}
PROBLEMATIC: overrides base class
</section>
);
}

⚡ IN THE WILD

Is children the same as the children of the render tree in Lecture 5? In Lecture 5, we learned that a component's children in the render tree are the components its own markup returns. With container composition, a parent writes child tags inside a container's JSX call. We might wonder whose child that nested component becomes in the tree. In the runtime render tree, content passed as children becomes a direct child of the container component that actually renders {children}. Even though App authored the <p> tag, the <p> sits underneath CardContainer in the render tree because CardContainer determines where and when that element renders.
Case Study

One frame, CardContainer, renders all three. The first article is the featured story, so the list marks it with a class and an accessibility label for screen readers. Each of the three steps applies one principle of this lesson, in the same order, and ends with what the page shows, so keep the dev server running and the Elements panel open.
