Component Summary

main

The entry file names <App /> as the root of the tree. No step changed it.

App

App renders ArticleList. ArticleList renders three CardContainer frames holding text, photo, and quote article bodies. CardContainer forwards attributes to article.

A developer coming from rigid parameter configurations expects to create separate props for every layout variation and assumes attributes on component tags reach HTML elements automatically. In React 19, the three steps established container composition: children captured diverse inner content, the title prop guaranteed consistent header placement, and prop spreading forwarded DOM attributes while preserving CSS class boundaries.

Where you will meet this

  1. Modal dialog containers: rendering custom form or alert content inside a standard overlay frame with backdrop styling.
  2. Global layout shells: wrapping page-level views between shared navigation headers and footers using a <PageLayout>{children}</PageLayout> wrapper.
  3. Design system button wrappers: forwarding standard HTML button attributes (type, disabled, onClick) to underlying <button> elements via {...rest}.
  4. Card grids and split panes: creating reusable layout grids that accept arbitrary cards, charts, or tables as children.
  5. Accessibility wrappers: building focus trap containers that augment nested elements with ARIA attributes without dictating their internal markup.

For the interview

The Interview Question: How do the children prop, spread attributes, and default values work?

1. The Hidden Signal

The interviewer wants to hear how you design reusable, maintainable component interfaces. A junior candidate reaches for dozens of boolean and string props to handle layout variations, creating brittle APIs. A senior engineer explains container composition using the children prop, separating layout framing from content presentation. They explain that children is an ordinary prop created by JSX compilation, that JSX spread forwards unconsumed attributes to underlying elements, and that default values prevent undefined values from leaking into class names.

2. The Classic Trap

The classic trap is spreading all props directly onto native DOM elements using <article {...props}>. Spreading props forwards children into the DOM as an attribute and leaks custom framework flags (like isFeatured), triggering React runtime warnings. Another trap is spreading {...rest} after className="card", which allows the caller's class to wipe out the base container class instead of joining them.

3. What is Actually Going On

When JSX compiles, any content placed between component tags becomes the children property of the props object. If one element is nested, children is an element descriptor object; if multiple siblings are nested, it is an array of descriptors. A container component renders this content wherever it places {children}. Using rest syntax (...rest) in parameter destructuring separates known container props from DOM attributes. Spreading {...rest} applies remaining properties to the root HTML element, while string concatenation with a default fallback (className = '') combines CSS classes safely.

4. Where It Gets Tricky

Why does children.map() throw an error when only one child element is passed?

Because children is not guaranteed to be an array. If a caller nests a single element, children is a single React element object, which lacks array methods like .map(). To manipulate children safely in legacy code, developers used React.Children.map, though modern React recommends container composition over children inspection.

Why does <article className="card" {...rest}> lose its styling when the caller passes a class?

JSX attributes evaluate from left to right, and whichever attribute is evaluated last overrides previous ones. If rest contains className="featured", it replaces className="card". The correct approach is to extract className separately and join them: className={'card ' + className}

What happens if you concatenate className={'card ' + className} without a default value?

If the caller omits className, the variable is undefined. In JavaScript, 'card ' + undefined evaluates to the string "card undefined". The browser sets class="card undefined", polluting the DOM. Providing a default className = '' ensures omitted classes evaluate to an empty string.

When should data be passed as a prop instead of children?

Use props when the container must dictate the layout, styling, and positioning of that specific data point across all instances (such as a card title or icon position). Use children when the caller should have complete freedom to choose the structure, tags, and formatting of the inner content.

Glossary

  • children: The specialized React prop containing elements, strings, or components nested between a component's opening and closing tags.
  • Composition: The software design pattern of building complex user interfaces by combining simple, flexible container components with nested content.
  • Array: An ordered, indexed collection of values in JavaScript enclosed in square brackets.
  • Rest syntax: The ...rest syntax in destructuring that collects all remaining, unextracted properties into a single object.
  • Spread syntax: The {...rest} JSX syntax that unpacks an object's properties as individual attributes onto an element.

Beyond the basics

  • Passing Props to a Component: Passing JSX as children and forwarding props with the spread syntax (see react.dev/learn/passing-props-to-a-component).
  • Understanding Your UI as a Tree: How container composition creates parent-child relationships in the render tree (see react.dev/learn/understanding-your-ui-as-a-tree).
  • Common components and children: The official definition of the children prop on native elements (see react.dev/reference/react-dom/components/common).
  • Children API and why children is opaque: Why modern React treats children as an opaque tree rather than inspecting it (see react.dev/reference/react/Children).

Summary

A component can be a frame the caller fills

❒ The children prop: the content between a component's tags arrives as one prop

➔ ALWAYS read nested markup by destructuring { children } in your container component.

➔ NEVER assume content placed between component tags appears automatically; the frame must render {children} explicitly.

❒ Composition: children when the caller decides the content, props when the frame decides its shape

➔ ALWAYS pass variable body content as children, while reserving props for fixed values the frame must position.

➔ NEVER create dozens of optional props for layout variations; let callers nest their own markup inside container slots.

❒ Prop spreading: the attributes the frame does not use pass on to its element

➔ ALWAYS extract container props, provide an empty default className = '', and spread {...rest} onto the underlying HTML element.

➔ NEVER spread raw {...props} onto DOM elements, and never place {...rest} after className without joining classes.

Content between the tags, a frame for the shape, and the rest passed on.

Lecture 8: Splitting Components with ES Module Imports and Exports

Interview Question

CORE

How do you split components across files, and how do default and named imports differ?

Imagine this scenario:

  1. The article site keeps every component in one file, App.jsx, and the file keeps growing.
  2. You move the article card into a file of its own, save, and the page goes blank with "ArticleCard is not defined".
  3. How does a component written in one file get used in another?

A project grows past one file

Since Lecture 2, every component we wrote has lived in one file, App.jsx. Each lesson said so, as a choice for learning: you could see every component at once. A real project does not stay that way. With a card, an article list, two badges, and a header in one file, every change means scrolling past code that has nothing to do with it, and two people who change the file at once get in each other's way. So every React developer meets the same question: how does a component written in one file get used in another?

The answer is one idea, and this chapter follows it from the first question to the last: each file is a module: its names stay inside until it exports them, and another file uses them only by importing them. The chapter follows one component's move to its own file: the file it lands in, the import that must match its export, the kind of export it gets, and the path that finds it.

This lesson answers four questions:

  • I moved ArticleCard into its own file. Why does App say it is not defined?
  • Do I write braces around the name or not?
  • Should the badges be default or named exports?
  • I moved the feed into components. Why can't it find the card?

The questions stand on what earlier lessons established:

  • Lecture 1 (What is React): export default in front of a component let another file use it; this chapter explains what that line does.
  • Lecture 5 (The render tree): A name used where it does not exist throws a ReferenceError, such as "topic is not defined": a function sees only its own names and those at the top of its file.
  • Lecture 7 (Children): CardContainer({ title, children }) draws the frame, and each story writes its body between the frame's tags.

Later in this track, Lecture 9 demonstrates how main.jsx imports App and mounts it with createRoot, and Lecture 12 examines why variables declared at module scope run once and must remain pure across renders.

A project is a folder of files

Two files need their names now, so the folders come first. Your project starts as one file, App.jsx, inside the src folder. When a component moves out, it goes into a folder named components that sits next to App.jsx.

A path names a file from where you stand

A file names another file by a relative path, a route that starts from its own folder. ./ means "this folder", so from App.jsx, ./components/ArticleCard.jsx means the components folder beside it, then the card's file. ../ means "the folder above". Two files in different folders reach the same file by different paths.

Relative routes to the badge file
from src/App.jsx                    ./components/Badges.jsx
from src/components/ArticleCard.jsx ./Badges.jsx

A name with no dot, such as 'react', is not a path at all: it names an installed package, and the build tool finds it in the project's dependencies.

Principles of React: Each File Is a Module

Everything in this lesson comes down to one idea: each file is a module, and its names cross to another file only by export and import. First, modules, which means each file keeps its names to itself until it exports them: a moved component is gone from the old file until the new file exports it and the old one imports it. Second, imports match exports, which means braces for a named export, none for the default: the wrong form stops the page before anything runs. Third, default and named exports, which means one default for the file's main component, named exports for the rest: a file has one default at most. Fourth, import paths, which means a path starts from the file that imports: a file in the components folder reaches its neighbor with a dot and a slash.

QUESTION 1

A moved component is not defined in the old file

A developer cuts ArticleCard from App.jsx and pastes it into src/components/ArticleCard.jsx but writes no export statement in front of the component function:

components/ArticleCard.jsx
1function ArticleCard({ title }) {
PROBLEMATIC: missing export keyword
2 return <article className="card">{title}</article>;
3}

In App.jsx, App still attempts to render the card tag directly without an import statement:

App.jsx
1export default function App() {
2 return <ArticleCard title="Rail Strike Ends" />;
WRONG: out of scope
3}

Save the file. The browser screen turns completely blank. Open the Console panel: the browser reports an uncaught runtime error, ReferenceError: ArticleCard is not defined

I moved ArticleCard into its own file. Why does App say it is not defined?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. ArticleCard is missing both an export in its new file and an import in App.jsx, so App cannot see it.

In traditional browser scripts loaded through separate <script> tags on an HTML page, all top-level functions share a single global scope. But in modern JavaScript applications, every file is an ES module. A module has its own local scope, just like the function scopes examined in Lecture 5.

When ArticleCard was moved into components/ArticleCard.jsx, its function name became private to that file. It no longer exists inside the module scope of App.jsx. When React attempts to evaluate <ArticleCard /> inside App, JavaScript searches the local scope of App.jsx, fails to find any identifier named ArticleCard, and throws a ReferenceError.

Moving a component between files requires both sides of the bridge:

  1. The source file must use an export statement to make the component available outside its own boundary.
  2. The consuming file must use an import statement to bring that identifier into its local module scope.

If an import statement targets a file that exports nothing, the browser halts before running any code with The requested module '/src/components/ArticleCard.jsx' does not provide an export named 'default'

Any helper function that only its own file needs, such as a title formatter formatTitle, stays unexported. Other files cannot reach it, keeping internal implementation details safe from accidental coupling.

Furthermore, a module's top level executes only once when the file is first imported, regardless of how many other files import it. A console.log placed at the top of a module file runs once during application startup. In contrast, a console.log placed inside a component body executes on every single render.

Under Vite, any module file containing JSX markup must end in .jsx. Naming the file .js stops the build immediately with [PARSE_ERROR] Unexpected JSX expression and Help: JSX syntax is disabled

The fix is to export ArticleCard from its own file and import it at the top of App.jsx:

components/ArticleCard.jsx
1export default function ArticleCard({ title }) {
2 return <article className="card">{title}</article>;
Exported default
3}
App.jsx
1import ArticleCard from './components/ArticleCard.jsx';
Imported into scope
2
3export default function App() {
4 return <ArticleCard title="Rail Strike Ends" />;
Renders card
5}
PRINCIPLE 1

Modules: each file keeps its names to itself until it exports them

We treat each file as a module: a component moved to its own file is exported there with export, and imported with import by every file that uses it; a function only its file uses stays unexported.

``jsx // src/components/ContactCard.jsx export default function ContactCard({ name }) { // exports component return <p>{name}</p>; } // src/App.jsx import ContactCard from './components/ContactCard.jsx'; // imports card ``

``jsx // src/components/ContactCard.jsx function ContactCard({ name }) { // **PROBLEMATIC:** unexported return <p>{name}</p>; } // src/App.jsx: **WRONG:** missing import throws ReferenceError ``

QUESTION 2

The braces of an import must match the export

A developer exports ArticleCard from components/ArticleCard.jsx using a named export:

components/ArticleCard.jsx
1export function ArticleCard({ title }) {
2 return <article className="card">{title}</article>;
Named export
3}

In App.jsx, the developer attempts to import it without curly braces:

App.jsx
1import ArticleCard from './components/ArticleCard.jsx';
WRONG: missing braces for named export
2
3export default function App() {
4 return <ArticleCard title="Rail Strike Ends" />;
5}

Save the file. The browser page stays completely blank. The console displays a fatal module resolution error: The requested module '/src/components/ArticleCard.jsx' does not provide an export named 'default' Running npm run build fails with [MISSING_EXPORT] "default" is not exported by "src/components/ArticleCard.jsx"

Do I write braces around the name or not?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. The import syntax asks for a default export without braces, but the module provides only a named export.

JavaScript ES modules provide two distinct export mechanisms:

  1. Default export: Declared with export default A module has at most one default export, and importers consume it without curly braces: import ArticleCard from ...
  2. Named export: Declared with export function Name or export const Name A module can have multiple named exports, and importers consume them inside curly braces: import { ArticleCard } from ...

The browser links module imports and exports statically before any application code executes. When App.jsx writes import ArticleCard from ... it explicitly requests the module's default export slot. Because ArticleCard.jsx used export function ArticleCard it populated a named slot called ArticleCard and left the default slot completely empty. The runtime halts immediately.

The mirror mistake fails just as decisively: writing import { ArticleCard } from ... when the source file used export default fails with does not provide an export named 'ArticleCard' Similarly, misspelling a named import, such as import { Articlecard } from ... fails because named imports must match the exact case-sensitive identifier exported by the module.

Because a default import binds to the file's single default slot, the importing file can assign it any local name: import StoryBox from './components/ArticleCard.jsx' works cleanly. In contrast, named imports must match the exported name, or use the as keyword to rename them: import { ArticleCard as StoryBox } from ...

Note that the curly braces in import { ArticleCard } are standard ES module syntax. They are not JSX expression curly braces from Lecture 4.

In older bundlers, an export and import mismatch was not caught at build time and evaluated to undefined at runtime. In React, passing undefined as a component type produces the classic error: Element type is invalid: expected a string (for built-in components) or a class/function (for composite components) but got: undefined. You likely forgot to export your component from the file it's defined in, or you might have mixed up default and named imports. Under Vite, this error appears if you import an entire module namespace with import * as Cards and render <Cards.ArticleCard /> when ArticleCard was actually a default export.

The fix is to match the named export with curly braces:

App.jsx
1import { ArticleCard } from './components/ArticleCard.jsx';
Matches braces
2
3export default function App() {
4 return <ArticleCard title="Rail Strike Ends" />;
Renders card
5}
PRINCIPLE 2

Imports match exports: braces for a named export, none for the default

We write each import in the form of its export: no braces for a default export, under any name we choose, and braces with the exact name for a named export.

``jsx // src/components/ContactCard.jsx export function ContactCard({ name }) { // named export return <p>{name}</p>; } // src/App.jsx import { ContactCard } from './components/ContactCard.jsx'; // matched braces ``

``jsx // src/components/ContactCard.jsx: export function ContactCard // src/App.jsx import ContactCard from './components/ContactCard.jsx'; // **WRONG:** missing braces // **WRONG:** does not provide an export named 'default' ``

QUESTION 3

A file has one default export

A developer keeps ArticleCard and a small Badge helper in components/ArticleCard.jsx, adding an export default keyword in front of both functions:

components/ArticleCard.jsx
1export default function ArticleCard({ title }) {
2 return <article className="card">{title}</article>;
First default
3}
4
5export default function Badge({ text }) {
6 return <span className="badge">{text}</span>;
WRONG: second default
7}

Save the file. The Vite error overlay immediately covers the browser window: [PARSE_ERROR] A module cannot have multiple default exports.

Should the badges be default or named exports?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. A JavaScript module has only one default export slot, so declaring a second default export is a syntax error.

Because App.jsx has had export default on its main function since Lecture 1, developers often assume every component should be exported as a default. But ECMAScript module specifications strictly limit each module file to a single default export.

In contrast, named exports have no numerical limit. A module can export tens or hundreds of functions, constants, or types by name.

The standard architectural convention across the React ecosystem is straightforward:

  • A file whose primary responsibility is a single major component exports that component as its export default
  • A file containing several smaller components or utility helpers exports each helper using named exports: export function LiveBadge() and export function NewBadge()

When a file exports both a primary default component and secondary named helpers, callers can import both in a single concise line: import ArticleCard, { Badge } from './components/ArticleCard.jsx' The default name sits outside the braces, while the named helpers sit inside the braces.

Every exported function should retain an explicit identifier. Writing an anonymous default export like export default ({ title }) => <article>{title}</article> is discouraged. An anonymous component function has its runtime name property set to "default", making stack traces and React DevTools component trees difficult to read.

The fix is to keep ArticleCard as the default export and export Badge as a named export:

components/ArticleCard.jsx
1export default function ArticleCard({ title }) {
2 return <article className="card">{title}</article>;
Single default
3}
4
5export function Badge({ text }) {
6 return <span className="badge">{text}</span>;
Named export
7}
App.jsx
1import ArticleCard, { Badge } from './components/ArticleCard.jsx';
Both forms
PRINCIPLE 3

Default and named exports: one default for the file's main component, named exports for the rest

We give a file at most one default export, for its main component, and we export its other components with names; a file of several small components uses named exports only, and every exported function keeps a name.

``jsx // src/components/ContactCard.jsx export default function ContactCard({ name }) { // one default export return <p>{name}</p>; } export function PhoneLine({ number }) { // named export for helper return <span>{number}</span>; } ``

``jsx // src/components/ContactCard.jsx export default function ContactCard({ name }) { // first default return <p>{name}</p>; } export default function PhoneLine({ number }) { // **WRONG:** second default return <span>{number}</span>; } // **WRONG:** module cannot have multiple default exports ``

QUESTION 4

A path copied from App.jsx breaks inside components

A developer moves the article list feed into src/components/ArticleList.jsx Inside this new file, the developer needs to render the card frame component CardContainer.jsx. The developer copies the import line directly from App.jsx without changing its text:

components/ArticleList.jsx
1import CardContainer from './components/CardContainer.jsx';
WRONG: copied path fails to resolve
2
3export default function ArticleList() {
4 return <CardContainer title="Rail Strike Ends">Story body</CardContainer>;
5}

Save the file. The Vite error overlay covers the page: Failed to resolve import "./components/CardContainer.jsx" from "src/components/ArticleList.jsx". Does the file exist?

I moved the feed into components. Why can't it find the card?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. The import path was copied from App.jsx and resolves to a nonexistent subfolder when evaluated from inside components.

Relative import paths in JavaScript always resolve relative to the folder containing the file that holds the import statement. They never resolve relative to the project root or relative to App.jsx.

When App.jsx (located in src/) writes ./components/CardContainer.jsx ./ represents src/. The build tool resolves the path to src/components/CardContainer.jsx where the file exists.

However, when ArticleList.jsx (located in src/components/) writes ./components/CardContainer.jsx ./ represents src/components/. The build tool appends the relative segment, resulting in src/components/components/CardContainer.jsx Because that directory does not exist, module resolution fails.

The Vite error message provides the diagnosis: it prints both the requested path ("./components/CardContainer.jsx") and the originating file (from "src/components/ArticleList.jsx").

Because CardContainer.jsx sits directly beside ArticleList.jsx in the same components directory, the relative route is simply ./CardContainer.jsx:

components/ArticleList.jsx
1import CardContainer from './CardContainer.jsx';
Neighbor in same folder

If a file inside components/ needs to reach a file in the parent src/ directory, it uses ../ to move up one folder level: import App from '../App.jsx'

The file extension .jsx may be omitted in modern projects (./CardContainer), though including it remains closest to native browser ES module standards. In contrast, package imports like 'react' or 'react-dom/client' contain no leading dot or slash, informing the bundler to look inside the project's installed package dependencies.

PRINCIPLE 4

Import paths: a path starts from the file that imports

We write each import path from the folder of the file that imports: ./ for a file beside it, ../ for the folder above, and no dot at all for a package such as 'react'.

``jsx // src/components/ArticleCard.jsx import { PhoneLine } from './PhoneLine.jsx'; // neighbor in same folder ``

``jsx // src/components/ArticleCard.jsx import { PhoneLine } from './components/PhoneLine.jsx'; // **WRONG:** wrong folder // **WRONG:** failed to resolve import from src/components/ArticleCard.jsx ``

What is the tree of files?

In Lecture 5, we visualized how React builds a render tree by evaluating component tags: App called ArticleList, which called CardContainer, which rendered its child elements.

Now that our project spans multiple files, our import statements create a second tree: the module dependency tree. A bundler (such as Vite during development or Rolldown during production builds) starts at the root entry point, main.jsx. It inspects each import statement, loads the requested file, inspects that file's imports, and recursively maps every module our project needs.

The module dependency tree vs the render tree
MODULE DEPENDENCY TREE (Static Files)     RENDER TREE (Runtime UI)
main.jsx                                  App
  └── App.jsx                               └── ArticleList
        └── components/ArticleList.jsx            ├── CardContainer
              ├── components/CardContainer.jsx    │     ├── NewBadge
              └── components/Badges.jsx           │     └── p (byline)
                                                  └── CardContainer
                                                        ├── LiveBadge
                                                        └── blockquote

Notice how the two trees differ: ArticleList.jsx imports CardContainer.jsx and Badges.jsx to assemble the UI. But CardContainer.jsx never imports ArticleList.jsx or Badges.jsx. The frame knows nothing about the badges placed inside it; it receives them at runtime through children.

Case Study
Let's Design a Practical Example

Now we split the whole article site feed of Lecture 7: the frame, two badges, and the article list itself leave App.jsx for the components folder, and App.jsx ends with four lines. The page must look the same after every step, so each step ends on a page that still works, or on the message that says why not. Keep the dev server running and the Console panel open.

First, we move the frame into its own file
<CardContainer.jsx>

This step applies Principle 1: Modules: each file keeps its names to itself until it exports them.

CardContainer is used by every article card and performs one clear visual role: rendering the card border, the title header, and the flexible children container. We cut CardContainer from App.jsx and place it in src/components/CardContainer.jsx as that file's default export.

What would happen if App.jsx forgot to import CardContainer? As shown in Question 1, the browser would throw ReferenceError: CardContainer is not defined and display a blank page. We add the default import line at the top of App.jsx.

In CardContainer.jsx, lines 1 to 8 declare the exported frame component:

CardContainer.jsx
1export default function CardContainer({ title, children }) {
2 return (

Wraps nested content

App.jsx

Imports frame

Next, we import the first badge by its name
<App.jsx>

The second card ("Rail Strike Ends") requires a "Live" badge. We create a utility file src/components/Badges.jsx and export LiveBadge as a named export. In App.jsx, we import it using curly braces matching its exact function name.

What would happen if App.jsx wrote import LiveBadge from './components/Badges.jsx' without braces? The page would fail to load with The requested module does not provide an export named 'default'

In Badges.jsx, lines 1 to 3 define and export the live status badge:

2 return <span className="badge live">Live</span>;

3}

<Badges.jsx>

The first card ("City Library Extends Its Hours") needs a "New" badge. Because NewBadge and LiveBadge are sibling utility widgets of equal standing, neither should be a default export. We add NewBadge to Badges.jsx as a second named export.

Inside ArticleList.jsx, we must import CardContainer and the badges. Component Summary

main

The entry file names <App /> as the root of the tree. No step changed it.

App

The root application component renders ArticleList in four lines of code.

ArticleList

Default export; imports CardContainer and Badges from its own folder.

CardContainer

Default export; renders the card border around title and children.

Badges

Named exports; provides LiveBadge and NewBadge helpers.

A developer accustomed to older script tags expects every declared function to be globally available across all files, assumes curly braces in import statements are optional, uses export default indiscriminately, and copies import paths from file to file without inspecting directory depths. In React 19 with modern ES modules, each file forms an isolated module scope, import syntax strictly mirrors export form, files maintain at most one default export, and every relative path resolves from the directory of the file that writes it.

Where you will meet this

  1. A components directory where every primary UI component occupies its own dedicated .jsx file.
  2. A utils or helpers file exporting multiple standalone calculation or formatting functions using named exports.
  3. Third-party UI libraries like Lucide or Material UI imported by name, such as import { Check, AlertCircle } from 'lucide-react'
  4. Team git workflows where feature branches avoid merge conflicts because developers edit separate modular files rather than a monolithic App.jsx.
  5. Debugging legacy codebases or third-party tutorials where mixing up default and named exports causes Element type is invalid: expected a string or a class/function but got: undefined

For the interview

  • Hidden Signal: The interviewer is testing whether you understand JavaScript module scope and build-time static linking versus runtime execution. Candidates who guess whether to use curly braces reveal a weak foundation in modern ECMAScript fundamentals.
  • Classic Trap: Claiming that default and named imports are interchangeable or that braces are merely an aesthetic preference. A mismatch halts execution before any component function runs.
  • What is Actually Going On: ES modules use static analysis to resolve bindings at build time. Default exports map to an internal property named default, while named exports map to explicit property keys on the module's namespace object.
  • Where It Gets Tricky: Can a file have multiple default exports? No, exactly one. Can a default import be renamed by the consumer? Yes, freely. Can a named import be renamed? Yes, but only with explicit as aliasing syntax (import { Card as StoryCard }). Where do relative paths start? Always from the directory of the importing file.

Glossary

  • Module: An isolated JavaScript file whose top-level functions and variables are private to that file until exported.
  • Default export: An export declared with export default that can be imported without curly braces under any local name.
  • Named export: An export declared with export function or export const that must be imported inside curly braces matching its exact identifier.
  • Relative path: A file path starting with ./ or ../ that resolves relative to the folder containing the file that writes it.
  • Package import: An import specifying a bare package name without dots or slashes that resolves to installed package dependencies in node_modules.
  • Module dependency tree: The static tree of file relationships formed by import and export statements, followed by build tools to compile the application.

Beyond the basics

  • Importing and Exporting Components (https://react.dev/learn/importing-and-exporting-components)
  • Understanding Your UI as a Tree (https://react.dev/learn/understanding-your-ui-as-a-tree)
  • MDN: export statement (https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Statements/export)
  • MDN: import statement (https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Statements/import)

Summary

Each file is a module

❒ Modules: each file keeps its names to itself until it exports them
  • ALWAYS export a component with export if another file needs to render it.
  • NEVER assume a function declared in another file is globally available.
❒ Imports match exports: braces for a named export, none for the default
  • ALWAYS use curly braces when importing named exports: import { LiveBadge } from './components/Badges.jsx'
  • NEVER use curly braces when importing a default export: import ArticleCard from './components/ArticleCard.jsx'
❒ Default and named exports: one default for the file's main component, named exports for the rest
  • ALWAYS export the primary component of a dedicated file as export default
  • NEVER declare more than one export default in the same module file.
❒ Import paths: a path starts from the file that imports
  • ALWAYS write relative paths starting from the importing file's directory: ./ for neighbors, ../ for parent folders.
  • NEVER copy import paths between folders without adjusting their relative steps.

One wall per file, an import that matches, one default, and a path from here.

DO THIS: export the primary component as default and utility helpers as named

code.txt
1export default function ArticleCard({ title }) {
2 return <article className="card">{title}</article>;
3}
4export function Badge({ text }) {
5 return <span className="badge">{text}</span>;
6}
7
8import ArticleCard, { Badge } from './components/ArticleCard.jsx';

DO NOT DO THIS: declare multiple default exports or mix up default and named syntax

code.txt
1export default function ArticleCard({ title }) {
2 return <article className="card">{title}</article>;
3}
4export default function Badge({ text }) {
5 return <span className="badge">{text}</span>;
6}
7
8import { ArticleCard } from './components/ArticleCard.jsx';
THE MONOLITHIC FILE HABITTHE MODERN ES MODULE RULE
VisibilityEvery function visible to entire fileFunctions private to module until exported
Default exportNot needed in single fileOne per file for primary component
Named exportsNot needed in single fileUnlimited named exports for utility helpers
Import matchingDirect invocation <Component />Braces for named exports, none for default
Path resolutionSingle flat fileResolves relative to importing file's directory

Lecture 9: Mounting the Root Component with createRoot and Vite Tooling

Interview Question

CORE

How does your root component attach to the browser DOM with createRoot, and how do build tools assemble it?

Imagine this scenario:

  1. Your article site now lives in several files: App.jsx and a components folder beside it.
  2. You double-click index.html to see the site, and the browser shows a blank white page.
  3. How do the files you write become the page the browser shows?

Every React app starts from one HTML page

Every website reaches the browser as an HTML page. Since Lecture 2 we have written components, and since Lecture 8 each one lives in its own file. But a browser knows nothing about our files. It opens one HTML page and runs the scripts that page names. So every React developer meets the same question: how does React get onto a real web page?

React's own documentation lists three ways to start, and developers choose between them based on project architecture. The first way creates the project with a full-stack framework such as Next.js:

Terminal
1npx create-next-app@latest
Creates a framework project

With a full-stack framework, we write page components, and the framework handles the rest: a server sends each page's HTML already filled, and the framework calls React's start-up code for us. It fits a site whose pages should arrive ready from the server, with routing built in. Lecture 45 compares full-stack frameworks and standalone build tools.

The second way is the one this chapter teaches. A build tool turns our files into code the browser can run, and one file of our own, the entry file, starts React with an explicit mount call:

Entry file with a build tool
1createRoot(document.getElementById('root')).render(<App />);
Mounts App

Read the line from the inside out. document.getElementById('root') finds one element of the HTML page, as in Lecture 1. createRoot hands that element to React. .render(<App />) tells React to show App inside it. Here we decide where React starts and what it shows, and the build tool prepares our files. It fits an app built from scratch, where one page is loaded once and React draws everything on it.

The third way starts from a page that already exists. A legacy website built with other backend tools can hand over one designated container to React:

One area of an existing page
1createRoot(document.getElementById('comments')).render(<Comments />);
Widget

The same two calls now take only the comments container. The rest of the page stays exactly as the backend server wrote it, and React never touches it. Lecture 1 explained that React can run an entire page or only a specific widget on an existing page. It fits a large legacy site that moves to React incrementally, one feature at a time.

Three ways to put React on a web page

(1) Start React with a full-stack framework (Lecture 45): the framework creates the project, renders HTML on a server, and calls React's start-up code for us.

(2) Start React with a build tool and an entry file (this chapter): the build tool prepares our modular files, and our own entry file hands one empty element to React.

(3) Add React to part of an existing page (this chapter): an existing page gives one area to React, and the rest stays as the server wrote it.

This chapter follows the second way, using Vite as the build tool, because it exposes every foundational step that frameworks hide. It follows one idea from the first question to the last: mounting, which means the browser loads one page, and React fills one element of it with our components. The steps follow the order of one page load: the page arrives, its code arrives, React takes one element, React fills it, and the app grows from there.

This lesson answers five questions:

  • index.html has only an empty <div id="root">. Where is the page I see, and where do I change it?
  • Why can't I just double-click index.html, like any HTML page I wrote before?
  • What does createRoot(document.getElementById('root')) do with the empty element?
  • My old tutorial writes ReactDOM.render(<App />, document.getElementById('root')) in one line. Why does our main.jsx use two steps?
  • I want a footer under the articles. Do I add a second createRoot for it in main.jsx?

The questions stand on what earlier lessons established:

  • Lecture 1 (What is React): index.html holds one empty element, <div id="root"></div>, which React fills. npm run dev starts the dev server, which serves the project during development. document.getElementById('root') queries the browser DOM for the element whose id is root, and the Elements panel inspects the live DOM tree.
  • Lecture 2 (Component anatomy): <App /> is a component tag: React calls the function App wherever JSX writes its tag. App without the tag is merely a function reference. A new Vite project wraps <App /> in <StrictMode>, a development-only verification tool.
  • Lecture 3 (JSX syntax): Browsers cannot parse JSX syntax natively. The build rewrites each JSX tag into a function call that returns a React element, a plain JavaScript object describing the UI. The Sources panel displays files as the browser received them, and main.jsx imports index.css. A Fragment, <> and </>, groups multiple sibling elements without introducing extra DOM nodes.
  • Lecture 4 (JavaScript expressions in JSX with curly braces): null represents the deliberate absence of any object value. Functions return null when a queried element is not found.
  • Lecture 5 (The render tree): App serves as the root component: every other component across the application descends from it in the render tree.
  • Lecture 6 (Props): npm run build compiles the production build, and npm run preview serves the compiled output locally.
  • Lecture 8 (Modules): Each file functions as an isolated module. import App from './App.jsx' is a default import with a relative path. In contrast, 'react-dom/client' is a bare package import pointing to an installed dependency.

The browser reads index.html first

When the browser requests our site, the first file it fetches is index.html. It parses the document from top to bottom. In a standard Vite project, the <body> of index.html holds only two items:

index.html
8 <body>
9 <div id="root"></div>
The one element React will fill
10 <script type="module" src="/src/main.jsx"></script>
Loads main.jsx
11 </body>

The <script> tag carries the attribute type="module". That attribute designates it as a module script: a script that can use standard import statements to load ES modules. Browsers defer execution of module scripts until the HTML document has finished parsing, guaranteeing that <div id="root"></div> already exists in the DOM when main.jsx runs.

The browser provides two distinct perspectives on a web page:

  1. View Page Source shows the raw HTML document sent across the network by the server.
  2. The Elements panel shows the live, active DOM tree inside browser memory after all scripts have executed.

On a static HTML site, both views look identical because no JavaScript modifies the DOM. On a React site, View Page Source displays an empty <div id="root"></div>, whereas the Elements panel reveals the full rendered component tree nested inside that same div.

The dev server sends the project from your computer

A web page can load in the browser through two distinct protocols. Opening an HTML file directly from the filesystem creates a file:// address, such as file:///Users/you/article-site/index.html In contrast, running npm run dev starts Vite's local HTTP server, delivering the page over a localhost address, such as http://localhost:5173/.

Terminal
1npm run dev
Prints the local address http://localhost:5173/

Third-party dependencies installed via npm install reside in the node_modules folder. React divides its responsibilities across two core packages:

  • react contains platform-agnostic primitives: component definitions, JSX runtime helpers, and state hooks.
  • react-dom provides the browser rendering backend. Its submodule react-dom/client exposes client-side mounting APIs like createRoot. React Native pairs the same core react package with a mobile renderer instead of react-dom.

When running npm run build, the bundler compiles the entire application into a static distribution directory named dist. This folder contains the optimized production assets (index.html, minified JavaScript, and CSS bundles) that a production web server hosts.

A method is a function stored on an object

In JavaScript, a function stored as a property on an object is called a method. Methods are invoked using dot notation: the parent object, followed by a dot, the method name, and parentheses:

Two methods
1document.getElementById('root');
Method of the global document object
2'latest articles'.toUpperCase();
Method belonging to string instances

When a function returns an object, we can chain a method call immediately onto that returned instance. That chaining pattern is how main.jsx is conventionally written:

main.jsx
1import { StrictMode } from 'react';
2import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';
Client-side renderer
3import './index.css';
4import App from './App.jsx';
5
6createRoot(document.getElementById('root')).render(
7 <StrictMode>
8 <App />
Mounts root component
9 </StrictMode>
10);

Lines 1 to 4 import dependencies. Line 6 performs two chained operations: createRoot(...) executes first and returns a React root object, and .render(...) immediately calls a method on that returned root. The same logic can be split across two statements: const root = createRoot(document.getElementById('root')); followed by root.render(<App />);.

Principles of React: Mounting the Root Component

Everything in this lesson comes down to one idea: mounting, which means the browser loads one page, and React fills one element of it with our components. First, the root element, which means the page arrives with one empty element: we leave that element empty in the HTML file and write every part of the page in our components. Second, the build tool, which means the page's code arrives as plain JavaScript: we open the project through the dev server, because a browser cannot read JSX or a package name by itself. Third, the React root, which means the page hands that one element to React: we find the element by the same id the HTML file gives it, and we hand React the element itself. Fourth, the initial render, which means the page shows the root component in that element: we ask the root to render once, with the root component written as a tag. Fifth, one root per app, which means the page grows inside the root component: a new part of the page is a new tag inside the root component, never a second root on the same element.

QUESTION 1

A title typed into the root element disappears

A developer wants to add a header title above the article list. Remembering standard HTML, the developer opens index.html and types <h1>Latest Articles</h1> directly inside <div id="root">:

index.html
9 <div id="root"><h1>Latest Articles</h1></div>
Typed by hand

Save the file and refresh the browser. The page displays the article list, but the typed <h1> heading is missing entirely. Opening View Page Source shows <h1>Latest Articles</h1> nestled inside the div, but the browser Elements panel shows only <div id="root"><main>...</main></div>

index.html has only an empty <div id="root">. Where is the page I see, and where do I change it?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. React clears all existing children inside the container element on its initial render, destroying any manually typed HTML.

When the browser parses index.html, it initially constructs the DOM element <div id="root"><h1>Latest Articles</h1></div> Moments later, the module script executes main.jsx. When main.jsx calls root.render(<App />), React takes complete ownership of the DOM subtree inside that container.

As part of the initial mount contract, React wipes out all existing child nodes inside the container element before inserting its own virtual DOM tree. Any HTML markup typed inside <div id="root"> is removed from the live document.

View Page Source continues to display the typed <h1> because it inspects the unmodified network payload delivered from the disk. In contrast, the Elements panel reveals the live, active DOM tree after React's render pipeline has wiped the container.

In a modern client-side React application, the root element in index.html serves exclusively as an empty mounting hook. All user-facing content belongs inside React components. Elements outside the root container, such as the <head> tag or <title>, remain untouched by React.

The proper fix is to create a dedicated SiteHeader component, render the heading inside it, and assemble SiteHeader alongside ArticleList inside App:

SiteHeader.jsx
1export default function SiteHeader() {
2 return (
3 <header className="site-header">
4 <h1>Latest Articles</h1>
Title lives in component
5 </header>
6 );
7}
App.jsx
1import SiteHeader from './components/SiteHeader.jsx';
New import
2import ArticleList from './components/ArticleList.jsx';
3
4export default function App() {
5 return (
6 <>
7 <SiteHeader />
Title above articles
8 <ArticleList />
9 </>
10 );
11}
PRINCIPLE 1

The root element: the page arrives with one empty element

We leave <div id="root"> empty in index.html and write every part of the page in our components; React fills that element when main.jsx runs, and replaces anything we typed inside it.

``html <!-- index.html: root container remains empty --> <div id="root"></div> <!-- React fills this element --> ``

``html <!-- index.html: typed content is wiped out on mount --> <div id="root"><h1>My Site</h1></div> <!-- React removes h1 --> ``

QUESTION 2

A double-clicked index.html shows a blank page

A newcomer navigates to the project directory in their operating system file manager and double-clicks index.html to view the site. The browser launches with an address starting with file:///Users/you/article-site/index.html The browser viewport is blank.

Open the Console panel: Chrome prints a fatal error: Access to script at 'file:///src/main.jsx' from origin 'null' has been blocked by CORS policy: Cross origin requests are only supported for protocol schemes: http, data, chrome-extension, https, chrome-untrusted.

Why can't I just double-click index.html, like any HTML page I wrote before?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. Browsers block ES module scripts loaded over the file:// protocol, and native browser runtimes cannot interpret raw JSX or bare package names.

Standard HTML pages containing vanilla JavaScript can open directly from local disk storage. However, React source files cannot run directly in the browser for three distinct architectural reasons:

  1. CORS policy on local modules: Web security standards block <script type="module"> tags loaded over file:// because local file schemes have an origin of null. Furthermore, an absolute path like /src/main.jsx on a file:// URL resolves against the root directory of the hard drive rather than the project folder.
  2. Native lack of JSX parsing: Even if served over plain HTTP, the browser parser stops at the first JSX element (<App />) with SyntaxError: Unexpected token '<' JSX is a language extension, not valid standard JavaScript.
  3. Bare package specifiers: Standard browser module loaders require relative paths starting with ./, ../, or /. A bare package specifier like import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client' halts browser resolution with TypeError: Failed to resolve module specifier "react-dom/client"

A build tool like Vite resolves all three obstacles. In development, running npm run dev launches a local dev server on http://localhost:5173/. On every file request, the server transforms JSX into _jsxDEV(...) function calls and maps bare package imports to concrete file paths inside .vite/deps/.

Source code vs browser delivery
WE WRITE:                         DEV SERVER DELIVERS:
import { createRoot }             import { createRoot }
  from 'react-dom/client';          from '/node_modules/.vite/deps/...';
<App />                           _jsxDEV(App, {})

For production hosting, running npm run build executes a full compilation pass, generating bundled static assets inside the dist folder. Production files can then be tested locally with npm run preview or uploaded to a static web server.

Terminal
1npm run build
Compiles files into production dist directory
PRINCIPLE 2

The build tool: the page's code arrives as plain JavaScript

We open the project through the dev server with npm run dev, never by double-clicking index.html, because the browser cannot read JSX or a package name; for a real server, npm run build writes the same plain JavaScript into dist.

``js // Terminal: npm run dev // Browser: http://localhost:5173/ // dev server transforms files ``

``js // Browser address bar: file:///Users/you/site/index.html // **WRONG:** CORS policy blocks file:// module scripts ``

QUESTION 3

A renamed id leaves the page blank

A developer decides to rename the container element in index.html to match another convention:

index.html
9 <div id="app"></div>
Renamed from root

However, main.jsx remains unchanged, continuing to query for the container using 'root':

main.jsx
6createRoot(document.getElementById('root')).render(
Still asks for root

Save both files. The browser displays an empty white screen. Opening the Console panel reveals an uncaught fatal exception: Uncaught Error: Target container is not a DOM element.

What does createRoot(document.getElementById('root')) do with the empty element?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. document.getElementById('root') found no matching element and returned null, which causes createRoot to throw an error.

The browser DOM method document.getElementById('root') queries the live document for an element matching the specified ID string. If no element in the HTML document possesses that ID attribute, the method returns null.

When createRoot receives null instead of a physical DOM element, it cannot initialize a mounting container. It halts execution immediately by throwing Target container is not a DOM element. Because execution crashes before .render() is called, nothing renders on screen.

When passed a valid DOM element, createRoot initializes and returns a React root object. This root object exposes two primary methods:

  • render(element): Mounts or updates the virtual DOM element tree inside the container.
  • unmount(): Teardowns the tree, cleans up event listeners, and empties the container.

Calling createRoot establishes the container boundary: React claims exclusive control over all DOM manipulation inside that designated element, while DOM nodes outside the container remain managed by traditional HTML and browser APIs. Note that passing a JSX tag directly into createRoot, such as createRoot(<App />), triggers the identical Target container is not a DOM element error because a React virtual element is not a real DOM node.

The fix is ensuring the query string in main.jsx matches the ID attribute declared in index.html letter for letter:

index.html
9 <div id="root"></div>
Matching ID attribute
main.jsx
6createRoot(document.getElementById('root')).render(
Matches index.html
PRINCIPLE 3

The React root: the page hands that one element to React

We call createRoot once in main.jsx with the element itself, found by the same id that index.html gives it; React then controls everything inside that element and nothing outside it.

``jsx const container = document.getElementById('root'); const root = createRoot(container); // React controls element ``

``jsx const container = document.getElementById('app'); // **PROBLEMATIC:** id mismatch const root = createRoot(container); // **WRONG:** throws Target container error ``

QUESTION 4

ReactDOM.render from an old tutorial stops the page

Following a tutorial found on an older blog, a developer imports ReactDOM and writes the single-line mount call:

main.jsx
1import ReactDOM from 'react-dom';
2import './index.css';
3import App from './App.jsx';
4
5const container = document.getElementById('root');
6ReactDOM.render(<App />, container);
WRONG: not a function

Save the file. The browser viewport stays blank. In the console, a fatal TypeError appears: TypeError: ReactDOM.render is not a function

My old tutorial writes ReactDOM.render(<App />, document.getElementById('root')) in one line. Why does our main.jsx use two steps?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. ReactDOM.render was deprecated in React 18 and completely removed in React 19.

Older versions of React exposed a legacy API named ReactDOM.render(element, container) that combined container discovery and initial rendering into a single synchronous call.

React 19 removed ReactDOM.render entirely. Importing from react-dom no longer provides a render function, causing legacy invocation attempts to crash with ReactDOM.render is not a function

Modern React decouples container initialization from rendering into two explicit operations:

  1. createRoot(container): Registers the host DOM element once and initializes concurrent rendering internal queues.
  2. root.render(element): Schedules the virtual DOM element tree to be rendered into that root.

A common mistake when migrating legacy code is passing the DOM container a second time into root.render:

main.jsx
6const container = document.getElementById('root');
7const root = createRoot(container);
8root.render(<App />, container);
PROBLEMATIC: container warning

While the page renders, the console warns: Warning: You passed a container to the second argument of root.render(...). You don't need to pass it again since you already passed it to create the root.

Another common mistake is passing the component function without JSX brackets: root.render(App). Because App is a JavaScript function reference rather than an evaluated React element, React prints: Warning: Functions are not valid as a React child. The argument must be an element: <App />.

Under the hood, createRoot initializes concurrent rendering queues, which Lecture 66 investigates. The initial call to root.render initiates what Lecture 15 defines as the initial render. Furthermore, React attaches its top-level synthetic event listeners to this root DOM container, as Lecture 79 explores. In development, Vite wraps <App /> with <StrictMode> to perform safety audits, which Lecture 46 details.

The fix is importing createRoot from react-dom/client and passing only the root element to .render(...):

main.jsx
1import { StrictMode } from 'react';
2import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';
Client API
3import App from './App.jsx';
4
5createRoot(document.getElementById('root')).render(
6 <StrictMode>
7 <App />
Passes element, not container
8 </StrictMode>
9);
PRINCIPLE 4

The initial render: the page shows the root component in that element

We call render on the root once, with the root component written as a tag, root.render(<App />), and nothing else; React 19 has no ReactDOM.render, and the element is never passed a second time.

``jsx import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client'; const root = createRoot(document.getElementById('root')); root.render(<App />); // mounts root element ``

``jsx import ReactDOM from 'react-dom'; const container = document.getElementById('root'); ReactDOM.render(<App />, container); // **WRONG:** not a function ``

QUESTION 5

A second root for the footer wipes out the page

A developer creates a Footer component and decides to mount it on the page by adding a second createRoot call directly underneath the first mount inside main.jsx:

main.jsx
5import Footer from './components/Footer.jsx';
Footer import
main.jsx
12const rootEl = document.getElementById('root');
13createRoot(rootEl).render(<Footer />);
PROBLEMATIC: overwrites root

Save the file. The browser renders only the footer text: "Latest Articles, 2026". The site header and article list have completely vanished. The console prints a warning: Warning: You are calling ReactDOMClient.createRoot() on a container that has already been passed to createRoot() before. Instead, call root.render() on the existing root instead if you want to update it.

I want a footer under the articles. Do I add a second createRoot for it in main.jsx?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. Creating a second root on the same DOM element destroys the existing component tree and replaces it with the footer.

In traditional jQuery or vanilla DOM manipulation, separate scripts find and populate distinct elements independently. In React, a root container maintains exclusive control over its target DOM node.

When createRoot is invoked a second time on <div id="root">, React takes over the container afresh, clears out all DOM nodes previously rendered by the first root (wiping out SiteHeader and ArticleList), and renders only Footer. Calling .render() twice on the same root instance produces the same result silently: each .render() replaces the entire contents of the root.

In an application built fully with React, the rule is absolute: one root per application. The entry file main.jsx initializes a single root container. Every new piece of user interface (a header, a feed, a modal, or a footer) is composed as a child component inside the component tree descending from App.

From then on, the page updates dynamically through state inside components (debuting in Lecture 14), never by calling createRoot or render again.

The only scenario where multiple roots belong in a single web application is when React is embedded into separate, independent sections of a legacy multi-page site. For example, if an existing server-rendered HTML page has <div id="header-widget"></div> and <div id="comments-widget"></div> each independent container receives its own dedicated createRoot call.

The fix is keeping a single createRoot in main.jsx and importing Footer inside App.jsx:

App.jsx
3import Footer from './components/Footer.jsx';
Imported where used
App.jsx
6 return (
7 <>
8 <SiteHeader />
9 <ArticleList />
10 <Footer />
New tag inside root component
11 </>
12 );
PRINCIPLE 5

One root per app: the page grows inside the root component

In an app built fully with React, we add each new part of the page as a tag inside App, never as a second createRoot or a second render; a page only partly built with React gives each separate React area its own element and its own root.

``jsx function App() { return <><SiteHeader /><ArticleList /><Footer /></>; // one tree } createRoot(document.getElementById('root')).render(<App />); ``

``jsx const container = document.getElementById('root'); createRoot(container).render(<App />); createRoot(container).render(<Footer />); // **PROBLEMATIC:** overwrites first render ``

Why is the page blank for a moment on a slow phone?

When inspecting the built production files, dist/index.html contains only an empty <div id="root"></div> and a <script> tag referencing the compiled JavaScript bundle.

On a low-powered mobile device or an unreliable 3G network, the browser must finish downloading the JavaScript bundle (often hundreds of kilobytes) and execute the entire initialization pipeline before React can render a single pixel of article content. Until main.jsx runs, the screen remains completely white. Furthermore, search engine crawlers that do not execute client-side JavaScript perceive an empty page.

To overcome this blank initial state, full-stack architectures employ server-side rendering. With server-side rendering, a server executes React components beforehand and sends a fully populated HTML document on the very first network response. When HTML is pre-rendered on a server, React attaches using hydrateRoot rather than createRoot (Lecture 104).

main

The entry file. Calls createRoot with the root element and renders App once.

A developer accustomed to older static web workflows expects HTML to live directly in index.html, opens files with a double-click, and assumes every distinct widget requires a separate mount call. In React 19 with modern build tooling, index.html provides only an empty container element, build tools translate modular code into browser-compatible JavaScript, main.jsx binds the container to React via createRoot, .render(<App />) displays the root component once, and all subsequent layout additions join the component tree descending from App.

Where you will meet this

  1. Every new Vite project: Running npm create vite@latest scaffoldings the identical index.html with an empty <div id="root"></div> and standard main.jsx entry file.
  2. Deploying static production builds: Uploading compiled assets to platforms like Cloudflare Pages or AWS S3 requires transferring the dist/ directory generated by npm run build.
  3. Embedding React into legacy systems: Adding an interactive component (such as a search autocomplete widget or interactive calculator) into an existing Rails or Django page uses createRoot targeted to that specific widget container.
  4. Upgrading legacy codebases: Modernizing older React 16 or 17 codebases requires replacing deprecated ReactDOM.render calls with createRoot.
  5. Architectural framework transitions: Migrating to full-stack frameworks like Next.js or Remix eliminates manual main.jsx files, as the framework manages mounting automatically.

For the interview

  • Hidden Signal: Interviewers use this question to assess whether a candidate understands the transition between physical browser DOM nodes and React's virtual component architecture. Strong candidates trace the complete path from network request to initial paint.
  • Classic Trap: Answering that React writes component HTML directly into index.html on disk. React builds the DOM dynamically in browser memory at runtime after scripts execute.
  • What is Actually Going On: The browser loads index.html, constructs an empty DOM container, and defers main.jsx via module script semantics. Vite transforms JSX into JavaScript function calls. createRoot initializes React's internal fiber root, and root.render initiates concurrent reconciliation to construct the physical DOM.
  • Where It Gets Tricky: How many roots does an application have? Exactly one for a pure React application; multiple roots only when embedding React widgets into separate areas of a legacy page. What happens if the query ID is misspelled? getElementById returns null, causing createRoot to throw an uncaught exception. Can code immediately following root.render inspect rendered DOM nodes? No, because render queues work asynchronously.

Glossary

  • Mounting: The process of initializing a React application and rendering its virtual component tree into a physical browser DOM container for the first time.
  • Build tool: A developer tool (such as Vite) that transforms modern JSX, TypeScript, and bare module imports into standard browser-executable JavaScript.
  • Module script: A <script type="module"> element that supports ES module imports and automatically defers execution until the HTML document has finished parsing.
  • createRoot: The mounting API provided by react-dom/client that initializes a concurrent React root container bound to a specific host DOM element.
  • React root: The controller object returned by createRoot that manages rendering and unmounting within a designated DOM container.
  • root.render: The method on a React root that schedules a virtual element tree to be rendered into the root container. Replaced legacy ReactDOM.render.

Summary

Mounting: the browser loads one page, and React fills one element of it with our components

❒ The root element: the page arrives with one empty element
  • ALWAYS leave <div id="root"> empty in index.html, and write everything the page shows in components.
  • NEVER type content inside the root element; React removes it on its first render.
❒ The build tool: the page's code arrives as plain JavaScript
  • ALWAYS open the project through npm run dev and its localhost address while you work.
  • IF the site goes to a server THEN send the dist folder from npm run build, checked first with npm run preview.
  • NEVER double-click index.html, in src or in dist; a file:// page stays blank.
❒ The React root: the page hands that one element to React
  • ALWAYS pass createRoot the element itself, found by the same id that index.html gives it.
  • NEVER call createRoot inside a component; it belongs in main.jsx, once.
❒ The initial render: the page shows the root component in that element
  • ALWAYS call render once, with one argument: the root component written as a tag.
  • NEVER copy ReactDOM.render from an old tutorial; React 19 removed it.
❒ One root per app: the page grows inside the root component
  • IF the app is built fully with React THEN add each new part of the page as a tag inside App, with one root and one render.
  • IF React runs only parts of an existing page THEN give each React area its own element and its own root.

One empty element, plain JavaScript, one root, one render, and the rest inside the root component.
