Lecture 10: Conditional Rendering in React

Interview Question

CORE

How do you show, hide, or switch JSX based on a condition?

  • Every article card on your site shows a title, an author, and a short summary.
  • Some parts belong only to some articles: a "New" label, a comment count, a sign-in prompt for visitors.
  • How does one component show a part in one case and leave it out in another?

Some parts of a page appear only in some cases

Look at any website and count the parts that appear only sometimes. An online shop marks certain products "Sale". A messaging client shows a counter only when unread messages have arrived. A blog asks visitors to sign in, while greeting subscribers by name. The overall layout stays the same, while underlying data determines which parts appear. Every React developer meets the same question: how does a component show, hide, or switch a part of the page based on a condition?

The first answer comes from HTML and CSS. Every standard DOM element can carry the hidden boolean attribute, operating like the disabled attribute from Lecture 4:

Hiding with CSS
1<span className="new-label" hidden={!isNew}>New</span>
Browser hides tag

When isNew evaluates to false, !isNew evaluates to true, causing the browser to apply the hidden attribute. The element remains in the live DOM tree: the Elements panel shows <span class="new-label" hidden="">New</span> and the browser rendering engine skips painting it. Applying a CSS class with display: none behaves identically. This is hiding with CSS: the DOM node exists, and only visual presentation is turned off. It fits a user interface widget that must retain its exact position and internal state while hidden.

The second answer is React's approach: omit the element from the JSX tree entirely:

Conditional rendering
1{isNew && <span className="new-label">New</span>}
Builds node if true

We read this as: if isNew is truthy, evaluate to the <span>; otherwise evaluate to false. When isNew is false, this expression hands React nothing to construct, so the Elements panel contains no <span> element. This mechanism is conditional rendering: each time a component executes, it decides which JSX elements to return, and React creates only those nodes in the DOM. React provides no proprietary template syntax for conditions; the choice relies entirely on standard JavaScript expressions and statements. Conditional rendering fits every dynamic element driven by data, and every element whose data might be missing, because unrendered JSX expressions never execute their children.

Two ways to show a part of the page only in some cases

1. Show a part only in some cases by hiding with CSS (HTML and Lecture 4): the element is always in the DOM, and an attribute such as hidden tells the browser not to draw it. 2. Show a part only in some cases with conditional rendering (this chapter): the component returns the element only when the condition holds, and otherwise React builds nothing.

This chapter focuses on conditional rendering. Everything follows one central anchor: conditional rendering, which means that each time it runs, a component chooses which JSX to return. The branching choices grow one piece at a time across our curriculum axis: none, one or nothing, one of two, and one of many. Lecture 73 returns to CSS-based hiding through React's <Activity> component, specifically for keeping user input and state alive while hidden.

This lesson answers four progressive architectural questions:

  1. Some days there is no featured article. How does the featured card show nothing instead of breaking the page?
  2. The "New" label should show only on new articles, and the comment count only when there are comments. Do I need an if for that?
  3. Signed-in readers see the summary, visitors see a sign-in prompt. Do I write two returns?
  4. The comment line needs three wordings: no comments, one comment, many comments. Can I put one ternary inside another?

What we build on

  • Lecture 1: What is React: document.getElementById locates an element by its id, and the Elements panel inspects the live DOM nodes currently constructed in the browser.
  • Lecture 2: Component anatomy: React executes a component function whenever a JSX tag invokes it. console.log writes diagnostic output to the Console panel, and in Strict Mode, component function bodies execute twice in development. A function lacking an explicit return value returns undefined.
  • Lecture 3: JSX syntax: An object stores key-value pairs as properties, accessed via dot notation: article.title. When a build fails to parse source code, Vite displays an error overlay covering the browser viewport.
  • Lecture 4: Curly braces in JSX: Curly braces inside JSX embed an expression that computes a value. JavaScript statements like if belong above the return statement. The ternary operator selects between two values: isLive ? 'Live now' : 'Recorded' Numbers render directly to the screen, whereas true, false, null, and undefined produce no visible output. The + operator concatenates strings.
  • Lecture 6: Props: A component receives props as a single object and unpacks properties using destructuring: function ArticleCard({ article }) Quoted attributes pass raw strings, whereas curly braces pass live values. Logical OR (||) and nullish coalescing (??) supply fallback values. Reading a property on a non-object throws a runtime TypeError.
  • Lecture 7: Children: The children prop receives elements passed between a component's opening and closing tags. An array stores multiple ordered values.
  • Lecture 8: Modules: Components such as ArticleCard reside in separate modular files, requiring explicit imports in parent files.

The card now receives one article object

Until now, ArticleCard received separate individual props: title and author. Because our article model now tracks summaries, publication status, and comment counts, each article travels as a single self-contained object passed via an article prop. These objects are defined at the top of ArticleList.jsx:

ArticleList.jsx
3const park = {
4 title: 'New Park Opens Today',
5 author: 'Mary Jones',
6 summary: 'The park on Main Street opens at noon.',
7 isNew: true,
A new article
8 commentCount: 3,
Three comments so far
9};

Our second article, rain, is authored by Oliver Brooks. It is not new (isNew: false) and has no comments (commentCount: 0). ArticleList renders both cards by passing their respective article objects alongside an isSignedIn authentication boolean: <ArticleCard article={park} isSignedIn={isSignedIn} /> Inside ArticleCard, dot notation accesses properties from the prop:

ArticleCard.jsx
1export default function ArticleCard({ article }) {
2 return (
3 <article className="card">
4 <h2>{article.title}</h2>
A property of the object
5 <p className="author">{article.author}</p>
6 <p>{article.summary}</p>
7 </article>
8 );
9}

On days when no featured story is selected, the featured data slot is empty. JavaScript represents the intentional absence of an object using null. Attempting to read a property from null immediately throws a TypeError: Cannot read properties of null The optional chaining operator (?.) allows safe navigation by evaluating to undefined instead of throwing when the target object is null:

Reading a property of null
1const article = null;
2article?.title;
Undefined, no error
3article.title;
WRONG: TypeError: Cannot read properties of null

JavaScript sorts every value into truthy or falsy

Conditional branching requires determining whether an expression evaluates to yes or no. When supplied with non-boolean values, JavaScript coerces them into a boolean. Exactly six values evaluate to false, known as falsy values: false, the number 0, an empty string '', null, undefined, and NaN. All other values evaluate to true and are called truthy: true, every non-zero number, any non-empty string, all plain objects, and all arrays (including empty arrays []).

Truthy and falsy
1if (0) { }
Falsy: the block is skipped
2if ('false') { }
3if ([]) { }
Truthy: an empty array is still an object

The logical NOT operator (!) inverts truthiness: !null evaluates to true, allowing if (!article) to read cleanly as "if there is no article". Comparison operators evaluate strictly to true or false: count > 0 checks if a counter exceeds zero, and strict equality count === 1 verifies that a value is identical in both type and value.

&& gives back one of its two sides

The logical AND operator (&&) evaluates expressions from left to right. When its left-hand operand is falsy, evaluation short-circuits and returns the left operand itself. When the left operand is truthy, evaluation continues and returns the right operand. It acts as the mirror of logical OR (||), which returns its left operand when truthy.

The logical AND
1true && 'New';
2false && 'New';
False: the left side itself
30 && 'New';
0: the left side itself, a number

Logical && does not inherently produce a boolean. It returns one of its two operands verbatim.

An if can end a function early

A return statement executed inside an if block immediately halts execution of the enclosing function, preventing any subsequent lines from running. This pattern is an early return.

An early return
1function firstLetter(name) {
2 if (!name) {
3 return '';
Ends here, the next line never runs
4 }
5 return name[0];
6}

When handling multiple discrete outcomes, if statements can be chained with else if and a terminal else. JavaScript evaluates each condition sequentially from top to bottom, executing exclusively the first matching block:

if, else if, and else
1let size;
2if (count === 0) {
3 size = 'none';
4} else if (count === 1) {
5 size = 'one';
6} else {
7 size = 'many';
Every other count
8}

Principles of React: Conditional Rendering

Everything in this lesson comes down to one idea: conditional rendering, which means that each time it runs, a component chooses which JSX to return. First, returning null, which means choosing to show nothing: when there is nothing to show, the component returns null at its very top, before any line reads the missing data. Second, logical AND, which means choosing one piece or nothing: we put a true or false value on its left side, never a bare number, because a zero shows up on the page. Third, the ternary operator, which means choosing between two pieces: we write the choice inside the JSX, so the parts both cases share are written only once. Fourth, an if statement and a variable, which means choosing among many pieces: we make the choice above the return and place the result in the JSX, instead of putting one ternary inside another.

QUESTION 1

A missing featured article blanks the whole page

On our article site, App.jsx mounts a featured article slot above the main article catalog. On days without an active breaking story, featured is set to null:

App.jsx
6const featured = null;
No featured article today
7
8export default function App() {
9 return (
10 <>
11 <SiteHeader />
12 <ArticleCard article={featured} />
Article is null

When this code runs, the entire browser window goes completely blank. The header and both standard articles vanish. In the Console panel, Chrome logs an uncaught runtime error: TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'title') followed by React's diagnostic warning: The above error occurred in the <ArticleCard> component

Some days there is no featured article. How does the featured card show nothing instead of breaking the page?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. An uncaught error during component rendering crashes React's entire component tree, wiping out all previously mounted UI.

Developers arriving from static HTML workflows often expect missing data to leave an empty placeholder box on the screen or assume that adding a CSS hiding class can suppress the element. In React, however, a component is an executable function. When ArticleCard runs with article={null}, execution reaches {article.title}, attempting to read the property title on null. This throws an unhandled JavaScript TypeError. Because the error occurs inside React's rendering pipeline without an error boundary (Lecture 72), React unmounts the entire application container to prevent displaying corrupted UI.

Attempting to hide the card using a CSS class name like <article className={article ? 'card' : 'hidden'}> fails completely. The function must still evaluate the nested {article.title} expression before producing the JSX element, triggering the exact same fatal crash. Similarly, attempting an imperative DOM query like document.getElementById('featured-card').classList.add('hidden') throws because the DOM node does not yet exist while the component function executes.

A common junior attempt uses optional chaining:

ArticleCard.jsx
4 <h2>{article?.title}</h2>
Undefined, no crash
5 <p className="author">{article?.author}</p>
6 <p>{article?.summary}</p>

Optional chaining prevents the crash because article?.title evaluates safely to undefined. However, React still constructs the outer <article className="card"> container. The Elements panel reveals a ghost card containing empty tags: <article class="card"><h2></h2><p class="author"></p><p></p></article> A blank card border and empty margins linger visibly on the page.

The senior solution is an early return returning null:

ArticleCard.jsx
1export default function ArticleCard({ article }) {
2 if (!article) {
3 return null;
No article: no card at all
4 }
5 return (

Placing if (!article) { return null; } at the very top of the function intercepts execution before any property reads occur. Because null renders no DOM elements, React leaves the featured slot completely empty. The rest of the page (the header, article list, and footer) renders cleanly.

The component still executes: a console.log placed at the top of ArticleCard prints diagnostic lines for the featured card. If the parent instead guards the tag using {featured && <ArticleCard article={featured} />} the component function never executes at all on days when featured is null.

The featured slot when article is null
code                 page                     Elements panel
article.title        blank, all of it         nothing in #root
article?.title       an empty box             <article class="card"><h2></h2>...
if (!article) null   header and two articles  no <article> for the slot
PRINCIPLE 1

Returning null: choosing to show nothing

When a component has nothing to show for its props, it returns null from an if at its very top, before any line reads the missing data; when the parent decides whether the component appears at all, the parent leaves out its tag instead.

``jsx function Profile({ user }) { if (!user) { return null; // nothing shows, the page stays } return <h2>{user.name}</h2>; } ``

``jsx function Profile({ user }) { return <h2>{user.name}</h2>; // **WRONG:** null user crashes render } ``

QUESTION 2

An article with no comments shows a bare 0

We enhance ArticleCard to display a "New" badge for recent stories and a comment counter for reader discussions:

ArticleCard.jsx
6 <article className="card">
7 {article.isNew && <span className="new-label">New</span>}
Label
8 <h2>{article.title}</h2>
9 <p className="author">{article.author}</p>
10 <p>{article.summary}</p>
11 {article.commentCount && <p>{article.commentCount} comments</p>}
12 </article>

We load the page. The park article renders as expected: it displays the New badge and "3 comments". But the rain article exhibits an unexpected flaw: while the "New" badge is hidden, a standalone, unformatted number 0 appears right beneath the summary.

The "New" label should show only on new articles, and the comment count only when there are comments. Do I need an if for that?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. Placing a numeric expression on the left side of && renders a literal 0 into the DOM whenever the count is zero.

Developers frequently conceptualize the logical AND operator (&&) as an inline if statement. But as demonstrated in our runway review, JavaScript's && operator does not return a boolean; it short-circuits and returns the operand itself:

The left side decides what && gives back
card   left side             && gives back   the page shows
park   isNew: true           <span>New</span>    New
rain   isNew: false          false               nothing
park   commentCount: 3       <p>3 comments</p>   3 comments
rain   commentCount: 0       0                   0

For the "New" label, article.isNew contains true or false. When false, && evaluates to false. Because React treats boolean values (false, true), null, and undefined as non-rendering tokens, nothing is inserted into the DOM.

For the comment counter, however, rain.commentCount contains the number 0. In JavaScript, 0 is falsy, causing && to short-circuit and return 0. But unlike false or null, numbers are legitimate render targets in React (as established in Lecture 4). React converts the number 0 to a text node and renders it directly to the browser DOM.

The fix is to ensure the left-hand side of && evaluates strictly to a boolean by using a comparison operator:

ArticleCard.jsx
11 {article.commentCount > 0 && (
12 <p>{article.commentCount} comments</p>
13 )}
Boolean comparison

Because 0 > 0 evaluates to false, the expression returns false, causing React to render nothing for stories without comments. Alternative conversions include Boolean(article.commentCount) or double negation !!article.commentCount.

Beware of other falsy traps: passing a string prop like isNew="false" passes a non-empty string, which is truthy and mistakenly displays the badge. Similarly, an empty array [] is truthy, meaning tags && <ul>...</ul> renders an empty list container; Lecture 11 guards {tags.length > 0 && <ul>...</ul>} around a list built with map.

PRINCIPLE 2

Logical AND: choosing one piece or nothing

To show a piece or nothing, we write condition && <Piece /> with a true or false value on the left, such as commentCount > 0, never a bare number.

``jsx const count = 0; {count > 0 && <p>{count} messages</p>} // shows nothing ``

``jsx const count = 0; {count && <p>{count} messages</p>} // **PROBLEMATIC:** renders a bare 0 ``

QUESTION 3

Two returns drift apart when one of them changes

We need to differentiate content for registered members and unauthenticated guests. Signed-in readers should see the full article summary, while visitors should receive a sign-in callout. A developer implements this requirement using two full return statements inside ArticleCard:

ArticleCard.jsx
1export default function ArticleCard({ article, isSignedIn }) {
2 if (!article) {
3 return null;
4 }
5 if (isSignedIn) {
6 return (
7 <article className="card">
8 <h2>{article.title}</h2>
9 <p className="author">{article.author}</p>
Added later
10 <p>{article.summary}</p>
11 </article>
12 );
13 }
14 return (
15 <article className="card">
16 <h2>{article.title}</h2>
PROBLEMATIC: author omitted
17 <p>Sign in to read this article.</p>
18 </article>
19 );
20}

Later, an editor requests that author bylines appear on article cards. The developer updates the component by adding <p className="author">{article.author}</p> to the first return block. When testing with isSignedIn = false, visitors see the article title and sign-in prompt, but the author's byline is missing.

Signed-in readers see the summary, visitors see a sign-in prompt. Do I write two returns?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. Duplicating shared markup across multiple return statements leads to maintenance drift where changes in one branch fail to reach the other.

Using an if statement with two distinct returns seems intuitive: it produces the correct initial DOM output, and each branch reads as an isolated block of markup. However, duplicating the shared wrapper elements (<article className="card">) and common header elements (<h2>{article.title}</h2>) creates architectural fragility. Whenever layout requirements change, developers must remember to apply identical edits in multiple locations. In our code, adding the author byline to the signed-in branch left the guest branch out of date.

The only piece of the component that differs between states is a single paragraph. Therefore, the conditional choice belongs inline inside the JSX tree. While an if statement cannot sit inside JSX curly braces, the ternary operator (? :) evaluates as an expression and can seamlessly branch between two JSX nodes:

ArticleCard.jsx
5 return (
6 <article className="card">
7 <h2>{article.title}</h2>
8 <p className="author">{article.author}</p>
Written once
9 {isSignedIn ? (
10 <p>{article.summary}</p>
11 ) : (
12 <p>Sign in to read this article.</p>
13 )}
14 </article>

By consolidating the component into a single return block, the outer <article>, the heading, and the author byline are declared exactly once. The ternary operator targets strictly the dynamic paragraph. When JSX branches span multiple lines, wrapping each branch in parentheses preserves formatting and visual clarity.

A ternary expression always requires both branches. Omitting the colon clause triggers a compiler syntax error: [PARSE_ERROR] Expected ':' but found '}' For cases requiring one branch or nothing, logical && remains the appropriate pattern. Two separate return statements remain valid only when the two branches share zero common structure, such as returning null when data is missing.

PRINCIPLE 3

The ternary operator: choosing between two pieces

To show one of two pieces in the same place, we write condition ? <A /> : <B /> inside the JSX and keep the markup both cases share written once; two whole returns fit only when the two cases share nothing.

``jsx <h2>{name}</h2> {isSignedIn ? <Summary /> : <SignInPrompt />} // only this differs ``

``jsx if (isSignedIn) { return <><h2>{name}</h2><Summary /></>; } return <><h2>{name}</h2><SignInPrompt /></>; // **PROBLEMATIC:** duplicate markup ``

QUESTION 4

Three comment wordings tangle into nested ternaries

Our design team updates the comment section specifications. The comment footer must now display one of three tailored messages depending on discussion activity: "No comments yet" when count is zero, "1 comment" when singular, and "5 comments" for plural counts. A developer writes nested ternaries inside the JSX:

ArticleCard.jsx
9 <p className="comments">
10 {count === 0
11 ? 'No comments yet'
12 : count === 1
13 ? '1 comment'
14 : count + ' comments'}
PROBLEMATIC: nested ternaries
15 </p>

Testing with articles containing 0, 1, and 5 comments reveals that the rendered output is visually accurate. However, during a team pull request review, senior engineers flag the construct as unmaintainable.

The comment line needs three wordings: no comments, one comment, many comments. Can I put one ternary inside another?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. Nesting ternary expressions creates convoluted syntax that obscures logic and increases cognitive overhead.

A single ternary operator cleanly models a binary choice. However, chaining multiple ternaries together requires the reader to mentally pair question marks with their respective colons. If a fourth condition is introduced (such as "Discussion closed"), the expression cascades into an impenetrable pyramid of conditions.

Because JavaScript statements are fully permitted above the return statement, multiple discrete branches are best handled using a standard if...else if...else chain that assigns its result to a local variable:

ArticleCard.jsx
5 const count = article.commentCount;
6 let commentText;
7 if (count === 0) {
8 commentText = 'No comments yet';
9 } else if (count === 1) {
10 commentText = '1 comment';
11 } else {
12 commentText = count + ' comments';
5 comments
13 }
ArticleCard.jsx
17 <p className="comments">{commentText}</p>
Placed in JSX

Each branching case now occupies a single, easily readable line above the return block. The JSX return then embeds the resolved text or element via {commentText}. This local variable can store plain strings, numbers, or full JSX element trees.

If the number of conditions expands further (such as handling ten different status types), the logic can be factored into a dictionary lookup object or delegated to a dedicated helper component. Remember that syntax shortcuts like && and the ternary operator are entirely optional conveniences; clean if statements remain a standard, robust architectural choice.

PRINCIPLE 4

An if statement and a variable: choosing among many pieces

When a choice has more than two cases, we pick the piece with if, else if, and else above the return, store it in a variable, and place the variable in the JSX, instead of nesting one ternary inside another.

``jsx let label; if (count === 0) { label = 'None'; } else if (count === 1) { label = 'One'; } else { label = 'Many'; } return <p>{label}</p>; // one case per line above ``

``jsx return ( <p>{count === 0 ? 'None' : count === 1 ? 'One' : 'Many'}</p> ); // **PROBLEMATIC:** nested ternaries obscure logic ``

Is hiding with display: none ever the better choice?

⚡ IN THE WILD

Hiding with CSS vs. Conditional Rendering

In Question 2, the rain article produced no <span> in the DOM, whereas the CSS hidden attribute retains <span class="new-label" hidden="">New</span> When is CSS hiding preferable to conditional rendering?

When an element is conditionally omitted from the JSX tree, React unmounts it completely. If that element is later re-introduced, React mounts a fresh DOM node, discarding any ephemeral DOM state (such as user-entered text, scroll position, or uncommitted form inputs).

Hiding with CSS maintains the element in the DOM tree, preserving its internal state and avoiding the lifecycle cost of re-initialization. For dynamic visibility toggles, Lecture 14 introduces stateful user interactions, while Lecture 73 introduces React's built-in <Activity> component, which hides views while preserving cached state. For data-driven display rules and guarding against missing objects, conditional rendering remains the essential and correct standard.

Case Study
Let's Design a Practical Example

Each question isolated a specific branching technique. Now we assemble the complete article site across our real component architecture. We support a featured article slot that is empty today, the park article (new with 3 comments), and the rain article (not new with 0 comments). Our card coordinates four concurrent decisions: whether to mount, whether to show the "New" badge, whether to render full text or a sign-in prompt, and which comment wording to display. Each step applies one principle in thread order. Keep the dev server running and inspect both the live browser output and the Elements panel.

Component Summary

App

The root component owns the featured slot. It leaves out the whole section, heading and card, when there is no featured article, because the heading is its own markup. Why not let the card decide? Because the card cannot remove a heading it does not own.

ArticleList

The list holds two article objects and isSignedIn, and passes them to two cards. It makes no choice of its own: the data it passes decides what each card shows.

ArticleCardarticle, isSignedIn

The card makes four choices, in order: nothing when there is no article, the label only when isNew is true, the summary or the prompt, and one of three comment wordings. Each choice sits where it belongs: the guard at the top, the wording above the return, the label and the summary inside the JSX.

A developer accustomed to older static web paradigms expects to toggle element visibility with CSS classes, reads && as a simple synonym for if, and copies markup across multiple return branches. In React 19, our featured slot rendered nothing without crashing the application, the "New" badge appeared exclusively on fresh content, the bare numeric 0 never leaked into the DOM, visitors and members shared a single robust card template, and three comment phrasings were evaluated cleanly as standard JavaScript lines. Each step fulfilled one foundational principle: returning null to show nothing, using boolean logical && for one piece or nothing, using the ternary operator for binary choices, and using if with a local variable for multi-branch logic.

Where you will meet this

  1. A notification badge with a count: Displaying an unread message badge only when notifications exist. The count is numeric, requiring count > 0 && <Badge /> rather than count && <Badge />.
  2. Visitor vs. member navigation bars: Presenting a "Sign in" button to unauthenticated visitors while displaying an account avatar and username to logged-in subscribers.
  3. Asynchronous data loading states: Rendering a loading spinner while data is fetching, returning null or a skeleton screen when data is empty, and rendering content once available.
  4. Multi-state workflow indicators: Displaying order tracking statuses ("Placed", "Processing", "Shipped", "Delivered") computed via an if...else if chain into a local variable or status lookup dictionary.
  5. Preserving form state in tab panels: Choosing between conditional rendering and CSS-based visibility toggles when hiding background panels without destroying user input (Lecture 73).

For the interview

  • The Hidden Signal: Interviewers assess whether a candidate understands how React interacts with JavaScript evaluation rules. Strong candidates immediately clarify that React has no special conditional syntax, explain how JSX unmounting affects the physical DOM versus CSS hiding, and proactively highlight the numeric zero trap.
  • The Classic Trap: Stating that {count && <Component />} is equivalent to an inline if. In JavaScript, 0 && <Component /> returns 0, causing React to render a literal text node 0 into the DOM. The solution is explicit boolean coercion: {count > 0 && <Component />} or {Boolean(count) && <Component />} Another common trap is attempting to hide missing data with CSS, which fails because property access on null crashes during component execution.
  • What is Actually Going On: React executes component functions to build virtual element trees. When a component returns null, React creates no physical DOM node for that component. Inside JSX, falsy values like false, null, and undefined produce no DOM nodes. The ternary operator evaluates strictly one expression, guaranteeing that shared surrounding markup remains deduplicated.
  • Where It Gets Tricky: What does a component return to render nothing? It returns null; in React 19, returning undefined from a bare return; also renders nothing without throwing, but returning null remains the intentional idiomatic standard. Is returning null identical to omitting the JSX tag in the parent? No: returning null still executes the component function (invoking logs and hooks), whereas omitting the tag prevents the component from running at all. Why does isNew="false" display the badge? Quoting the attribute passes a string, and non-empty strings are truthy; passing isNew={false} in braces supplies a real boolean. What happens to unmounted DOM nodes? React completely destroys them; when re-rendered, they are re-created from scratch without preserved state.

Glossary

  • Conditional rendering: The process of choosing which JSX elements to return and mount in the DOM based on runtime conditions using standard JavaScript syntax.
  • Early return: A pattern where a function terminates immediately via a return statement inside a top-level condition, preventing subsequent logic from running.
  • Truthy and falsy: The inherent boolean classification of JavaScript values in conditional contexts. Falsy values include false, 0, '', null, undefined, and NaN; all other values are truthy.
  • Logical AND (&&): An operator returning its left operand if falsy, and its right operand otherwise. Used in JSX to conditionally render an element when the left operand is a boolean.
  • Ternary operator: An inline expression (condition ? exprIfTrue : exprIfFalse) that resolves to one of two values based on a condition.
  • Hiding with CSS: Retaining an element in the browser DOM while toggling its visual visibility via attributes like hidden or CSS properties like display: none.

Beyond the basics

  • Every form of conditional rendering (https://react.dev/learn/conditional-rendering)
  • How a choice changes the tree (https://react.dev/learn/understanding-your-ui-as-a-tree)
  • MDN: Logical AND (https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Operators/Logical_AND)
  • MDN: Optional chaining (https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Operators/Optional_chaining)
  • MDN: The hidden attribute (https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/HTML/Global_attributes/hidden)

Summary

Conditional rendering: each time it runs, a component chooses which JSX to return

❒ Returning null: choosing to show nothing
  • IF a component has nothing to show for its props THEN return null from an if at its very top, before any line reads the missing data.
  • IF the parent owns the markup around the component THEN the parent leaves out the tag instead.
  • NEVER hide a part whose data may be missing with CSS alone; its JSX still runs and throws.
❒ Logical AND: choosing one piece or nothing
  • ALWAYS put a true or false value on the left of &&, such as count > 0.
  • NEVER put a bare number on the left of &&; a 0 shows up on the page.
❒ The ternary operator: choosing between two pieces
  • IF two cases share markup THEN write the ternary inside the JSX, around the part that differs.
  • IF the two cases share nothing THEN two whole returns are fine.
❒ An if statement and a variable: choosing among many pieces
  • IF a choice has more than two cases THEN choose with if, else if, and else above the return, and place the variable in the JSX.
  • NEVER put one ternary inside another; each new case adds a level to untangle.

Nothing, one or nothing, one of two, and one of many.

DO THIS:

code.txt
1function ArticleCard({ article, isSignedIn }) {
2 if (!article) {
3 return null;
4 }
5 return (
6 <article className="card">
7 <h2>{article.title}</h2>
8 {isSignedIn ? <p>{article.summary}</p> : <p>Sign in to read.</p>}
9 {article.commentCount > 0 && <p>{article.commentCount} comments</p>}
10 </article>
11 );
12}

DO NOT DO THIS:

code.txt
1function ArticleCard({ article }) {
2 return (
3 <article className="card">
4 <h2>{article.title}</h2>
5 {article.commentCount && <p>{article.commentCount} comments</p>}
6 </article>
7 );
8}

(the hidden attribute)		CONDITIONAL RENDERING
(this chapter)

or a hiding class		No element at all
when the condition is false
When the data is missingThe JSX still runs:
article.title throws		An if at the top returns null
before any line reads it
What is inside the partKept while it is hiddenBuilt again when it comes back
The forms it takesOne attribute:
hidden={!isNew}		null, &&, the ternary,
or a variable chosen with if

Lecture 11: Rendering Lists and Keys

Interview Question

CORE

How do you render a list from an array, and why does React demand a key on every item?

  • Your article list writes one <ArticleCard /> tag by hand for every article on the site.
  • Thirty articles would mean thirty tags, and the console warns about a "key" as soon as you shorten them.
  • How does one array of articles become one card per article, and what is the key for?

A page shows many items of the same kind

A site shows the same kind of item many times: articles in a list, comments under an article, products in a shop. Every item has the same design, and only its data differs. So every React developer meets the same question: how does a component show one piece of markup for each item? Until now we have answered it by hand. ArticleList writes three <ArticleCard /> tags, one per article, and a fourth article would need a fourth tag.

This chapter turns the data itself into the cards. It follows one idea from the first question to the last: rendering a list, which means that an array of data becomes an array of elements, each with its own key. It goes in two stretches. First the items become elements: every item, then only some items. Then the elements get names: what a name does, and where it goes.

This lesson answers four questions:

  1. I have the articles in an array. How do I show a card for each without writing every tag?
  2. Each topic gets its own section with only its articles, and an empty section needs a message. How?
  3. The cards show fine. Why does React insist on a key?
  4. I put the key in, and the warning is still there. Where does it go?

What we build on

  • Lecture 1: What is React: With npm run dev running, a saved file updates the open page, and text typed into a box on the page stays where it is.
  • Lecture 2: Component anatomy: console.log prints to the Console panel, and a function that ends with no return value gives back undefined, which shows nothing.
  • Lecture 3: JSX syntax: Each tag becomes a React element, a plain object. A Fragment, <> and </>, groups elements and adds nothing to the page, and it takes no attributes.
  • Lecture 4: Curly braces in JSX: Braces hold an expression, code that gives back a value; a statement such as if or for cannot go inside them. An array of texts in braces shows its items one after another.
  • Lecture 6: Props: A component receives its props as one object and reads them by name, such as { article }.
  • Lecture 7: Children: An array holds several values in order, and {...rest} writes every property of an object as a prop.
  • Lecture 8: Modules: A file shares a value with a named export, export const articles and another file brings it in with braces, import { articles } from '../articles.js'
  • Lecture 10: Conditional rendering: A number on the left of && shows on the page, so count > 0 turns it into true or false. The ternary chooses between two pieces, and name[0] reads the first item of a text by its position.

The articles move into a file of their own

The three tags in ArticleList differ only in their data, so the data moves out of the JSX into one array, and the array goes into a file of its own, src/articles.js, with a named export from Lecture 8. Each article is an object with four properties: an id, a number that belongs to that article and to no other, then its title, its author, and its topic.

articles.js
1export const articles = [
2 {
3 id: 1,
Belongs to this article only
4 title: 'New Park Opens Today',
5 author: 'Mary Jones',
6 topic: 'City',
7 },
8];

The second article is "Rain Expected This Weekend" by Oliver Brooks, id: 2, topic Weather; the third is "Five Soups for Cold Days" by Samantha Robinson, id: 3, topic Food. ArticleList imports the array and still writes one tag per article, reading each article by its position: articles[0], articles[1], and articles[2], counted from 0. For this lesson, each card displays the title, the author, and an interactive comment box, <input placeholder="Write a comment" />

ArticleList.jsx
6 <main>
7 <ArticleCard article={articles[0]} />
The first article
8 <ArticleCard article={articles[1]} />
9 <ArticleCard article={articles[2]} />
One tag per article
10 </main>

An arrow function is a short way to write a function

Every function so far began with the word function. JavaScript has a shorter way to write a small function, the arrow function: the parameters, then =>, then what the function gives back. When nothing but an expression follows the arrow, the function gives that expression back by itself, with no return.

Two ways to write one function
1function double(n) {
2 return n * 2;
The classic form
3}
4const double = n => n * 2;
The arrow form: n in, n * 2 back

When a curly brace follows the arrow, the function has a block body: room for several lines, and a return is needed to give anything back. Without it, the function gives back undefined. An arrow function gives back the expression right after =>; after => {, it gives back only what return names.

The block body
1const half = n => {
2 return n / 2;
With a curly brace, return is needed
3};
4const broken = n => { n / 2; };
PROBLEMATIC: yields undefined

Three array methods take a function

An array has methods, functions that belong to it (Lecture 9), and three of them take a function and call it once for each item. forEach() only calls the function and gives back undefined. map() collects what the function gives back for each item into a new array of the same length. filter() keeps the items for which the function gives back true, in a new, often shorter array. length, a property with no parentheses, counts the items.

Three array methods
1articles.forEach(article => article.title);
PROBLEMATIC: returns undefined
2articles.map(article => article.title);
3articles.filter(article => article.topic === 'Food');
One article
4articles.length;

map() turns every item into something new, filter() chooses which items stay, and forEach() gives back nothing at all.

Principles of React: Rendering Lists

Everything in this lesson comes down to one idea: rendering a list, which means that an array of data becomes an array of elements, each with its own key.

First, mapping, which means turning every item into an element: we call map on the array, and the arrow function gives back one element for each item.

Second, filtering, which means turning only some items into elements: we filter the array before we map it, and when nothing is left, we show a message instead of an empty space.

Third, keys, which means naming each element so React can tell the items apart: each key comes from the item's own id, so a new item at the top leaves every other item with its own element.

Fourth, the key's place, which means naming the element the map gives back: the key goes on the tag written inside the map, never inside the child component.

QUESTION 1

A map with curly braces shows no cards

To stop writing one tag per article by hand, we replace the three tags of ArticleList with a call to articles.map(). We add a curly brace after the arrow to leave room for a second line later:

ArticleList.jsx
6 <main>
7 {articles.map(article => {
8 <ArticleCard article={article} />;
PROBLEMATIC: missing return
9 })}
10 </main>

When we open the page, the header and footer render, but no article cards appear on screen. The page shows an empty space where the catalog should be, and the browser Console panel reports no warnings or errors.

I have the articles in an array. How do I show a card for each without writing every tag?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. An arrow function with a curly brace creates a block body, requiring an explicit return statement to produce an element.

In plain JavaScript, developers often turn to loops when processing collections. But a standard JavaScript for loop is a statement, not an expression, so it cannot be placed inside JSX curly braces. The array method forEach() is an expression, but it always evaluates to undefined, so writing {articles.forEach(...)} inserts nothing into the JSX tree without any diagnostic message.

The array method map() solves this because it is an expression that returns a brand-new array. When JSX curly braces evaluate an array of React elements, React renders each element sequentially in order, matching how an array of text strings displays its values.

In the broken implementation, however, a curly brace immediately follows the arrow: article => { ... }. In JavaScript, this syntax defines a block body. A block body does not automatically return the expression inside it; it requires an explicit return keyword. Without return, the function body evaluates and returns undefined for each item. Consequently, articles.map() returns an array of three undefined values: [undefined, undefined, undefined] Because React renders undefined as empty visual output, the cards vanish completely.

The fix is to return the React element. We can wrap the returned element in parentheses directly after the arrow, or write an explicit return inside the block body:

ArticleList.jsx
7 {articles.map(article => (
8 <ArticleCard article={article} />
Given back for every article
9 ))}

With this change in place, all three cards appear on the page. Because the items lack keys, Chrome logs React's classic warning: Each child in a list should have a unique "key" prop which Question 3 addresses.

The same map, two bodies
article             => { <ArticleCard ... />; }    => ( <ArticleCard ... /> )
New Park ...        undefined                      <ArticleCard> element
Rain Expected ...   undefined                      <ArticleCard> element
Five Soups ...      undefined                      <ArticleCard> element
the page shows      no card                        three cards
PRINCIPLE 1

Mapping: turning every item into an element

To show one element per item, we call map() on the array inside the JSX, and its arrow function gives back the element: right after =>, or with return when the body starts with a curly brace.

In plain JavaScript, a loop writes one thing per item. But a for loop is a statement and cannot go inside the braces, and forEach() gives back nothing. map() is an expression: it calls a function for each item and gives back a new array of what the function returned. React shows an array of elements in order, so one map() gives one element per item. The function must really give the element back. After =>, the expression is given back by itself; after => {, only return gives it back, and without it every item becomes undefined and nothing shows, with no message. Each element still needs a key, as Principle 3 shows.

We should do this:
{items.map(item => (
<Item item={item} />
one element per item
))}
We should not do this:
{items.map(item => {
<Item item={item} />;
PROBLEMATIC: missing return renders nothing
})}
QUESTION 2

An empty topic shows a bare 0

We organize our home page into sections by topic, such as City and Sport. ArticleList receives a topic prop, filters articles.js with articles.filter(), and renders the cards using shown.length && shown.map(...)

ArticleList.jsx
4export default function ArticleList({ topic }) {
5 const shown = articles.filter(article => article.topic === topic);
6 return (
7 <section>
8 <h2>{topic}</h2>
9 {shown.length && (
10 shown.map(article => <ArticleCard article={article} />)
11 )}
PROBLEMATIC: bare length renders 0
12 </section>

In App.jsx, we mount two sections, one for City and one for Sport:

App.jsx
9 <ArticleList topic="City" />
10 <ArticleList topic="Sport" />
No Sport articles yet

The City section displays "New Park Opens Today". But the Sport section, which contains no matching articles, displays the heading "Sport" with a literal, unformatted digit 0 rendered directly beneath it.

Each topic gets its own section with only its articles, and an empty section needs a message. How?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. When the filtered array is empty, shown.length evaluates to 0, causing the logical AND operator to return 0 directly into the DOM.

The filtering strategy works correctly for the City topic. As introduced in our runway, filter() evaluates each item against a predicate test (article.topic === topic) and returns a new array containing only the items that pass. Calling map() afterwards transforms solely those retained items into React elements.

For the Sport category, however, zero articles match. The filter() method returns an empty array []. Calling shown.map() on an empty array would evaluate to another empty array, rendering an empty white gap below the heading without explaining the absence to the reader.

To avoid an empty gap, the code attempted to guard the list with {shown.length && shown.map(...)} But in JavaScript, the logical AND operator (&&) does not produce a boolean. When the left operand is falsy, && short-circuits and evaluates directly to the left operand. Because shown.length is the numeric value 0, the expression evaluates to 0. And as established in Lecture 10, React treats numbers as visible content, painting a literal 0 into the page markup.

The solution is to ask an explicit comparison question, shown.length > 0, and use a ternary expression to render an informative fallback message:

ArticleList.jsx
9 {shown.length > 0 ? (
10 shown.map(article => <ArticleCard article={article} />)
11 ) : (
12 <p>No {topic} articles yet.</p>
No Sport articles yet.
13 )}

With the ternary operator in place, the Sport section renders the heading "Sport" followed cleanly by the fallback paragraph: "No Sport articles yet."

What filter and && give back
section   filter() gives back         shown.length   && gives back    page
City      [New Park Opens Today]      1              [<ArticleCard>]  one card
Sport     []                          0              0                0
PRINCIPLE 2

Filtering: turning only some items into elements

To show only some items, we call filter() before map(); when the filtered array can be empty, we test its length with > 0 and show a message instead.

filter() runs a test for each item and gives back a new array of the items that passed. map() then turns only those into elements, so the filter goes first. A filter can leave nothing: then the array is empty, its length is 0, and map() gives back nothing to show. A bare length on the left of && puts that 0 on the page, because React shows numbers. A real question, length > 0, and a ternary give the reader a message instead.

We should do this:
const shown = items.filter(item => item.isOpen);
{shown.length > 0 ? (
shown.map(item => <Item item={item} />)
cards
) : (
<p>Nothing here yet.</p>
shown when array is empty
)}
We should not do this:
const shown = items.filter(item => item.isOpen);
{shown.length && shown.map(item => <Item item={item} />)}
PROBLEMATIC: renders 0 on page
QUESTION 3

A typed comment jumps to another article

We render ArticleList using articles.map() without specifying any key prop on <ArticleCard />. In the browser, Chrome logs a warning: Each child in a list should have a unique "key" prop Aside from this console message, the catalog appears to render properly.

With the dev server running, we type the phrase "Great news!" into the comment input box of "Rain Expected This Weekend", which currently sits as the second card on screen. We then open articles.js, prepend a brand-new breaking story, "Library Opens on Sundays" by James Smith with id: 4, to the very top of the array, and save the file:

articles.js
1export const articles = [
2 {
3 id: 4,
A new article, first in array
4 title: 'Library Opens on Sundays',
5 author: 'James Smith',
6 topic: 'City',
7 },

Vite pushes the update to the browser. The page re-renders to show four articles. But the comment "Great news!" has vanished from the weather card and now appears inside the comment box of "New Park Opens Today", which is now the second card on screen.

The cards show fine. Why does React insist on a key?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. Without unique keys, React matches elements across renders strictly by array position, mapping existing DOM nodes and their uncommitted input states to different items.

Developers frequently assume that React's key requirement exists merely to quiet compiler warnings. Because the initial visual layout looks identical with or without keys, the requirement can appear purely decorative. The bug reveals itself the instant the collection order changes.

When a component re-renders, React reconciles the newly returned element tree against the tree produced on the prior render pass. To avoid rebuilding the entire DOM from scratch, React attempts to preserve existing DOM nodes and updates only the attributes that changed.

Without keys, React relies on positional matching: it pairs the first new element with the first old element, the second with the second, and so on. When a new article is prepended at index 0, every existing article shifts down by one position. React inspects position 1. Previously, position 1 rendered "Rain Expected This Weekend". Now, position 1 holds "New Park Opens Today". React keeps the existing second DOM <article> container (along with the text "Great news!" typed into its <input> node), and merely overwrites its <h2> title and author paragraph to match the new park data. The user's typed comment is permanently attached to the wrong article.

A common junior impulse is using the array index as the key:

ArticleList.jsx
7 {articles.map((article, index) => (
8 <ArticleCard key={index} article={article} />
The position again
9 ))}

Passing key={index} silences the console warning, but the defect remains completely unchanged. Because the index is nothing more than the item's positional coordinate, React continues matching by array position, moving "Great news!" to the wrong article upon every prepend or reorder.

A key is a stable identifier that names each element across renders. By assigning key={article.id} using the item's unique database identifier, React tracks element identity regardless of layout position:

ArticleList.jsx
7 {articles.map(article => (
8 <ArticleCard key={article.id} article={article} />
Its own name
9 ))}

With key={article.id}, React recognizes that the card with key={2} has moved from position 1 to position 2. React moves the physical DOM node downward, preserving its internal input state, and constructs a fresh DOM node at position 0 for the new library story. The comment "Great news!" remains securely attached to "Rain Expected This Weekend".

Keys operate like file names inside a desktop directory: renaming or reordering files preserves each file's contents, whereas addressing files purely by their visual slot index causes contents to scramble whenever files are added. Generating dynamic keys on the fly using Math.random() breaks reconciliation completely: because the key changes on every render pass, React destroys and recreates every single DOM node on every update, wiping out all active focus and input values. Lecture 12 explores component purity, showing why generating values during a render breaks pure rendering.

The array index is acceptable as a key only for static collections that never insert, delete, or reorder, such as the fixed lines of a poem or hardcoded navigation links.

Where the typed comment goes after the save
by position (no key, or the index)       by key (article.id)
old element 1 -> Library Opens ...       new element      -> Library Opens ...
old element 2 -> New Park ... [Great]    old element id 1 -> New Park ...
old element 3 -> Rain Expected ...       old element id 2 -> Rain ... [Great]
new element   -> Five Soups ...          old element id 3 -> Five Soups ...
PRINCIPLE 3

Keys: naming each element so React can tell the items apart

We give each element a key from the item's own id, so React matches every item with the same element the next time the list is shown; the array index fits only a list that never changes order, and a key made while rendering fits nothing.

When a list is shown again, React matches each new element with one it already built, keeps it, and changes only what differs. Without a key, it matches by position: the first with the first. An item added at the top shifts every item down, so each old element receives the next item's data, and whatever the user typed stays behind under the wrong item. The index is the position again, so it fails the same way. A key taken from the item's own id names each element, and React matches by name: every item keeps its element, and only the new item gets a new one. A key made while rendering, such as a random number, matches nothing, so every element is built again.

We should do this:
{items.map(item => (
<Item key={item.id} item={item} />
follows the item
))}
We should not do this:
{items.map((item, index) => (
<Item key={index} item={item} />
PROBLEMATIC: index tracks position
))}
QUESTION 4

A key inside the card leaves the warning in place

Having learned that repeated items require keys, we inspect the page in Chrome's Elements panel. The repeating element is the <article> tag. We place key={article.id} on the root <article> tag inside ArticleCard.jsx:

ArticleCard.jsx
1export default function ArticleCard({ article }) {
2 return (
3 <article key={article.id} className="card">
Not an array item
4 <h2>{article.title}</h2>

Inside ArticleList.jsx, the map remains written as {articles.map(article => <ArticleCard article={article} />)} We reload the page. All cards render, but the browser Console panel continues logging the exact same warning: Each child in a list should have a unique "key" prop. Check the render method of ArticleList

I put the key in, and the warning is still there. Where does it go?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. The key must be placed on the outermost JSX tag returned directly inside the map() call, not on elements nested inside the child component.

When developers inspect rendered HTML in developer tools, they see <article class="card"> repeating in the DOM tree, leading to the assumption that the <article> tag needs the key. But React reconciles element arrays where they are produced. In ArticleList, articles.map() returns an array of <ArticleCard> React elements. It is this array of child elements that React reconciles, and the console warning explicitly points to ArticleList as the culprit.

Inside ArticleCard, the <article> tag is simply a single root element returned by that component. It does not exist as an item within an array of siblings, so placing a key prop on it does not assist React's list reconciler.

The key belongs directly on the tag generated within the map() expression:

ArticleList.jsx
8 <ArticleCard key={article.id} article={article} />
An array item

Furthermore, React reserves key for internal reconciler identification. React never forwards the key attribute as a standard component prop. If a child component attempts to access props.key, JavaScript returns undefined, and React issues a console warning: key is not a prop. Trying to access it will result in undefined being returned If a child component requires the ID value for its own logic, pass it explicitly under a distinct prop name, such as <ArticleCard key={article.id} articleId={article.id} />

Similarly, hiding a key property inside an object and spreading it with {...props} triggers a compiler warning in modern React: A props object containing a "key" prop is being spread into JSX Always declare key directly and visibly on the JSX tag.

When a list item consists of multiple sibling tags without an enclosing wrapper element, such as a title followed by an author paragraph, wrap them in a keyed Fragment. While the short syntax <>...</> cannot accept attributes, the fully named <Fragment key={article.id}> imported from 'react' provides the required key anchor:

A list of Fragments
1{articles.map(article => (
2 <Fragment key={article.id}>
Fragment takes key
3 <h2>{article.title}</h2>
4 <p>{article.author}</p>
5 </Fragment>
6))}
The array React receives, and the card's own markup
ArticleList returns   [ <ArticleCard />, <ArticleCard />, <ArticleCard /> ]
                        ^ the items of the array: the key goes here
ArticleCard returns   <article> ... </article>
                        ^ one element, not an array item
PRINCIPLE 4

The key's place: naming the element the map gives back

We write the key directly on the tag the map() call gives back, never inside the child component and never inside a spread object, and when the child needs the id, we pass it again as a prop of its own.

React needs the key on the items of the array it receives, and that array holds the elements map() gave back. A key on an element inside the child component sits on the child's own markup, not on an array item, so the warning stays. React also keeps the key for itself: the child receives no key prop, and reading it gives undefined. So the key goes on the tag written inside map(), and a child that needs the id receives it again under another name. An item made of several elements uses <Fragment key={...}>, because <> takes no key.

We should do this:
{items.map(item => (
<Item key={item.id} item={item} />
on the array item
))}
We should not do this:
function Item({ item }) {
return <li key={item.id}>{item.name}</li>;
PROBLEMATIC: warning stays
}

⚡ IN THE WILD

Why does the index work in so many tutorials?

In many online tutorials, you see lists rendered with key={index}, and nothing appears broken. The index fails only when an item is inserted, deleted, or reordered, and only when a DOM element holds uncommitted client-side state, such as text typed into an input or active focus. A fixed navigation menu with five static links never inserts items at the top and holds no user input, so its index keys never exhibit visible bugs. But on an article catalog where breaking news is saved at the top every day, index keys immediately scramble user comments. Lecture 61 returns to key strategies, examining sorting, deletion, and what makes a truly stable key.

Component Summary

App

The root component shows four topic sections with one component, ArticleList, and a different topic each time. It holds no data of its own: adding a topic is one more tag, and adding an article touches no component at all.

ArticleListtopic

The topic section filters the articles of articles.js, maps the rest into list items, and names each item by its id. Its empty case is a message, so a section with no articles still says something to the reader.

ArticleCardarticle

The card shows one article: its title, its author, and a comment box. It never sees its key; React keeps the key, and the card keeps whatever the reader typed, because its element stays with its article.

A developer who comes from plain JavaScript expects a loop that writes the cards, && that hides an empty list, and a key that only quiets the console. In React 19, five articles became five cards from one tag, each topic section showed only its articles and a message when it had none, a new article at the top left every typed comment under its own article, and the key sat on the tag map() gave back. Each step applied one principle: every item became an element, only some items did, each element got its name, and the name sat on the right element.

Where you will meet this

  1. Every list on every site: Comments, search results, shopping cart items, and direct messages; each collection originates from an array, transforms via map(), and binds a key from each item's unique database identifier.
  2. Sections and categorized feeds: Pages that partition content by category or timestamp filter a single source array per category, displaying an empty state message when a partition contains zero items.
  3. Data fetched from servers: REST and GraphQL endpoints return database records containing immutable primary IDs, which map directly to React keys without client-side transformation.
  4. Lists holding active user input: Checkboxes, quantity inputs, and draft text fields; in these components, using index keys or omitting keys causes active user entries to jump to adjacent rows during sorting or deletion.
  5. Console key warnings in development: React's diagnostic key message points directly to the component whose map() call needs the key attribute, indicating exactly which file to inspect.

For the interview

The Interview Question: How do you render a list from an array, and why does React demand a key on every item?

1. The Hidden Signal

Interviewers ask this question to evaluate whether a candidate understands the fundamental connection between JavaScript expressions and React reconciliation. A junior developer views map() as boilerplate loop syntax and assumes keys exist merely to satisfy linter rules. A senior engineer explains that map() is an expression producing an array of React element descriptors, which React evaluates natively. More importantly, they demonstrate how React uses keys during the reconciliation phase to track component identity across renders, differentiating between node reuse, positional shifts, and structural destruction.

2. The Classic Trap

The classic interview trap is answering that "the array index is unique, so key={index} is always safe". The index is unique within a single render, but it reflects array position rather than data identity. When items are prepended, removed, or sorted, the index of every shifted item changes. Because React reconciles nodes by position when index keys are used, client-side input state (such as text typed into input fields, checkboxes, or focus) remains bound to the old DOM node and shifts to the wrong record. Another fatal trap is using key={Math.random()}, which generates a new key on every render, forcing React to destroy and rebuild every DOM node on every update pass.

3. What is Actually Going On

Writing articles.map(article => <ArticleCard key={article.id} article={article} />) provides React with an array of element objects, each stamped with an immutable identifier. When application data updates and triggers a re-render, React compares the new array of descriptors against the previous render tree.

By matching elements by key rather than array index, React recognizes when an existing element has merely changed its position. React moves the physical DOM node to its new slot in the tree, preserving its internal browser state and active input contents. Only genuinely new items trigger DOM node creation.

Without keys, React defaults to index-based reconciliation. When an item is added at index 0, React overwrites the properties of existing DOM nodes in place. The DOM node that held the second article receives the third article's text, while any text typed into its nested input elements lingers visibly on screen.

4. Where It Gets Tricky

Can a child component read its own key prop? No. React strips key during element creation. If a component reads props.key, JavaScript returns undefined and React logs a console warning. When a child needs its identifier, pass the value explicitly under a separate prop name, such as articleId={article.id}.

Where does the key go when a card is wrapped in a list tag? The key must sit on the outermost tag returned directly inside the map() callback. If you wrap <ArticleCard> in an <li>, the key moves to the <li>.

How do you key an item composed of multiple sibling elements without a container tag? Use a keyed Fragment: <Fragment key={article.id}>. The shorthand tag <> cannot receive attributes.

Must keys be globally unique across the whole page? No. Keys must be unique only among immediate sibling elements within the same array. Multiple independent lists may reuse the same IDs without collision.

When is the array index acceptable as a key? The index is safe only when the list is strictly static: it is never filtered, sorted, paginated, prepended, or deleted, and items contain zero internal state or form inputs.

Why does an empty list with length && render a zero? In JavaScript, 0 && <Component /> evaluates to the falsy left operand 0. React renders numbers into the DOM as visible text. Always write length > 0 to produce a clean boolean.

Glossary

  • Rendering a list: Transforming an array of data into an array of React element descriptors, typically via map(), so that React renders one element per item.
  • Arrow function: A concise function syntax (item => <Item item={item} />). An expression directly following the arrow returns automatically; a block body enclosed in curly braces requires an explicit return.
  • map(): A standard JavaScript array method that executes a callback on each item and returns a new array of transformed results of identical length.
  • filter(): A standard JavaScript array method that tests each item against a predicate and returns a new array containing only the items that returned true.
  • Key: A unique string or number attribute assigned to JSX tags returned in a list, used by React's reconciler to match element identity across render passes.
  • Index as key: Using an item's array position as its key. This defaults reconciliation to positional matching, causing form state and focus to attach to the wrong items upon reordering.

Beyond the basics

  • Rendering data from arrays: Complete official guide covering list rendering, filtering, and key rules (see react.dev/learn/rendering-lists).
  • Rendering a list of Fragments: How to group multiple sibling tags per item using keyed Fragments (see react.dev/reference/react/Fragment).
  • Array.prototype.map(): Comprehensive documentation of JavaScript's map method and its callback arguments (see developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Array/map).
  • Arrow function expressions: Deconstruction of arrow function syntax, implicit returns, and block bodies (see developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Functions/Arrow_functions).
  • Preserving and resetting state with keys: Advanced component identity control and subtree state resets using keys (see react.dev/learn/preserving-and-resetting-state).

Summary

Rendering a list: an array of data becomes an array of elements, each with its own key

❒ Mapping: turning every item into an element
  • ALWAYS call map() inside the JSX, and give the element back right after =>, or with return after => {.
  • NEVER use forEach() or a for loop inside the braces; they give back nothing the page can show.
❒ Filtering: turning only some items into elements
  • ALWAYS call filter() before map() when only some items should show.
  • IF the filtered array can be empty THEN test length > 0 and show a message instead.
❒ Keys: naming each element so React can tell the items apart
  • ALWAYS take the key from the item's own id.
  • IF the list never inserts, deletes, or reorders THEN the index is a safe key; otherwise it moves typed text to the wrong item.
  • NEVER make a key while rendering, such as Math.random().
❒ The key's place: naming the element the map gives back
  • ALWAYS write the key on the tag written inside map(), directly, not inside a spread object.
  • IF the child needs the id THEN pass it again as a prop of its own; the child never receives key.

Every item, only some items, one name each, and the name on the right element.

6 <ArticleCard article={article} />
7 </li>
8 ))}
9 </ul>
10) : (
11 <p>No {topic} articles yet.</p>
12);
